### 29 August 2026, 16:48:17 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5502394621

Created by Phase 37 (the eight data protection response letters, item 12927850552). Actionable without that conversation.

The duty. DPA 2018 s.164A(2), read from legislation.gov.uk on 29 August 2026: "A controller must facilitate the making of complaints under this section by taking steps such as providing a complaint form which can be completed electronically and by other means." It was inserted by DUAA 2025 s.103(2) and has been fully in force since 19 June 2026 (S.I. 2026/82 reg. 3(a), with reg. 7). It is not triggered by anyone complaining — it applies whether or not a complaint is ever made. Ledgerstone has taken no step under it: no form, no dedicated address, no page.

Why this item exists. The Phase 35 pack (item 12927908435) records this at its readiness item C1 as "the only readiness item on this board that names a duty already in breach", and its C3 sets out an interim step. C1 and C3 sat in a readiness table with no board item, so nobody owned them. This item is that owner.

What to do — two things, neither of which waits for Q3.

1. A monitored mailbox. A shared, dedicated mailbox — not a personal one, so that monitoring survives absence — reachable by anyone who asks, monitored by the person handling data protection. This is also readiness item R1 in the Retention and Rights-Request Operating Procedure (item 12818099921, Document 2, §5.2) and C2 in the Phase 35 pack, both NOT SET. Both statutory clocks run from when Ledgerstone receives, not from when anyone reads — Art 12A(2)(a) for a rights request, s.164A(3) for a complaint acknowledgement.

2. A printable complaint form. The content is already drafted, field by field, at Phase 35 §4.3 (item 12927908435) — eight fields, ready to drop onto a PDF or a printed sheet. Nothing needs writing. The acknowledgement that follows it is drafted at Phase 35 §4.7, and the outcome letter at Phase 37 §9 (item 12927850552).

Why this is not blocked by Q3 (the brand-name collision). Neither step asserts a trading name, a domain or a logo. The full public page is blocked — it needs a website, which needs a name — and that stays blocked. This is not full compliance and should not be recorded as such. It is a step under s.164A(2) that is available this week, on a duty that has been unmet for over two months.

Owner: Lakhbir, with the DPO. Done when: the mailbox exists and is monitored; the printable form exists and someone can be sent it on request; and both are recorded against Retention Procedure R1 and Phase 35 readiness items C1, C2 and C3.

### 31 August 2026, 08:55:28 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5504875672

Phase 47 sweep, 31 August 2026 — building the ICO breach-report answer sheet (item 12927942615) surfaced that this one cheap action is now the single blocker on FOUR separate duties, not one.

This item is framed as the interim DPA 2018 s.164A(2) step. It is that, and the duty has been live and unmet since 19 June 2026. But the same missing thing — a monitored, shared, dedicated data protection address — is now what stops four different obligations being performable:

1. DPA 2018 s.164A(2) — the duty to take steps to facilitate complaints, "such as providing a complaint form which can be completed electronically and by other means". Live and unmet for over two months.
2. UK GDPR Article 33(3)(b) — a breach notification to the ICO must give a contact point. §4.5 of the new answer sheet has this field marked NOT SET, and it is identified there as the field most likely to stall a submission at 2am on a 72-hour clock that cannot be paused.
3. UK GDPR Article 37(7) — the DPO's contact details must be published and communicated to the Commissioner. There is nothing to publish.
4. Retention and Rights-Request Operating Procedure, readiness item R1 — the primary intake route for every rights request, and the address that goes on the public page required by Item 5 condition C8. C8 is a condition of the lawful basis itself, so this is not only a service gap.

Why the convergence matters rather than being a coincidence. Each of the four documents records the gap in its own words, in its own workstream, as its own blocker. None of them says the other three are waiting on the same thing. A reader of any one of them sees a small administrative blank; the four together are the reason three statutory routes are currently unperformable.

It must be a shared, dedicated mailbox, not a personal one — the Retention Procedure §5.2 gives the reason: monitoring has to survive an absence. A personal address reintroduces the single point of failure that Q23 already flags on the 72-hour clock.

Nothing here is new research and nothing is blocked on Claude. The recommended local part (privacy@) is already in the Retention Procedure; the domain is board item 12927507563 (professional email provisioning, drafted and awaiting a purchase decision). This is the cheapest item on the whole board measured against what it unblocks.

### 8 September 2026, 07:54:14 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5527419503

A fifth duty now waits on this mailbox — Phase 98, 8 September 2026.

Reading the suppliers' published data-processing terms established where a breach notification would actually arrive, and the answer is a problem.

Microsoft notifies "one or more of Customer's administrators", by email. monday.com notifies "Customer" — its DPA does not define which address. Neither is a monitored data-protection address, because there isn't one.

And an unread notification still starts our clock. The breach procedure's own rule at section 3.1 is that awareness is a firm-level fact: if a processor tells us on Friday, we are aware on Friday, whether or not anybody read it until Monday. So the gap is not that we might be told late — it is that we might be told on time and not know, and discover the 72 hours started three days ago.

This mailbox is the single highest-value item in the whole data-protection workstream, and two separate documents written today reach it from opposite directions: the supplier-duties table via where notifications land, and the four-facts record via our near-total inability to become aware of a breach by our own means.

Once it exists there is a follow-on that takes minutes: nominate it as the data-protection contact on the Microsoft and monday.com accounts, so the notification goes somewhere deliberate rather than to whoever happens to administer the tenant.

### 12 September 2026, 18:52:20 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5542871668

Phase 129, 12 September 2026 — ICO registration does not need the company to exist. Status changed from "Blocked - incorporation" to "Ready - Lakhbir action".

What the ICO says. Read on ico.org.uk on 12 September 2026:

* ico.org.uk/for-organisations/data-protection-fee/ — under the Data Protection (Charges and Information) Regulations 2018, organisations that use personal information must pay the fee unless exempt, and the page says in terms that this includes sole traders.
* ico.org.uk/for-organisations/data-protection-fee/register/ — the registration service is for all data controllers, sole traders and companies alike. You need a card, the organisation's name and address, and staff and turnover figures. It takes about 15 minutes.
* ico.org.uk/for-organisations/data-protection-fee/register/new-registration/ — the form starts by asking the organisation type: individual or sole trader, partnership, limited company, LLP, charity, or other bodies such as clubs and societies. A Companies House number is asked for only if you pick limited company. The form also says each data controller organisation must register and pay separately.
* ico.org.uk/for-organisations/data-protection-fee/faqs-data-protection-fee-payment-and-online-registration/ — tier 1 (turnover up to £632,000, or no more than 10 staff) is £52 a year, £5 less by direct debit. A registration that is no longer needed has to be closed with the ICO. Not paying when you should can mean a fine of £400 to £4,000.
So the company is not what is in the way. The real question is who registers. A registration belongs to one legal person, the controller, and cannot be moved to another. Today there is no company, so the only person who could register now is Lakhbir, as a sole trader. When the company is incorporated it is a separate legal person, and it needs its own registration and its own fee.

A worked example. Register now as a sole trader: £52, or £47 by direct debit. If the company is incorporated later, it registers too, for another £52, and the sole-trader registration is closed. That is £104 in the first year. Or wait for the company: £52 once, but no registration at all until the company exists, and incorporation has no date. The name is in doubt as well: CAP REBATE LTD (company 17307313, incorporated 29 June 2026) is already on the Companies House register. One more point: the ICO publishes the organisation name and any trading names on its public register, so do not enter "Caprebate" as a trading name until the name is cleared.

Our recommendation. Take the ICO's two-minute self-assessment (ico.org.uk/fee-checker) in Lakhbir's own name and keep the result. If personal data is already being handled for the business (contacts, test data, anything held on a business device), register as a sole trader now, and register the company again when it exists. If the self-assessment says no fee is due yet, record that, and the date.

Carried over from "Confirm whether the ICO registration was actually applied for", which is now closed and points here. On 1 September Lakhbir said the registration would be applied for that day. Nothing on the board records whether it was: no application, no fee, no registration number, and the subitem "Apply for ICO registration" is still blank. Settle that first, in one line: was it applied for, in whose name, and what is the reference? If it was done in Lakhbir's own name, it covers today, and the company registers separately later. This registration is also how the data protection officer's contact details reach the Commissioner, the second half of Article 37(7).

What waits on whom. Lakhbir: say whether it was applied for. If it was not, take the self-assessment and register in the right name. The wording for every field is already in the attached ICO registration content file. Owner: Lakhbir.

Created 31 August 2026. Both emails are written and attached — copy, paste, send.

We are not allowed to use either commercially without asking — the Valuation Office has said in terms that their data is not covered by the usual free-to-reuse government licence, and it is the only source in our whole system where that is true.

What the Valuation Office email releases: three known errors in our numbers get fixed. The biggest is that we add 18% for site overheads on top of costs that already include them — we are counting it twice on every single job. We also apply a flat 15% for professional fees regardless of job size, and we treat all equipment as if it were new.

An important correction that should not get lost. The 18% double count is our own arithmetic mistake. It should be fixed whatever the Valuation Office replies, and it does not need anyone's permission. Do not let it sit behind a licence answer.

What the Ordnance Survey email releases: automatic site size instead of asking the client, and a map in the client report. This one is a quality improvement, not a correctness fix — if they say no, we carry on as we are. That is the honest difference between the two.

What this relies on: nothing. Neither email depends on anything else being finished. Both are written to be sent by Lakhbir personally on behalf of a business being set up, which is normal and honest — we are not claiming to be a registered company we are not.

Cause and effect on timing: government data teams are slow, so expect a few weeks. The wait starts when we send, not when we decide. That is the whole argument for sending them today. The attached document also sets out what to do on every possible answer, including silence — chase once, then treat it as a no and take the fallback, so an unanswered email cannot sit looking like an open question for six months.

An earlier version of this system was designed to look up public records about a property — the energy certificate, the care regulator entry, the Companies House record — before the client had agreed to anything. Why it still matters even though the design changed

• We need a written view on record, so the same question does not get raised for a fourth time

Some of these records contain named individuals — a care home's registered manager, an energy assessor, a company director. Looking those up without a lawful reason is where the exposure sits. A short written opinion closes it permanently.

### 28 August 2026, 14:58:48 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5500200746

Phase 6 — a pre-solicitor research note is now attached as a second doc on this item, answering Lakhbir's question directly: the two questions were researched as far as published UK law and official guidance allow, and both narrowed. Part A shrank. A personal data breach is defined at Article 4(12) as "a breach of security leading to…" — so processing without a lawful basis is an infringement of Article 6 but is not, on its own, a personal data breach, and the 72-hour Article 33 duty attaches only to a breach. That takes the reporting limb, and the urgency, out of the question as it was framed; what survives is an evidential question (did any lookup ever run — and because Article 4(2) makes a single retrieval "processing", the whole of Part A rests on §A4 of the brief, which Ledgerstone can improve and a solicitor cannot) and a class-by-class lawful-basis question where planning objectors are the sharp end. DPA 2018 s.170 also looks off-point, because it turns on obtaining data without the source controller's consent. Part B closed the other way. Regulation 11(d) MLR 2017 covers "material aid, or assistance or advice … whether provided directly or through a third party" — wording inserted in 2020 that meets the "a regulated professional stands between us and HMRC" position head-on; HMRC's own published test makes a study of a client's particular circumstances producing a recommended course of action advice, not information; and the ATT publishes in terms that capital allowances advice requires AML supervision. HMRC would be the supervisor, registration is a few hundred pounds, and a business in this category may trade while its application is processed. The note states that as Ledgerstone's reading, not a conclusion, and lists what genuinely still needs a solicitor — eight questions, of which the sharpest is that regulation 56(1)'s prohibition does not name tax advisers even though HMRC's guidance calls unregistered trading a criminal offence. It closes with six concrete edits to the brief. No legal conclusion is stated, nothing has been sent, and no solicitor has been instructed.

## SURVEYOR · STEP 1 of 3 — book the free 45-minute call

`12830181616` · 7 comments

### 26 August 2026, 07:16:57 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5492258650

What this is
A single phone call. It is probably the highest-value hour on this entire board, and it is free.

In plain English
Book 45 minutes with a chartered surveyor who does capital allowances work, and ask two questions:

1. Would you sign a valuation based on desktop evidence — photos, floor plans, a video walkthrough — without visiting the property?
2. If yes, what exactly would you need to see?

Why this matters so much
Our entire model assumes the answer to the first question is yes. Site visits are roughly a third of a surveyor's time on a job, so removing them is what makes the numbers work. If a real surveyor says "no, I would always need to attend," then the cost base is very different and several months of planned work would be built on a false assumption.

One free call retires that risk. It should happen before the surveyor CRM, the report templates, or the video capture protocol get built any further.

Original wording: "FREE 45-min sanity-check call with a RICS capital-allowances surveyor BEFORE building the review CRM. Two questions: would you sign on desktop evidence, and what would you need to see. Retires the one risk that could invalidate months of build."

What this is, and what it is not. The free 45-minute call already has its own item (12830181616) and its own agenda. This is the first paid engagement — a different conversation, and it had no board item until now.

• The free call asks: is the desktop-first model viable at all, in the abstract? Would you ever sign on desktop evidence; where would the value bands sit.
• This session asks: here is a finished pack for a specific property — is it good enough that your job becomes checking rather than building?

Sequencing. Run the free call first. If it returns a firm no from two or three independent surveyors, this session should not be booked at all — that is a finding about the cost model, not a run of bad candidates.

Format. Three hours, paid at the surveyor's rate, remote and screen-shared, recorded with written consent. Two Ledgerstone people — one leading, one on the capture sheet. The capture sheet is the deliverable and it cannot be done well while running the conversation. The surveyor must be told in writing beforehand that the case is fictional, nothing is being signed, and no client exists.

The one thing that cannot be re-run. Segment 1 is a blind commitment: the surveyor writes down their own position before seeing any of our views. Once they have seen what we think is wrong, every later opinion is contaminated for calibration purposes — and under the ad-hoc model there is no second uncontaminated meeting with the same person. Send Part A of the walkthrough with sections A.6.1 and A.8 removed, and put no figures or opinions in the covering email.

The number this session exists to produce. Segment 1 questions 1.3 and 1.4 — how long the qualifying-percentage work takes from our pack versus from a blank page. The difference is the only quantified answer to whether any of this preparation is worth doing. Capture both separately; do not accept a ratio.

What this is
A person you need to hire. This one blocks more work than any other appointment on the board.

In plain English
When we split a purchase price between land, building and claimable equipment, that split has to be signed by a chartered surveyor (RICS). Without a named surveyor willing to put their name to it, we have estimates, not a claim. HMRC would not accept our figures on their own.

What is waiting on this person
• The valuation report template — it has to be built with them, not handed to them
• The choice between two valuation methods (a separate item on this board)
• The decision on when a video walkthrough can replace a site visit — which is the single biggest cost saving available to us
• The whole calibration exercise, because their corrections to our estimates are the only real evidence we will ever have that our numbers are right

Suggested first step
There is a separate item on this board for a free 45-minute call with a surveyor. Do that before you commit to hiring anyone — it answers whether the desktop-first model is viable at all.

## Write the process for engaging a one-off tax adviser or surveyor

`12927537258` · 5 comments

### 29 August 2026, 14:05:31 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5502282477

Phase 28 — new item, drafted this phase. The 28 August decisions to use no retained adviser on either side were both sound, and neither had a process written behind it. A retained professional is a relationship you can lean on; an ad-hoc one is a transaction you have to specify. This is that specification, and it is the missing half of both decisions.

The finding that matters most: the two roles stop being symmetrical under ad hoc, and the board has been treating them as a matched pair. The CTA review buys a review of the rules, once. The surveyor buys a valuation of this building, every time. But the hybrid advise-vs-support decision creates a third thing nobody has scoped — a per-case CTA sign-off for clients with no accountant, which is a different product from the one-off rules review, on a different letter, at a different fee, carrying professional risk on a named client's filing position. It has no board item. §2.1 says so plainly and §10 puts it as a question: the first such client cannot be accepted without an answer.

What else is in it. Step-by-step processes for both roles. A recommendation for a small named panel of three to five surveyors on the signed framework letter — none retained, none guaranteed work — because ad hoc does not have to mean starting from nothing every time, and because the incident plan (12927557335) needs someone reachable to classify a defect. A ten-item instruction-pack checklist, of which items 4–8 do not currently exist as attachable artefacts. A section on what "sign-off" means when there is no continuing relationship: a signature is against a version, and does not travel — if the pack changes after signature, re-instruction is the only honest answer, because the adviser may be unreachable. Conflicts and data protection. Cost. And §9, what genuinely breaks under ad hoc, including the one nobody names: half-questions become expensive, so the temptation to guess rather than ask goes up.

Two hard dependencies already on the board. Anchor quarantine (12830183464) is the rule most likely to be broken accidentally under ad hoc, because a hurried covering email is exactly where a client's own estimate leaks. And the five phase9/ straw men are still not attached to their items — the Phase 10 walkthrough states that until they are, a second ad-hoc surveyor cannot pick the work up at all.

What you need to do: answer the five questions in §10 — in particular whether the panel model is what you intend, and who signs the filing position for a client with no accountant. Nothing has been sent and no adviser has been approached.

Phase 146, 22 Sep 2026: the fee-versus-benefit model re-run at the flat 3% fee, company by company. This supersedes the 4 September update below, which was written at 5%.

That update said a company's best year-one relief (4.77% of the allowances) is below our fee, so "there is no pool split at which a company client's fee does not exceed their year-one benefit". At 3% that is no longer true. The engine's own benefit model was run on £100,000 of allowances for every tax position it knows. As a check it was run at 5% first, and it gave back the old figures exactly (4.77%, 3.42%, 3.60%, 7.20% and 8.10%). At 3% the fee is £3,000.

Where the client is now ahead in year one (writing-down allowances only, no first-year allowance):

* A company at 25% or 26.5% on main-pool plant: ahead by £500 to £1,770.
* A higher-rate or additional-rate sole trader or partner on main-pool plant: ahead by £2,600 to £5,640.
* A small-profits company (19%) or basic-rate trader (20%) on main-pool plant, but only in periods before April 2026 (18%): ahead by £420 and £600.
Where the fee is still bigger than year-one relief:

* Special-rate plant, for every client at every tax rate. The fee is bigger by £120 for a Scottish top-rate partner and by £1,860 for a small-profits company. A 3% fee needs a 50% tax rate to be covered at 6%.
* Small-profits companies and basic-rate traders from April 2026, even on pure main-pool plant. 14% × 19% = 2.66% and 14% × 20% = 2.80%, so the fee is bigger by £340 and £200.
* Mixed plant, which is what real buildings have. From April 2026 a company at 25% falls behind once more than 25% of the claim is special-rate, and a company at 26.5% once more than 33.5% is. A claim split like the competitor file (46% main, 54% special) leaves every company behind, by £430 to £1,158.
In all, the fee is bigger than year-one relief in 21 of 44 combinations of tax position and plant, against 34 of 44 at 5%.

Worked example. A dental company paying 25%, with £100,000 of allowances in its year from April 2026: 60% main pool, 40% special-rate. Year-one relief is 25% × (14% × £60,000 + 6% × £40,000) = £2,700. The fee is £3,000, so the company is £300 behind in year one. Over five years it relieves £10,604.55. On the competitor file (£73,740, a 40% taxpayer) the client is now £1,193.16 ahead on headline figures. On that client's real profits the fee is still 2.19 times the year-one cash (3.65 times at 5%).

By sector: the model cannot give a sector answer. Sector changes the result only through the mix of plant and the client's tax position, and neither is captured for any client today, so the system reads "undetermined" (for a 26.5% company, a range of 1.59% to 3.71%).

What this means for your decision. The recommendation (warn, adjust the percentage, do not cap) is not changed by these numbers on their own. But two things it rested on no longer hold. First, the statement that no company is ever ahead is now wrong. Second, a cap would no longer hit every company client. It would hit special-rate-heavy claims, small-profits companies, basic-rate traders from April 2026, and most mixed claims. The choice is still yours, and both switches stay off. The full note, with the table, is written under "Do we cap the fee, warn about it, or adjust the percentage?" in CAPREBATE QUESTIONS. The script that produced these figures is in the Phase 146 working folder and re-runs the shipped engine.

The address lookup is the very first thing a client touches. If it is unreliable or unexpectedly expensive, that is felt at the top of the funnel where it does the most damage.

## DPO to sign that the audit log is tamper-evident, not tamper-proof

`12949297803` · 3 comments

### 1 September 2026, 17:25:40 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5510652403

Built by Phase 61, 1 September 2026. Draft — for the DPO to adopt, not in force.

Why this exists as its own record rather than a line in the developer brief. Lakhbir answered Q53 on 1 September with "DPO will log". That is a real answer and this document does not argue with it — but it is the tamper-EVIDENT option, not the tamper-proof one, and the two are one word apart. A limitation recorded only in a brief handed to a developer is a footnote. A limitation recorded in the governance corpus is a control.

The control is three sentences (§2), and they are the whole substantive answer: the audit log is tamper-evident, not tamper-proof; administrators of the WordPress installation sit inside the trust boundary and are trusted; the log is evidence of what happened, not proof against an administrator who alters it.

Three conditions attach, and one is not met. C-1 requires the administrator set to be enumerated and known — by named person, including everyone with database access by any other route, and the host's own support staff, who are inside that boundary whether or not anyone intended them to be. Nobody has made that list, and the account is understood to be shared with several unrelated businesses. Until the list exists, "administrators are trusted" names nobody, and a trust boundary drawn around an unknown set is not a trust boundary.

Six things this does NOT mean (§5), stated as refusals because that is the half most likely to be misread. Above all: it is not permission to build a thinner log, or to skip the AuditSink port. The port exists so that funding an external sink later is an adapter and not a retrofit — building without it forecloses the better answer.

The hash chain has the same exposure and is covered by the same determination. verifyChain detects inconsistent edits; it does not detect a consistent rewrite of the whole chain, because its head is not anchored anywhere WordPress cannot reach.

How it sits with the DPIA. This is the measure DPIA v2.0 risk R9 already names — R9's own measures column says the Medium rating "is contingent on the administrator set being small and known. It is not currently known." The two documents agree, including about the gap. If C-1 is not closed before go-live, R9 is not a Medium and the DPIA should say so.

Cross-referenced from Developer Brief v3.3 §3.0.4, §11 Auditability and §12 item 18. Cannot be adopted before the DPO instrument (12927221812) is executed — same nine-step chain, step 4.

## DPO to approve the document-pipeline impact assessment

`12910861459` · 6 comments

### 27 August 2026, 12:51:54 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5496496775

What this is
A data protection impact assessment for the pipeline that reads client-uploaded documents. It has never existed, and two pieces of work are stuck behind that fact.

In plain English
Two of the four new document types we want to extract from — replies to standard pre-contract enquiries (CPSE), and the sale contract itself — cannot be built yet. Both name the parties to a transaction, and knowing who sold a property to whom is exactly the fact the tax rules need. Our document pipeline currently refuses to send anything resembling a person's name to the extraction model, which is the right instinct, but it means the one fact these two document types exist to supply is the one thing the pipeline currently cannot read.

Why this sat unresolved
The pipeline's own build notes flagged the need for this assessment when it shipped — which model is used, where it is hosted, how long it keeps data, and whether it trains on what we send it. Nobody wrote it down anywhere on the board. Searching the whole board for a DPIA before this item returned nothing.

The part that makes this bigger than two blocked document types
The same unanswered question — which model, hosted where, on what terms — applies equally to the seven document types already built and shipped. This assessment is not only new-work gating; it is the record that should have existed before any of the seven went out, and did not.

What it does and does not decide
It writes down what the pipeline processes, whose personal data is at stake, the risks and the controls already built against them. It does not decide whether to relax the parties rule for CPSE replies and the sale contract — that is a DPO judgement, offered here as an option with its cost, not a recommendation. It also does not decide the model question itself; that needs an actual answer from whoever holds the API account, which this document cannot supply on its own.

Original wording: "the DPIA for the pipeline — which model, hosted where, what retention, what training-use position, which the pipeline records as materially affecting whether even the permitted segments may be sent" (item 12902240772 §7).

## 🔒 Breach register — where it lives and who may write to it

`12946269151` · 2 comments

### 1 September 2026, 13:57:57 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5509608851

-----------------------------------------------------------------
The Art 33(5) breach register now lives on monday.com. Built 1 September 2026, Phase 56.
-----------------------------------------------------------------

Q21 asked where the register physically lives and who can write to it. Lakhbir answered: Monday.com. That answer is right — the register was otherwise sitting in the OneDrive tree, where BCP scenario E1 (ransomware) encrypts it along with the data it exists to be evidence about, and Monday is separately hosted and already paid for. But a location is not a control, so this is what was actually built.

1. Where it is
--------------

* The register: private board 18429145787 — "🔒 Personal Data Breach Register — Art 33(5) [RESTRICTED]". One item per incident, incident_ref (PDB-nnn) as the item name, 30 columns taken from sections 2.2 and 2.3 of the register document (board item 12927581028). It is empty, and that is a statement about this business, not an omission.

* The annex: a second, separate private board 18429145822 — "🔒 Breach Register Annex — affected individuals [RESTRICTED, NAMES]". This is the only place a name of an affected individual is recorded. The register carries annex_ref and nothing more. That separation is in the existing design (2.6, Trap 2) and it survived the move deliberately: a register that is easy to read is not an argument for putting names in it.

2. How the write restriction is enforced — mechanism, not intention
-----------------------------------------------------------------

Three platform settings, all set by API on 1 September 2026 and all read back afterwards:

* board_kind: private on both boards. A private board cannot be found, opened or edited by anyone who is not a subscriber. It does not appear in the workspace to other users. This is what removes the 6 subscribers of the Health Capital board — a shared board with permissions: everyone — from having any access at all.

* permissions: owners on both boards, set with set_board_permission(basic_role_name: viewer), which returned edit_permissions: "owners". Only a board owner can write. Anyone later added as a plain subscriber gets read access and no more, unless a board owner explicitly promotes them with update_users_board_role.

* Subscribers and owners: Lakhbir Dhillon only, on both boards, verified by read-back.

Why the register is not an item on this board. The phase brief said "restricted board item (group 08)". monday.com has no per-item permission: an item on the Health Capital board is readable and writable by everyone who can see that board, and that board is board_kind: share with permissions: everyone and six subscribers. The only place a write restriction can actually be enforced is at board level. So the register is a restricted board, and this item in group 08 is the pointer to it — which is what makes the restriction real rather than declared. §2.7(2) of the register document requires access to be limited to the DPO and the controller; on the Health Capital board that requirement could not have been met.

3. THE FINDING THAT MATTERS MOST: the DPO has no monday.com account
-----------------------------------------------------------------

Saddique is not a user of this monday.com account. All 198 users on account 1740732 were enumerated on 1 September 2026 and there is no Saddique. Every decision field in Table B — art33_decision, art33_reasoning, art34_decision, art34_reasoning, decided_by, decided_at — is the DPO's to complete, and the DPO cannot currently open the board they are supposed to write to.

This is not fixed by moving the register somewhere else; it follows the register wherever it goes. Two consequences, both Lakhbir's:

* Inviting Saddique costs a seat and is an admin action — it was not done here, because adding a person to a restricted register is the controller's decision and not Claude's. Until it is done, a real breach would be worked by Lakhbir writing down what the DPO said, which is a different record from the DPO's own.

* decided_by, countersigned_by and closed_by are TEXT columns, not people columns, precisely for this reason. A people column could not hold the name of the person who actually makes the decision. This is deliberate and should not be "tidied up" later.

Note this compounds the existing position that the DPO instrument (12927221812) is drafted and not executed, and that on 1 September the appointment moved behind incorporation.

4. The residual risk, recorded rather than glossed
--------------------------------------------------

Monday removes the ransomware risk and introduces a smaller one that is not zero. This board lives on the same monday.com account, so a compromise of that account takes the register with it — and takes the annex too, because "held separately" on Monday means separated by access, not by hosting. Both boards are in the same tenant, reached by the same credentials, and administered by the same account admins.

Two things follow that are worth stating plainly:

* Account admins were not enumerated. The API version in use has no is_admin field on User, so who can administratively reach a private board on this account is not verified and is recorded as unknown rather than assumed to be nobody. This account is shared with several unrelated businesses.

* The trade is still clearly worth making. E1 is the most likely incident this business will have and it destroys an OneDrive-hosted register by design. Account compromise is less likely, and unlike ransomware it does not silently destroy the evidence of its own occurrence. But the register document now says this rather than presenting Monday as unconditionally safe.

The mitigation that is NOT built: nothing takes an off-platform copy of these two boards. If the answer to "what if the Monday account is lost" is a periodic export, that is a decision and a task, and it does not exist yet.

5. What is still open
---------------------

* Q21 is answered and now closed by this build — readiness item B3 in the register document moves from "NOT DECIDED" to "DONE".

* Q22 / RET-5 — derived at six years from closed_at on 1 September (Phase 55), still not set by the DPO. The annex is expressly NOT covered by RET-5.

* Q23 — who decides when the DPO is unreachable — untouched and still open. It is now sharper: the DPO cannot reach the register at all.

* B1 — the procedure itself is still not approved.

* A UI convenience not built: two saved views ("A — THE FACTS", "B — THE DECISIONS") would reproduce the document's two-table presentation. The register works without them.

6. Two departures from the document, both deliberate and both recorded
-----------------------------------------------------------------

* clock_start is not a column. The document restates awareness_at as clock_start in Table B so the deadline sits next to the decision it governs. On one item both are already on the same row, so the restatement has no function — and duplicating the single field the whole 72-hour clock depends on creates two values that must be equal and can diverge. awareness_at serves both.

* awareness_at is split into two columns — a date, and awareness_basis for the prose the document requires in that field ("where the two differ, the reason is stated in this field"). A date column cannot hold prose. This is one document field represented as two Monday columns, not a new field.

And one defect found in the document while reading it: §2.6 requires each entry to reference the annex by annex_ref, but annex_ref does not appear in the §2.2 column table. It is built here, and the register document has been corrected.

Built by Claude, Phase 56, 1 September 2026. Nothing here is approved. The register is empty because no breach has occurred.

WRITTEN 8 September 2026, Phase 98. Attached as "Caprebate-Four-Facts-a-Breach-Decision-Turns-On-v1.md".

The four facts were already specified on this item. The half that was missing — and the half this document is actually about — is how we would establish each one inside 72 hours with the people and systems that exist today.

The finding: three of the four cannot be answered inside 72 hours today, and two of them cannot be answered at all after the event.

Device encryption — there is no device-management record and no attestation. After a laptop is gone there is nothing to inspect and nothing recorded its state beforehand. Unanswerable after the event, which is the only time it is asked. Backup restore — never tested; a first-ever restore of an unknown backup during an active incident is not a plan. Publication channel — decided (the website), unbuilt, so today there is no channel and a 34(3)(c) case could not be performed. Identity standard — this one is answerable in minutes, and the answer is weak: the proportionate rule is to match what we already hold, and for an E1 record that is a name plus birth month and year, all of it on a public register and quotable back by anyone. Matching held data authenticates nobody.

And the prior problem, which the procedure already states and this document does not soften: the realistic route to awareness is that somebody tells Lakhbir directly. A 72-hour clock that starts on awareness is a light obligation for a controller that cannot become aware — that is the gap, not the comfort.

Six actions would change these answers, and none of them is a project. Two of them stop being possible later: evidencing device encryption must happen before a device is lost, and the monitored mailbox is the difference between a clock that starts and one that never starts. Both have been added as updates to the existing items that own them rather than duplicated here.

THE KNOWN LIMITATION IS RESTATED, NOT DESIGNED AROUND. The breach procedure allocates "assess and decide" to the DPO and "countersign the decision to report or not to report" to Lakhbir as controller — a two-person control. Lakhbir is also the DPO's deputy, so on the deputy route those two rows are the same person. A two-person control performed by one person is not a control; it is a record of who decided. The mitigation is not a workaround: the deputy route is used only when the DPO is genuinely unreachable, its use is recorded with the reason, and the decision is reviewed when they return. A second weakness travels with it — the DPO instrument is still unsigned, so the authority behind that table is thinner than the table looks.

## Write the list of who we pass client data on to

`12927931400` · 7 comments

### 29 August 2026, 17:26:37 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5502412704

<p><b>Why this exists.</b> UK GDPR Article 19 requires the controller to communicate any rectification (Art 16), erasure (Art 17(1)) or restriction (Art 18) <b>to each recipient to whom the personal data have been disclosed</b>, unless that proves impossible or involves disproportionate effort. <b>That duty is unperformable by a controller which has not written down who its recipients are</b>, and no document anywhere on this board records the list.</p>

<p>Phase 37 found the same gap from the other direction — Article 15(1)(c) requires an access response to name the recipients, and its placeholder <b>P9</b> says "NOT ESTABLISHED. Do not write 'none' without checking" — but <b>no board item owned it</b>, so it sat in a placeholder table belonging to nobody. This item owns it. The same list also answers <b>Article 14(1)(e)</b> in the Phase 39 Article 14 direct notice.</p>

<p><b>One thing that does NOT gate this, and is often assumed to.</b> Item 5's question Q9 asks whether an external surveyor is a processor or an independent controller. <b>Article 4(9) defines a "recipient" as anyone to whom personal data are disclosed, whether a third party or not</b> — so a surveyor is a recipient either way. Q9 decides whether they owe <i>Ledgerstone</i> an Article 33(2) breach notification. It does not decide whether Ledgerstone owes <i>them</i> an Article 19 communication. <b>Do not wait for Q9.</b></p>

<p><b>What to do.</b> Produce a short table — recipient, what categories of personal data reach them, on what occasion, and by what route — covering at least:</p>
<ul>
<li>An external surveyor (none appointed yet — record the intended position)</li>
<li>A CTA, on a review or sign-off</li>
<li>A client's own accountant</li>
<li>HM Revenue and Customs, where a claim has been filed</li>
<li>The extraction model provider, once one exists (currently unidentified — pipeline DPIA risk R5)</li>
<li>Any address-lookup or data supplier</li>
<li>Storage and workflow processors — OneDrive/M365, Monday.com</li>
</ul>

<p><b>Two rules for filling it in.</b> (1) A recipient that has never actually been sent anything is not owed an Article 19 communication — say "none disclosed to date" rather than leaving a blank. (2) <b>HMRC is the awkward one:</b> a name in a filed return cannot be erased, so record what a communication to them would realistically ask for. §6.6 of the Phase 39 pack deals with this.</p>

<p><b>Where the answer goes.</b> Post it as an update here. It closes placeholder P14 in the Phase 39 pack (12927894775) and P9 in the Phase 37 letter pack (12927850552), and it is review trigger 11 of the Phase 39 pack.</p>

<p><i>Created by Claude, Phase 39, 29 August 2026. Owner type: Lakhbir, with the DPO.</i></p>

The 30 August reading was right: this was assembly, not discovery. The components were in four documents nobody in the data-protection workstream opens — Governance Part C section C10, Part D sections D4 and D5, Part B section B5, and the Developer Brief. The honest previous position was not "there is no list" but "there are four partial lists, none of them called a recipients list, and none written for Article 19".

What the document contains: five recipients we disclose to (surveyor, tax adviser, the client's own accountant, HMRC — and the registers, listed only to say they receive nothing); seven processors who hold the data and are recipients too under Article 4(9); and, for each, whether anything has actually been disclosed to date.

Today the honest Article 15(1)(c) answer to any client is that no personal data of theirs has reached any recipient, because none of those relationships is live. That is true, and it stops being true on the first engagement.

TWO FINDINGS THAT NEED A DECISION, and they are the real content.

1. The engagement letter does not permit this list. Clause 7 promises data goes only to the surveyor and tax adviser. The client's own accountant — a core part of the business model, and named in the published privacy notice — is not permitted by it. And read literally the clause is breached the moment a client file is saved to OneDrive, because it admits no processors at all. The two documents contradict each other and the client signs one of them. Raised as its own item, "Clause 7 of the engagement letter forbids what the privacy notice promises".

2. The privacy notice lists sources as recipients. Its "Who We Share Data With" section names HM Land Registry, Companies House and sector regulators. We read from those; they receive nothing. The same section names no processor at all, while three of them hold client personal data today. This is exactly the source-versus-recipient merge the 30 August note predicted a first pass would make — it had already been made, in the published document.

What this document cannot do. Nothing records, per data subject, which recipients actually received their data. Article 19 is owed to "each recipient to whom the personal data have been disclosed" — a per-record fact, not a per-firm one, and a static list of categories does not discharge it. Something must log the disclosure when it happens. That capability does not exist and lands on the same systems decision as the Rules-Defect plan's "which clients are affected?" gap.

Q9 — whether a surveyor is a processor or an independent controller — was checked and does not gate this: Article 4(9) makes them a recipient either way.

Two of these have a deadline that is not a date — Phase 98, 8 September 2026.

The four-facts breach record (attached to "Record the four facts a breach decision turns on") found that two items inside this one stop being possible later, and are cheap now.

1. Evidence device encryption NOW, while the devices are in front of you. Article 34(3)(a) removes the duty to tell individuals about a breach only where protection measures were implemented and applied to the data affected — both limbs. After a laptop is lost there is nothing to inspect, and "it was a work laptop" is an assumption, not evidence. What is needed is small: a dated note of each device, its encryption state, and how it was checked. It cannot be produced retrospectively, which is the only time it is ever wanted.

2. Run one restore test and record the date and outcome. The continuity plan records that no restore has ever been tested. Article 34(3)(b) — the high risk is no longer likely to materialise — is reachable in a ransomware case only if restoration is verified. A first-ever restore test of an unknown backup, during an active incident, inside 72 hours, is not a plan.

3. And while you are in there: switch on and find out what audit logging OneDrive and monday.com already provide. It costs nothing and it is currently the only thing that could tell us what happened after the event.

None of the three is a project. All three change a breach answer from "we could not say" to "here is the evidence".

### 14 September 2026, 07:23:53 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5543995948

Phase 131, 14 September 2026 — what audit logging OneDrive and monday.com already provide
-----------------------------------------------------------------

What was open. The 8 September note on this task asked, as its third point, to "switch on and find out what audit logging OneDrive and monday.com already provide". Nobody had found out. The Cyber Essentials readiness pack now has Appendix C, researched on 13 September 2026 from Microsoft Learn, monday.com's developer documentation and read-only queries of our monday.com account. Nothing has been switched on; the two admin consoles need a person to sign in.

OneDrive (the Aqlios LTD Microsoft 365 organisation):

* The standard audit log comes with every Microsoft 365 Business plan and with E1, E3 and Microsoft 365 E3. It keeps records for 180 days. The premium audit log needs E5 or an add-on, and keeps OneDrive records for a year (ten years with a further add-on).

* Microsoft says auditing is not switched on by default on Business Basic, Standard or Premium. Which plan the Aqlios organisation has is not recorded anywhere, so it needs looking up, and auditing should be assumed off until checked.

* File access is logged: opening a file (repeat opens by the same person within five minutes are not re-logged), previews, downloads, edits, deletions and recycle-bin deletions. Sharing, anyone-links and company links being created, and an anyone-link being used, are logged too.

* Appendix C gives the exact check (one PowerShell command, or the banner on the Audit page in Microsoft Purview), the role needed, and how to switch it on. Nothing before the switch is recovered, so record the date it was confirmed.

monday.com: our account is on the Pro plan. The audit log — sign-ins, IP address, user and event — is Enterprise only, and a test query from this account was refused. What Pro has is each board's activity log, which records changes to boards, not who signed in or downloaded a file. So on Pro, nobody can see who opened the breach register boards. monday.com's support articles returned 403, and two commonly quoted points (downloads and exports being logged, and records never expiring) are marked unverified.

## ⏰ VAT check, monthly — register when turnover crosses the threshold

`12950693863` · 3 comments

### 1 September 2026, 19:03:08 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5511143994

Why this item exists
--------------------

On 1 September 2026 Lakhbir answered the VAT question: "no, not yet as we are not earning enough to be VAT registered. When we earn enough then we will apply." That is the right answer — the company is not yet incorporated, so there is nothing to register.

But an answer of "later" with no trigger is how this gets missed. The board previously carried the VAT subtask at "Working on it" — the only task in that state — which asserted work that had never started. That is corrected (subitem 12552667534, now cleared). This item is the other half: the thing that makes "later" resurface.

The two tests that force registration
-------------------------------------

1. The historic test. Taxable turnover over the VAT registration threshold in any rolling 12-month period — not a tax year, not an accounting period, a rolling window checked every month.

2. The future test, and it is the one that will catch this business. If taxable turnover is expected to exceed the threshold in the next 30 days alone, registration is required immediately — the historic 12 months are irrelevant.

Confirm the current threshold on gov.uk before acting. It has been £90,000 since 1 April 2024 and figures in this note must not be relied on as current without checking.

Why the future test is the live risk here, specifically
-------------------------------------------------------

The fee is a percentage of tax saved on capital-allowances claims. That is a standard-rated supply of services, and the amounts are large and lumpy — a single successful claim can invoice more in one month than the whole preceding year. A business with modest rolling turnover can therefore be required to register with almost no notice, on the strength of one signed engagement. Check this at the point an engagement is signed, not only at month end.

The check, monthly
------------------

* Add up invoiced fees for the last 12 months. Compare to the threshold.
* Look at engagements signed but not yet invoiced. Would any single coming month, on its own, exceed the threshold?

* If either is close, register. Late registration carries a penalty and HMRC charges the VAT that should have been collected — which comes out of the fee, because the client's invoice has already gone out without it.

One thing worth deciding before the threshold forces it, not after: many of the clients are healthcare businesses making exempt supplies, so they may not be able to reclaim VAT charged to them. Registration therefore makes the fee effectively more expensive to a part of the client base. That is a pricing conversation, and it is better had in advance than in the month registration becomes compulsory.

Linked: subitem 12552667534 under HMRC tax registration (12552682452). Not blocked by incorporation — but nothing can be registered until the company exists (12552682418).

### 14 September 2026, 07:16:17 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5543985124

Phase 131, 14 September 2026 — what VAT registration does to our fee for a client who cannot recover VAT
-----------------------------------------------------------------

What was missing. This task's opening note of 1 September said that registering would make the fee "effectively more expensive" to healthcare clients who make exempt supplies, and that this is a pricing conversation to have in advance. Nobody had worked the numbers. That note also described the fee as a percentage of tax saved. The fee was decided on 3 September as 5% of the capital allowances identified, and the new note uses that basis.

What is attached: Caprebate VAT Registration and Exempt Healthcare Clients v1, a short note. Every rule in it was read on GOV.UK on 13 September 2026: the VAT rates page, "Register for VAT: when to register", the VAT thresholds page, and VAT Notices 701/57 (health professionals), 701/2 (welfare and care homes) and 706 (partial exemption).

* The threshold is confirmed: register when taxable turnover for the last 12 months goes over £90,000, or when it is expected to go over £90,000 in the next 30 days alone. Deregistration is optional below £88,000. On our fee basis, £90,000 of fees is £1.8 million of allowances identified.

* A worked example. £400,000 of allowances identified gives a fee of £20,000, plus £4,000 VAT, so an invoice of £24,000. A client that can recover VAT pays £20,000 in real terms, which is 5%. A dental practice doing clinical work only, a GP surgery or a care home generally cannot recover it, and pays £24,000 — 6% of the allowances. A partly exempt practice whose taxable work is 15% of its supplies gets back about £600 and pays about £23,400.

* The fee-versus-benefit comparison in the questions document is re-run at 6% for a client who cannot recover VAT. A limited company at the marginal rate gets about £19,080 back in year one on £400,000. The fee is £920 more than that without VAT, and £4,920 more with VAT it cannot recover. VAT moves no client from "fee smaller" to "fee bigger". It widens the gap for the three kinds of client already behind in year one, and narrows the margin for the two ahead.

* One recommendation, about disclosure only: once we are registered, any fee-versus-benefit figure shown to a client who cannot recover VAT should use the VAT-inclusive fee. Whether to cap, warn or adjust the fee is already an open question for Lakhbir, and the note does not pre-empt it.

* Left open for advisers: how a partly exempt client treats VAT on our fee, and whether a client can deduct our fee and any VAT it cannot recover in its own tax.

Nothing has been registered and no client asked anything. Status unchanged: Parked - deliberate, owner Lakhbir.

* After a surveyor is instructed, £995 leaves us £1,035 (dental) to £3,455 (private hospital) down.

* Recommendation: £995 per property, plus the surveyor's charges we are liable for under the instruction, at cost.

* Nil abort fee. On a £500,000 dental job, a nil abort after the survey absorbs £2,030. That is the profit on one completed job at 100 jobs a year, and on 8.6 completed jobs at 25 jobs a year.

* Fixed fee. The engine can only charge 5% of allowances, so the recommendation is to take the fixed-fee option out of clause 4.

Found by Phase 94, 6 September 2026, on reading the letter rather than on a report of it.

The engagement letter was written on 4 September 2026 and has thirteen clauses. None of them is a clawback. Clause 4 fixes the fee at 5% of the capital allowances identified and never revisits it if that figure is later reduced on enquiry. Clause 5 runs the other way, charging the client a break fee if they walk away. Clause 10 caps our liability at the fees paid, which reaches the same money only if the client sues us and proves a claim — it is not an automatic credit and no client would experience it as one.

Two live documents specify the mechanism and neither is an instrument. The business plan, under the risk headed "a claim collapses on enquiry after we have been paid", recommends "a clawback mechanism in the engagement letter, proportionate and computable: fee is a stated share of a stated figure, so a reduction produces a proportionate credit anyone can calculate". The rules-defect incident and client correction plan goes further and states it as a rule rather than an intention — "the fee follows the corrected figure, always. Where a fee has been invoiced or paid on an over-stated claim, the difference is credited or refunded. This is not discretionary and is not a goodwill gesture." That document also identifies why it matters: a correction reduces our own fee, so the firm has a direct financial interest in not finding the defect, and the credit rule is the control that removes the interest.

Why the shape is easy and the number is not. Because the fee is a stated percentage of a stated figure, the credit computes itself — if the allowances fall from £73,740 to £50,000, 5% falls from £3,687 to £2,500 and £1,187 is owed back. What is not obvious is the trigger and the boundary: does it fire on any reduction or only a material one, does it survive an HMRC settlement the client chose to accept, and is it time-limited. Those are commercial decisions and they are now a question for Lakhbir in CAPREBATE QUESTIONS, titled "If a claim is reduced after we have been paid, do we give the money back?"

What Claude can do without waiting. Draft the clause with the trigger in square brackets, exactly as clauses 4 and 5 already carry bracketed commercial terms, so the letter is complete in shape and only a number is outstanding. No client has signed anything, so this is a redraft rather than a renegotiation.

The letter itself is on the item "The client engagement letter — written, unreviewed, and on no register", which is with the solicitor.

## Clause 7 of the engagement letter forbids what the privacy notice promises — and neither of them mentions a processor

`12993832839` · 3 comments

### 8 September 2026, 07:54:14 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5527419495

Found by Phase 98, 8 September 2026, while assembling the recipients list. Both documents are live: one is signed by clients, the other is published.

Engagement Letter clause 7 says, in terms: "Data will be shared only with the surveyor and tax adviser engaged in connection with the Client's claim, and will not be disclosed to any other third party without the Client's consent, save where required by law."

Three problems, and the second is the serious one.

1. The client's own accountant is not permitted by clause 7. The accountant referral channel is a core part of the business model, and the privacy notice names the accountant explicitly as someone we share with. Clause 7 permits the surveyor and the tax adviser and nobody else absent consent. The two documents contradict each other and the client signs one of them.

2. Read literally, clause 7 is breached the moment a client file is saved. Storing a document in OneDrive, or a client name on this board, is a disclosure to a processor. "Only with the surveyor and tax adviser" admits no processors at all — and Microsoft, monday.com and IONOS hold client personal data today.

3. HMRC is covered only by "save where required by law", which is a strained fit for a claim the client chooses to make.

And the privacy notice has its own defect. Section 4, "Who We Share Data With", lists "public registers such as HM Land Registry, Companies House and relevant sector regulators". We do not share data with those registers — we read data from them. They are the largest sources in the system and they receive nothing. A data subject reading that section is told their data goes somewhere it does not go. The same section names no processor at all.

Recommendation. Amend clause 7 rather than narrowing the business to fit it. A clause permitting (a) the surveyor and tax adviser engaged on the claim, (b) the client's own accountant where the client has introduced or nominated them, (c) HMRC in connection with a claim, and (d) processors acting on our instruction under Article 28 terms, would describe what actually happens. Then rewrite privacy notice section 4 from sections 1 and 2 of the recipients document: recipients in one list, processors in a second, registers moved to wherever the notice describes where data comes from.

Do not publish a recipients list that the signed letter forbids. The full analysis is the attachment on "Write the list of who we pass client data on to".

### 26 August 2026, 07:16:04 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5492257522

What this is
An open decision. Only you can make it. It is one of the two most valuable unanswered questions on this board.

In plain English
We have agreed we charge 5%. What we have not agreed is 5% of what. There are two very different answers:

• 5% of the cash the client gets in year one. Smaller fee, easy for the client to understand, and they pay it out of money they have actually received.
• 5% of the total tax relief over the life of the claim. Much bigger fee, but the client is paying today for a benefit that arrives over ten or more years — which is harder to sell and harder to defend if challenged.

The gap between these two is large. On a typical care home the first might be £5,000 and the second £13,000 for identical work.

Why it is urgent
Every client-facing document we write has to state the fee basis. Until this is settled, the engagement letter, the client report and the website pricing page all stay unfinished.

Also unresolved: whether there is a minimum fee. That is tracked separately on this board.

Claude can help by writing an options paper setting out both bases with worked examples at three job sizes, and the advertising-standards risk of each. Say the word and it goes in the plan.

Original wording: "D3 — DECIDE: fee basis. 5% agreed in principle. STILL OPEN: 5% of year-one cash or lifetime relief? And what minimum fee?"

### 26 August 2026, 08:52:02 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5492435051

Options paper drafted. Your decision — item ownership and status left untouched.

Doc: Options paper — the fee basis: 5% of year-one cash, or 5% of lifetime relief?

Recommendation: 5% of lifetime relief. Year-one cash is not just smaller, it is unusable, for three independent reasons — any one of them decides it.

1. There is barely any year-one cash on the route that will be most of our work. On a second-hand purchase the claim comes in via current-period pooling, and AIA and first-year allowances are not available on that route (Module A §4, from s.51A/s.52/s.58 read directly; CTA confirmation pending as A-Q1). Year one is a writing-down allowance on the pool and nothing else. 5% of that is £135–£405 on the dental job and £608–£1,823 on the care home — against costs of £2,630 and £5,290. Every worked example loses money at every job size and every pool split. Best case on the biggest job is a £3,467 loss.

2. The base cannot be computed. Year-one relief depends on the main-rate/special-rate pool split, and our own pool model refuses to assert a default because guessing would move money between a 14% pool and a 6% pool on no evidence. We would be invoicing on a number we have told ourselves we cannot calculate, and could not calculate it until after the survey — i.e. after most of the cost is spent.

3. The base swings 52x on a route the client did not choose. A £500k dental fit-out yields a £7,000 fee; a £500k dental purchase yields £135. Same sector, same money, comparable work. Worse, it is backwards — the purchase job is the harder one (entitlement chain, pooling position, historic elections, s.185 cap) and Option A pays least for it.

One correction to the item's framing. The note here estimates year-one cash on a care home at ~£100k giving a £5,000 fee. On a purchase it is £12,150–£36,450, giving £608–£1,823. The £100k figure is what you get if a large first-year deduction is available, and on the purchase route it is not. The real gap is roughly £1,000 vs £10,000, not £5,000 vs £13,000. Your £2.2k dental figure, though, reconciles exactly — £2,250 at 5% of lifetime relief for a 40% payer.

Three conditions on the recommendation: never state 5% without the base (that is the CAP exposure, and it is common to both options); trigger payment on delivery of the report, not receipt of benefit; and cap the first invoice against year-one relief. Without a cap the fee consumes 28%–83% of the client's first-year cash, and we cannot tell them which end until after they have signed.

Two things flagged, not decided:
• Your 18 Aug note records 5% as a placeholder with higher rates for larger or more manual jobs. The base and the rate are separable — settling one does not settle the other, and nothing in the paper assumes 5% is fixed.
• This does not fix small jobs. A £500k dental purchase still loses £380 at 5% of lifetime relief. Break-even prices: dental ~£584k, GP ~£860k, care home ~£1.41m — the care home threshold is highest despite the best band, because corporation tax is lower than income tax and its costs are higher. So a single minimum price would be wrong for two of three sectors. Those figures feed the minimum-fee paper on 12830205390; the two decisions want taking together.

Weakest input, and I want to flag it plainly: the surveyor and CTA costs are my estimates, not quotes. They drive every break-even figure. The model is saved and can be re-run the moment you have real numbers. Section 12 lists what would change the recommendation — only one thing genuinely would.

Status and owner unchanged. "Claimed by (machine)" cleared.

What is now true on the board, and what is true on disk
-------------------------------------------------------

The four subitems — complaints policy, privacy policy, terms & conditions, consent policy — read Done. The documents themselves are unchanged and still say "DRAFT — NOT APPROVED" in their own headers. Nothing was approved on 1 September; no signature was added; no policy was published.

So the board and the documents now disagree, and the disagreement is deliberate. If they are ever read side by side, the documents are the accurate record and this item is the decision to present them as complete.

The two things that follow, and they are the reason this is written down
-----------------------------------------------------------------

1. Nothing downstream should now be read as approved because this item is Done. Developer Brief v3.3 §12 item 19 already states the general rule — do not treat board-Done as DPO-approved on any data protection document — and it applies here with full force. Thirteen data protection documents are in the same position and none of them has been signed.

2. Pilot Plan condition C8 is unaffected. It records the privacy notice as NOT MET because there is no published privacy notice, and moving a subitem to Done does not publish one. C8 remains unmet. The gap that Q16 was asking about — approved and published have not happened — is still there; what changed is how the board describes it.

The honest one-line summary: this closes the gap by asserting completion rather than by approving them. Approving them is still available at any time and is still cheap — it needs a signature, not more drafting.

## Caprebate G5 — write lawful basis / legitimate interests assessment for register lookups (third-party personal data in EPC, CQC, Companies House)

`12818099921` · 10 comments

### 26 August 2026, 14:32:22 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5493333919

Lawful basis / legitimate interests assessment delivered: Item 5 — Lawful Basis and Legitimate Interests Assessment: public register lookups

Conclusion: Article 6(1)(f) IS available for the two retention exceptions (Companies House PSC, HMLR individual proprietor) and for the transient handling of professional names in EPC/care-regulator records — subject to 11 stated conditions. It is NOT available, and is not claimed, for planning applicants, agents, objectors and neighbours; that data must stay out of the system entirely.

Three findings that change how this must be written up:
1. The law moved. The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 restructured the provisions this rests on. Article 14(5)(b) — the familiar "disproportionate effort" exemption — is now OMITTED from the UK text; it sits at Article 14(5)(e), and new Article 14(7) turns it into an active duty to make the information publicly available. Any template-based LIA or privacy notice written against the old numbering will be wrong.
2. The new Article 6(1)(ea) "recognised legitimate interests" shortcut does not apply. Annex 1 covers crime, safeguarding, emergencies, national security and public-task disclosures. A commercial property lookup is none of them, so the full three-part test is mandatory.
3. The transparency obligation is currently UNMET. The lawful basis reasoning is sound but condition C8 fails today: there is no published privacy notice. Recommended fix is cheap — publish the register-sources section as a standing public page with the Article 21 objection right in its own visible block. That discharges Article 14(7) directly.

Left for humans: nine questions in §13. The sharpest is Q1 to the solicitor (a PSC of an associated company who is not the client and gets nothing from the processing). Q6 deliberately does NOT answer whether the old pre-engagement design was a breach — that stays with item 12830181812. Q7 flags that Articles 22A–22D were not read. §14 lists exactly what could not be verified, including ICO guidance (site blocks automated requests) and the CAA 2001 AIA citation, which the CTA must supply.

Route B, at 5.5.3. ## Caprebate — data minimisation: strip named individuals at ingestion (CQC, EPC assessor); two justified exceptions (PSC common control, HMLR personal proprietor)

`12818210932` · 2 comments

### 26 August 2026, 14:52:29 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5493422736

<p>Drafted the operational rule: <a href="https://seveneightsixmediagroup.monday.com/docs/18428279094">Item 6 — Data Minimisation Rule</a>.</p><p>It states the strip-at-ingestion rule (not report-generation), defines the awkward personal-name cases (assessor IDs, sole-trader names, signature blocks, embedded free text), and sets the "avoid the endpoint, don't just filter it" principle as the preferred pattern over fetch-then-strip. Exception 1 (Companies House PSC: name, birth month/year, nationality only, confirm-only, corroborated matches) and Exception 2 (HMLR proprietor, natural persons only) are each justified on the facts and specified as two separately-held, name-searchable, independently-deletable stores with per-record purpose/basis/source/expiry metadata and hard restrictions on reporting, marketing, reuse and model input.</p><p>It cross-refers to the LIA (doc 46389172) for the legal balancing and to board item 12818313893 for the automated enforcement test, rather than duplicating either. Five open questions are left for the DPO and Lakhbir, covering the third-party proprietor classification schema, the trustee/beneficiary edge case, breach reporting procedure, the objection contact route for non-clients, and the retention-expiry figures that depend on the CTA's enquiry-window input.</p>

<p><b>Blank 4 — the dedicated contact address.</b> Determined in substance: healthtaxpartners.com is live on IONOS with mail configured, so this is a control-panel task (item 12927874161), not a purchase and not a decision. <b>The local part — privacy@ — is still a recommendation and not a decision</b>, and should be confirmed when the mailbox is created rather than left inferred. <b>The blank closes when the address is MONITORED, not when it exists.</b> Chain step 3.</p>

<h3>3. WHAT §6.7 ADDS, AND WHAT IT COSTS</h3>

<p><b>The deputy for breach decisions is Lakhbir Dhillon</b> — closing Q23 and readiness item B5 of the breach procedure. §6.7 sets seven rules bounding the route (D1–D7): it opens only where the DPO cannot be reached in time to decide within the Article 33(1) deadline; attempts to reach him are recorded first; it covers the Art 33(1) and Art 34 decisions, fixing awareness_at and opening the entry <b>and nothing else</b>; it confers no entitlement to the title; it does not suspend Article 38(3); the decision is handed back and confirmed or corrected on the record when the DPO is reachable; and every deputy-route entry is reviewed at the next quarterly review.</p>

<p><b>The limitation is written into the instrument, not into a comment.</b> The breach procedure's design is a two-person control — the DPO proposes, the controller approves. <b>On the deputy route it collapses: the same person proposes and approves, and the countersignature adds nothing because it is the same signature.</b> Claude's own recommendation at breach-procedure §7.1 Q23 was that the deputy could not be Lakhbir alone, for exactly this reason. <b>That recommendation was put, considered and declined. The decision was the controller's to take and it has been taken</b>, and it is defensible in a two-person business — the realistic alternative was no weekend route at all. It is recorded this way so a reader in a year sees a limitation the business knew about, rather than a control the business thought it had.</p>

<p><b>Two facts about the route that are worth reading before relying on it.</b> First, <b>no contactability undertaking was given</b> — the alternative Q23 offered was for the DPO to undertake to be reachable within 72 hours including weekends, and it was not taken. So the deputy is not a rare fallback; it stands behind every weekend and holiday. Second, <b>the DPO has no monday.com account</b> (breach procedure ADDENDUM 2 §A2.3), and the register now lives there — so until chain step 8, the deputy route is the <b>only</b> operable route into the register.</p>

<p><b>What would remove the limitation, and it is cheap.</b> Any second person with no commercial interest in the engagement could countersign — the CTA, the solicitor, or an external DP adviser bought in under §6.2. The countersignature is a review, not a decision, and it can be given <i>after</i> the notification has gone, so it does not have to fit inside 72 hours. No such person is named in the instrument, because naming one who has not agreed would be the same defect in a different place.</p>

<h3>4. WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT DONE</h3>

<p><b>The "DRAFT — NOT APPROVED" headers on the thirteen documents were not touched.</b> That mismatch is closed by a signature, not by editing headers. It is chain step 7.</p>

<p><b>Q28 was not answered and the response-letters rule was not relaxed.</b> Naming a designated officer in a transparency notice, with the caveat attached, is a different act from signing a statutory letter as "Data Protection Officer". The conservative rule at §0.4 of item 12927850552 stands unchanged — statutory letters are signed for and on behalf of the controller, the person dealing with the matter is named, and nobody is described as DPO while the instrument is unsigned and Article 37(7) is undischarged. <b>The letters pack already carries that rule correctly and needed no edit.</b></p>

<h3>What changed in the document</h3>

<ul>
<li><b>§3.7's second structural weakness rewritten.</b> It said "There is no deputy." That was true on 29 August and is not true now.</li>
