<li><b>ADDENDUM 3 added</b> — the route, the seven rules D1–D7, the limitation, what would remove it, and what it does not change.</li>
</ul>

<h3>The limitation, and why it is recorded rather than glossed</h3>

<p>§3.2 and §3.7 describe a two-person control: the DPO decides, the controller countersigns, and the countersignature is what makes a decision reviewable by somebody who did not make it. <b>On the deputy route that collapses into one person</b> — Lakhbir is controller, countersignatory and now decision-maker, so the countersignature adds nothing because it is the same signature.</p>

<p><b>This procedure recommended against it.</b> §7.1's Q23 entry said in terms: "If a deputy is named it cannot be Lakhbir alone, because the controller countersigns rather than decides." <b>That recommendation was put, considered and declined</b> — the decision is the controller's to take. It is defensible in a two-person business: the realistic alternative was no weekend route at all, and a business with no weekend route reliably discovers the clock started three days earlier, which is the exact failure §3.1 is written against. <b>A single-person decision that is recorded and reviewed beats a two-person control that exists only on paper because one of the two could not be reached.</b> It is written up as a known limitation so that a later reader sees a gap the business knew about rather than a control it thought it had.</p>

<h3>The finding this addendum produced</h3>

<p><b>The deputy route is not currently the fallback. It is the only operable route.</b> Two facts already in this document meet: the register moved onto monday.com on 1 September (ADDENDUM 2 §A2.1), and the DPO has no monday.com account (§A2.3). <b>Until he has one with write access to board 18429145787, Saddique cannot open a register entry or fix awareness_at at all</b> — so every entry opened before then is opened by the deputy, reachable or not. It is cheap to fix, it is now step 8 of the incorporation chain on item 12552682418, and it should not be discovered during an incident.</p>

<p><b>And it holds out of hours even after that is fixed.</b> The alternative Q23 offered was for the DPO to undertake to be contactable within 72 hours including weekends. That was not taken, and nothing obliges Saddique to be reachable out of hours. So the deputy is not an exception — it is what stands behind every weekend and holiday until such an undertaking is given.</p>

<h3>What is unchanged</h3>

<p><b>B1</b> — this procedure is still not approved. <b>B2</b> — the DPO instrument is still not signed, and is now <i>more</i> load-bearing: the deputy route is created by §6.7 of an unexecuted instrument, so what actually stands behind both routes today is the informal designation of 28 August 2026. <b>B6</b> — there is still no monitored contact address, so §3.1's finding is untouched: <b>naming a deputy improves the decision, not the detection.</b> The DRAFT header was not edited.</p>

## Pre-filled ICO breach-report answer sheet — the form cannot be saved and resumed, so it is a transcription job inside 72 hours

`12927942615` · 8 comments

### 29 August 2026, 17:26:21 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5502412572

<p><b>Why this exists.</b> The practical route for a UK GDPR Article 33(1) breach notification to the Information Commissioner is the ICO's online personal data breach reporting form. <b>Nobody at Ledgerstone has ever seen it.</b> ico.org.uk returns HTTP 403 to automated requests, so Claude could not read it for the Phase 39 communications pack (board item 12927894775) and deliberately did not guess at its fields. The Article 33(1) notification template there (T1) is therefore drafted as content organised by the limbs of Article 33(3) — not as a map of the form.</p>

<p><b>Why it matters now rather than later.</b> Article 33(1) gives 72 hours from awareness, and they are <b>calendar hours</b> — a breach discovered on a Friday evening has a Monday evening deadline. Discovering on the day of a breach that the form wants an account, a registration reference nobody has, or a field nobody has an answer to, is how a manageable breach becomes a late notification.</p>

<p><b>What to do — 20 minutes, no breach required.</b></p>
<ol>
<li>Open the ICO's report-a-breach page in an ordinary browser and walk the form as far as it goes <b>without submitting anything</b>.</li>
<li>Write down <b>every field it asks for</b>, in order, including any it asks that Article 33(3) does not require — sector, registration reference, whether individuals have been told, whether the police are involved, a contact telephone number.</li>
<li>Record whether an <b>account or login</b> is needed, and if so <b>who holds the credentials</b> and where they are kept. A credential only Lakhbir has is a single point of failure on a 72-hour clock, which is the same shape as open question Q23.</li>
<li>Record whether the form can be <b>saved and resumed</b>, and whether it issues a reference on submission.</li>
<li>Record the <b>fallback route</b> (telephone or postal) for the day the form is unavailable. Article 33(1) requires notification, not a particular channel.</li>
<li>Note that the form will ask for an <b>ICO registration reference</b> and Ledgerstone has none — registration is outstanding on board item 12552682424. Record what the form does when there is no reference.</li>
</ol>

<p><b>Where the answer goes.</b> Post it as an update on this item. It is then folded into §2.7 of the Phase 39 pack (12927894775) as a revision — that section is written to be replaced by what you find, and review trigger 2 of the pack names this item.</p>

<p><b>What not to do.</b> Do not submit a test notification. Do not create an account in a personal name that only one person can reach.</p>

<p><i>Created by Claude, Phase 39, 29 August 2026. Owner type: Lakhbir.</i></p>

## Caprebate — client document ingestion minimisation: strip on receipt per document type, the name guard on the upload path, and deleting the raw file

`12928074627` · 3 comments

### 29 August 2026, 18:56:48 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5502451091

<b>Phase 41 built, tested and attached. Deliverable is in the Document column; the code is in <code>04-phase-work/phase3/</code>.</b><br><br>

<b>THE FACT FIRST, because it changes the shape of everything else (item 12928031577, now closed).</b> The raw uploaded file is retained <b>by design</b> — AWS S3 eu-west-2, SSE, per the Developer Brief §3 — and <b>nothing is built</b>. No upload handler, no storage adapter, no file write, no text extraction, no deletion mechanism in any form. The pipeline library begins at <code>segment(pages)</code> and nothing anywhere constructs a <code>doc_id</code>. <b>This is NOT the "documents are not retained" finding Phase 40's review trigger 3 anticipated, so its §7 and §10 do not need re-running</b> — the question was undecided because the component does not exist. Both halves of what that means are recorded: the Article 14(3)(a) clock cannot have started, and equally <b>none of this phase enforces anything until somebody writes the upload handler</b>.<br><br>

<b>What was built</b><br>
1. <b>A receipt policy per document type</b>, derived from <code>DOC_SPECS.permitted_segments</code> at module load rather than transcribed, so it cannot drift from the field sets (test C2). Worked from the fields, not from a general idea of what is sensitive.<br>
2. <b>Condition D4, done and absolute.</b> Representations, consultee responses and correspondence are removed from an uploaded planning document <b>on receipt</b> — from every type including the two human-read ones, checked before the mode branch, under every setting, with no override, and re-asserted against the output. Reason <code>NO_LAWFUL_BASIS</code>, kept distinct from <code>NO_FIELD_NEEDS_IT</code>, because unlawful and unnecessary are different arguments.<br>
3. <b><code>assertNoUnauthorisedName</code> wired onto the upload path</b> via a <code>CLIENT_DOC</code> entry at subitem 13, <code>riskLevel: 'highest'</code>, <b>no third exception</b>. The register's own assertion is called, not a second copy of it.<br>
4. <b>The human-capture rule</b> (D3) — role-token substitution plus a reviewer attestation, so it is enforceable rather than advisory, and the evidential wording a CPSE reply turns on survives intact.<br>
5. <b>The per-upload transparency record</b> (D1, D2, D5), per person because the 5 Feb 2026 chapeau makes it a per-person assertion.<br>
6. <b>A raw-file retention mechanism</b> distinct from RET-1/RET-2, where fail-closed means <i>delete sooner</i>, and where a file with <b>no computable deletion date</b> throws just as hard as an overdue one.<br><br>

<b>Three things worth flagging even though they are not what the phase was set to do</b><br>
• <b>The design has a tension I could not resolve and did not paper over — Q37.</b> Stripping a witness's details on receipt and writing them a letter are <b>mutually exclusive</b>: you cannot notify somebody whose address you have deleted. Q17 and Q19 both land on this item, and they pull in opposite directions. Applied 1 September 2026 by Phase 62.
-----------------------------------------------------------------

Fire safety training (12552684629) — REMOVE-. Q17, Lakhbir: "re tag them". It is a premises duty and there are no premises. Marking it Done would assert training was delivered; it was not. Returns if premises are ever taken.

Information governance training (12552684628) — KEPT, and this is the exception that was written into the answer itself. Q19 was "remove the HR and training subtasks until a first hire", and Lakhbir answered remove. The recommendation he was answering carried an exception on its face — except information governance training — and it is kept for a reason that does not depend on headcount:

* The data protection framework requires it regardless of how many people work here. UK GDPR Article 39(1)(b) puts awareness-raising and training of staff involved in processing among the DPO's own tasks, and Article 32 security measures are not met by a workforce that has never been trained.
* It applies to Lakhbir today, as the only person doing the work. A sole worker who is also the controller, the breach deputy and the person who will handle rights requests is precisely the person the training is for. "No employees" removes an HR obligation; it does not remove a data protection one.
* It is load-bearing on documents that already exist. The breach procedure, the rights-request routes and the retention procedure all assume somebody knows how to follow them.
So this parent is not fully retired — one live subitem remains, and its name now says so rather than leaving a future sweep to work out why one of two survived.

Phase 132a, 15 September 2026 - claims C6 and C11 answered, and both are off the site.

C6, "Up to 4 years". The audit asked which law supports four years. Read on legislation.gov.uk today: none.

* Individuals and partnerships amend a return within twelve months of the filing date (Taxes Management Act 1970, s.9ZA(2) and s.12ABA(2)).
* A company's capital allowances claim can be made or amended up to the first anniversary of the filing date (Finance Act 1998, Schedule 18, paragraph 82).
* The four-year limit belongs to overpayment relief (TMA 1970, Schedule 1AB, paragraph 3). Case A in paragraph 2(2)(b) and (c), and FA 1998 Schedule 18 paragraph 51A for companies, shuts that route to a missed claim.

## Rules-defect incident and client correction plan — when a defect surfaces after a client's report has shipped

`12927557335` · 5 comments

### 29 August 2026, 14:05:49 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5502282635

Phase 28 — new item, drafted this phase. I checked the Business Continuity & Disaster Recovery Plan (12552682536) first, as instructed. It does not cover this and does not partly cover it: every one of its scenarios — document store, supplier, key person, equipment, comms, cyber — is about availability, whether we can keep working. This is about correctness, whether what we already shipped was right. So this is built, not duplicated, and the BCP's section 10 should cross-refer to it once both are approved.

The core finding. The board's standing shipping rule (a claim-reducing correction is safe to ship on Claude's reading; a claim-increasing one is held) is forward-looking, and it inverts after a report ships. Before shipping, a reduction is safe because it is conservative. After shipping, the reduction is the dangerous one — the client has already claimed the larger number, so the filed position may be wrong, with interest and possibly penalties behind it. The plan classifies every defect by direction first (Type R reduces, Type I increases, Type N is reasoning-only), then crosses that with filing status — not filed / filed with the amendment window open / window closed — to set the response. The amendment window is ours to watch, not the client's: a Type I client told two weeks after their window closed has been told nothing useful.

The conflict I have written as a rule rather than an intention. Our fee is a percentage of tax saved, so a Type R correction reduces our own fee — the firm has a direct financial interest in not finding, not classifying and not disclosing exactly the defects that matter most. Three controls: the fee follows the corrected figure always, with refunds, non-discretionary; materiality is never assessed by the person whose fee moves with the answer; and every Type R is registered even when later found immaterial, so a pattern of near-misses stays visible. This needs to be in the engagement letter before the first client signs — it is far harder to introduce afterwards, and the letter is not written yet, so the timing is fortunate.

The ad-hoc gap, and the interim rule. Since 28 August there may be no adviser under instruction when a defect surfaces. So: Lakhbir may pause without a CTA; Lakhbir may not un-pause, may not issue a correction, and may not tell a client their filed position is wrong, without one. Pausing new intake is cheap and narrow and should be done on suspicion; un-pausing has a higher bar than pausing. That asymmetry is the whole design.

A gap this exposed that is worth acting on independently. The first question in any incident is "which clients are affected" — and there is currently no way to answer it. Nothing stamps a shipped case with the engine version, rulebook module versions, gate flag values or adviser sign-off references it was computed against. At two pilot clients that is a non-problem. At twenty it is the difference between a two-hour notification exercise and an unanswerable question, and it is far cheaper to build before there are cases. Added to the Go-Live Checklist as a new section E line.

What you need to do: six questions in §10, the first two being whether you accept the fee rule and the pause asymmetry. Never invoked; no client has been engaged.

## Take the five decisions the data protection officer's appointment needs — none of them waits on the company

`13033247305` · 5 comments

### 12 September 2026, 18:56:01 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5542872859

Phase 129, 12 September 2026 — split out of "Sign the data protection officer's appointment — 13 documents and 3 live duties wait on this signature". The signature still waits on the company, because the appointment names the company as the controller. These five decisions do not. They are the blanks in section 10.2 of the draft "Instrument of appointment — Data Protection Officer" (in the documents folder, 08-monday-doc-exports). Answer them now, and the instrument can be signed the day the company exists instead of waiting for another conversation. Four of the five can be settled in one talk between Lakhbir and Saddique. Answering signs nothing.

* Saddique's data protection background (section 3, first row). Lakhbir and Saddique. What we think: nothing is recorded, and the law says the officer is chosen for their knowledge of data protection. "None" is a complete answer, and a more useful one than a blank. Example of a good answer: "No formal training or qualification; has worked from the data protection documents on this board since 28 August 2026." Recommendation: write the honest sentence, even if it is "none", because it decides how much the next answer has to carry.
* What outside data protection support the officer can call on, and the budget for it (section 3, second row, and section 6.2). Lakhbir. What we think: the test is proportionate. Our processing is small and narrow, but some of the open questions on this board are not simple. Example: "No retained adviser. The officer uses the documents on this board and the ICO's free helpline for small organisations (0303 123 1113), and may spend up to a stated sum a year on a one-off written opinion." Recommendation: name at least the ICO helpline and a figure for a one-off opinion. If the answer to 1 is "none", then "none" here is not enough.
* Employee or service contract (section 1, "Basis of engagement"). Lakhbir. What we think: either is allowed, and the choice changes nothing about what the officer does or is protected from. It is a blank only because nobody has written it down. Recommendation: write whichever matches how Saddique is actually engaged. If he is not on the payroll, that is "service contract".
* Is the list of Saddique's other roles in section 7.1 complete? Lakhbir and Saddique. What we think: section 7.1 lists one other role. He negotiates bespoke client fees above the 5% baseline for larger and multi-site clients, and flags any expected fee of £25,000 or more for VAT threshold monitoring. That role sets prices and does not decide what data we collect, so there is no conflict on the current facts, but only if the list is complete. Example of what would change it: a directorship, a shareholding, or any say over what the assessment tool collects or how long we keep things. Recommendation: answer "yes, complete", or give the corrected list.
* The notice period for ending the appointment (section 9.3). Lakhbir and Saddique. What we think: it must be long enough to find a successor, correct the published contact details and tell the Commissioner. Worked example: someone asks for their personal data on the day notice is given. We have one month to answer, and up to two more months if the request is complex, so three months in all. A notice period shorter than three months could end the appointment with that request still open and nobody in the role. Recommendation: three months.
What answering unblocks. Sections 1, 3, 7 and 9 of the instrument stop being blanks. Signing then waits only on the company and the privacy mailbox. Where to answer: write the five answers as a reply on this task. Status: Ready - Lakhbir action. Owner: Lakhbir.

Why it matters. Without the mailbox, replies from clients bounce. Without DKIM and DMARC, our emails are more likely to land in spam, and it is easier for someone to fake an email from us.

Related. Which service sends the email is asked in CAPREBATE QUESTIONS: "Which email service should send our emails from contactus@caprebate.com?" (recommendation: IONOS). ## Flag to the tax adviser — one of our fixes makes claims bigger, not smaller

`12851910641` · 8 comments

### 26 August 2026, 07:18:35 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5492260799

What this is
Something to put in front of the tax adviser deliberately, rather than letting it slip past unnoticed. Honesty item.

In plain English
Most of our recent corrections made claims smaller — we found places where the system was letting people claim things they should not. That is the safe direction to be wrong in.

One correction went the other way. Previously, a building split into several self-contained flats would stop the assessment dead. We changed it so that only a genuinely single home stops, and blocks of flats now continue and can produce a claim. That makes some claims bigger.

Why we are flagging it rather than burying it
It rests on our reading of one piece of HMRC guidance. Every other change in that batch reduced claims, so this one could easily be waved through as part of a general tightening. It is the opposite, and it carries more risk than the rest.

What to do
Name it explicitly when the tax adviser reviews the rulebooks. Ask them to confirm the reading directly rather than approving the batch as a whole.

Original wording: "E-3 DISCLOSURE — the E-1/E-2 fix INCREASED claims in one respect: blocks of self-contained flats now proceed instead of stopping. Rests on CA11520. Name it explicitly at CTA review rather than letting it pass as part of a reduction."

## Rulebook E — the dwelling-house rule and the residential carve-out

`12830037617` · 5 comments

### 20 August 2026, 07:48:05 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5476422363

Rulebook E delivered — 20 August 2026
-------------------------------------

File attached to this item (also added to the CTA review pack, item 12830043701, so the reviewer has A–E in one place). Same locked template as A/C/D: 7 sections, 22 sourced authorities, 5 rule groups, 15 engine defects, 8 CTA questions.

The board note said E "may cut more than Module D adds, for supported living". That is half right — the engine is wrong in both directions, and the two worst errors are over-claims sitting in client-facing question wording.

The two blockers
----------------

E-1 — communal is not common. Supported Living S6a offers "communal lounge/kitchen" to the client as claimable common parts. Per CA11520, R&C Brief 45/10 and Hora Tevfik, shared living space that completes the residents' living arrangement is part of the dwelling-house. Common parts (lobby, corridors, stairs, lifts) are not. The two words are opposites and the engine uses them as synonyms.

E-2 — "for use in" is not "located in". The same question offers "plant rooms" without asking what the plant serves. CA23060's worked example is ground-mounted solar in the garden of a let house. A central boiler in a common-part plant room serving the flats is excluded — that is the single largest special-rate item in the building.

Three doors the engine cannot currently reach
---------------------------------------------

E-4: CA11520 now accepts that specialised supported housing may not be a dwelling-house at all, where the level of care leaves residents very little privacy. No branch exists for the sector's highest-value sub-segment.

E-8: s.187A only engages where the past owner "was entitled to claim". A landlord barred by s.35 never was — which on its face removes the pooling requirement on purchases from residential landlords. Nil claims become live ones. Low confidence; gated on E-Q4.

E-5 / E-6: dwelling_factor is applied to Dental, GP and Private Hospitals. s.35(1) cannot reach a trade or a profession (s.15(3)). A care-home manager's flat is an s.11 / private-use question, not this one.

Two citation errors found
-------------------------

CA20020 is archived — cited as live in Modules 04 and 05 and two data models. "Ordinary UK property business" no longer exists — FA 2025 Sch 5 removed the qualifier with the FHL repeal, so from April 2025 every property business is in scope.

Where I am weakest
------------------

E-Q1. Every authority reasons from cluster flats or HMOs, where the private unit is not self-sufficient. A block of genuinely self-contained flats with a shared lounge is unresolved, and it is a large slice of the stock. I have also not read the Tevfik judgment — E-1 and E-3 both turn on it and it should be read before either is remediated.

Next in sequence: Rulebook F (contributions & grants) cuts the supported-living base independently and often harder. Rulebook H owes an answer on whether LRR really is unrestricted by the dwelling-house rules — the Supported Living flow asserts that today and E makes no finding on it.

### 14 September 2026, 07:20:21 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5543991683

Phase 131, 14 September 2026 — Rulebook E: the Hora Tevfik decision read in full and set against the flats and shared-lounge switches; the archived HMRC manual page replaced. The file was edited on 13 September and attached here today. Its correction lines are dated 13 September.

What was wrong.

* The rulebook rests two rules on Hora Tevfik v HMRC and said in terms that the decision had not been read.

* It cited HMRC's manual page CA20020, which is archived.

* It said that page was archived "as part of the FHL-repeal tidy-up", which the evidence does not show.

What the decision holds. First-tier Tribunal, [2019] UKFTT 0600 (TC), released 24 September 2019, read from the PDF on Find Case Law.

* The facts: three houses in multiple occupation, with bedrooms sharing a kitchen, bathroom and lounge. Not self-contained flats.

* The meaning: the tribunal agreed with HMRC's 2010 brief that "dwelling-house" takes its everyday meaning. A communal kitchen and lounge are part of the dwelling-house, because the bedrooms alone do not give what is needed for daily private life. Common parts are not: the entrance lobby, corridors, stairs, lifts, and parts with no living facilities.

* Why the taxpayer lost: he had not separated the common parts from the communal areas, so he did not prove his claim. His annual investment allowance also failed because the spending was before 6 April 2008.

* How much weight it carries: he did not attend, and neither side argued the dwelling-house points. A First-tier decision binds no one.

How it bears on the two switches. Off is the live reading for both, and neither moves.

* The flats switch (several self-contained homes). The decision is not about flats. What it says fits today's reading, that a building of several self-contained homes can have a common-parts claim, and not the switched one. HMRC's own officer, in a letter the decision records, accepted that hallways and stairs between converted flats are not part of any home. That is weak support, so the switch stays off.

* The shared-lounge switch (a shared lounge or kitchen outside self-contained homes). The decision does not decide this either. Its reason for putting the lounge inside the home was that the bedrooms were not self-sufficient, and that reason is absent in a scheme of self-contained homes. It gives no support for switching on. The switch stays off, and the question stays with the tax adviser.

Not adopted. The tribunal also said mains and service installations are not a dwelling-house. Read alone, that would make claims bigger. The rulebook does not adopt it: the test in the Act is whether plant is provided for use in a home, and the tribunal itself went on to apportion. The point is added to the tax adviser's question on shared plant.

What changed, and where.

* The Tevfik source row is rewritten with what the decision holds.

* A new passage at the end of section 6 sets the decision against the two switches.

* Two discrepancy notes are corrected. One said the judge "disagreed" with HMRC and "expressly held" the point; the decision does neither in terms. The other said CA20020 was archived "as part of the FHL-repeal tidy-up"; the web archive shows the page live in September 2020 and archived by April 2025, with the replacement pages last revised in September 2021.

* The CA20020 source row now cites CA23060, the current page carrying the same dwelling-house material, checked on GOV.UK on 13 September.

* Question 1, question 3 and the scrutiny log are updated to match.

Already fixed: nothing. All three points were still open in the file.

No switch, no code and no row outcome changed. The combined rulebooks document held with the tax adviser's review pack was updated on disk to match, but is not uploaded from here.

File attached: Ledgerstone-Statutory-Rules-Register-F-Contributions-And-Grants-v1.md. Locked seven-section template. 39 sources, 36 rules in 7 groups, 16 engine defects, 9 open CTA questions. Status set to Awaiting CTA review; claim column cleared.

What changed, and it is not what the item predicted
---------------------------------------------------

This item said Rulebook F would cut the supported-living base harder than E. It does not. The questions in this project were already close to right. Every sector flow asks about grants; GP already states the NHS mutual-exclusivity rule element-by-element at G17; G18 already keeps rent reimbursement apart from capital grants; the dental flow already tells clients UDA income is trading income. On contributions the build is further ahead than it was on anything D or E looked at.

The defect is in the arithmetic, not the questions. Stage 1(a) of the estimate engine spec carries this comment and then this line:

« remove grant-funded spend (GP: any cost element funded by an NHS improvement grant is excluded entirely — mutual exclusivity, not pro-rata) »
B = B * (1 - grant_fraction)

The comment states the rule and the next line does the opposite. Four artefacts describe a per-element strip; the one that computes applies a proportion. That is F-1, BLOCKER.

Why it runs against us in GP specifically
-----------------------------------------

Direction 8(1) of the 2024 Directions is a list of what an NHS improvement grant may fund, and read next to Module D's taxonomy it is close to a list of integral features — heating, ventilation and lighting installations, statutory fire and security fabric works, infection-control specialist floor covering, generator connection, water meter, car parking, tenant fit-out. Direction 9 then bars grant funding of land, buildings, repairs, restoration, residential quarters and fair wear and tear. The grant is aimed at the plant and starved of the structure. A practice reporting 30% of works grant-funded may have had 80–90% of its qualifying expenditure met, and the engine strips 30%. In supported living the same defect runs the other way, because SAHP buys dwellings that Module E has already removed — so the grant is deducted twice for one payment.

The two BLOCKERs
----------------

F-1 — pro-rata strip where the rule is per-element. Over-claim in GP. F-2 — an unknown grant defaults to nil. GP and Supported Living say so explicitly; Care Homes Q17 and Dental D17 state no default at all, which is worse. This is the same failure pattern as the inverted s.187A routing: unknown facts routing to the most favourable branch, in the sectors with the highest exposure.

What is now weak
----------------

F-R10 and F-Q1 are the softest load-bearing thing in the module, and they are also the most valuable. Where PropCo and OpCo are connected, s.537(2)(c) denies the contributor a contribution allowance and a capital contribution is not deductible as revenue — so both limbs of s.536(3) appear satisfied and the occupier's expenditure is not reduced at all. HMRC's own worked example at CA14400 reaches exactly that result. But the example is a married couple, a scriptwriter and a shopkeeper — not a property group — and I found no authority applying it to a PropCo/OpCo structure. It increases claims across four of five sectors and contradicts what four of our own artefacts currently say. Held, not coded.

Three retrieval gaps that matter. (1) CA14400 was read in a full-text search rendering, not fetched as a page — and F-R10 rests on it. Fetch it before answering F-Q1. (2) s.62 was not read in this session at all; F-R17 depends on it, and there is already an open item in group 02 (12851633377) recording that s.62 has only been read as-enacted and s.62A not at all. F-R17 must not ship before that closes. (3) Cyril Lord Carpets v Schofield 42 TC 637 was not read — only a case summary. Its holding that grants payable in respect of specific items are related to that expenditure is load-bearing for the whole tracing argument. Read it before remediating F-1.

Not verified: SAHP programme detail and the Homes England Capital Funding Guide recovery/recycling chapters come from search results, not the source documents. The Care and Support Specialised Housing Fund and local-authority capital routes were not researched. Whether s.538A has manual coverage outside CA14000 was not checked. F-14 (NHS fee reimbursement against our preliminaries-and-fees uplift) is stated conditionally — I confirmed the reimbursement caps and that a fees factor exists in the costing work, but not that it is applied on the GP path.

Housekeeping — one thing I could not do
---------------------------------------

The item rename did not take. I attempted it three times (change_simple_column_value and change_multiple_column_values, with and without em-dashes); the API returned success each time and the name is unchanged. This item's title still reads "NEXT UP" even though the work is done and awaiting review. Flagging rather than leaving it silent — a stale title on a completed item is the E-1/E-2 pattern in miniature. Someone with UI access should retitle it.

Scope this module did not touch
-------------------------------

No rates are stated anywhere in it. It makes no finding on Land Remediation Relief (F-Q9, handed to Rulebook H — do not read F's silence as clearance) and none on repairs versus capital where a grant funded work that turns out to be revenue (handed to G). Yield bands and R-B8 are untouched, except that F-1 interacts with the GP band because a band calibrated on unsubsidised refurbishments cannot be applied to a grant-funded one without the element-level strip.

## Rulebook G — repairs versus capital

`12830061107` · 3 comments

### 24 August 2026, 12:54:48 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5485537965

<p><b>Rulebook G drafted</b> — v1, ready for CTA review: <a href="https://seveneightsixmediagroup.monday.com/docs/18427873138">Rulebook G — Repairs vs Capital</a>. Built from primary sources read in full: ITTOIA s.33/s.57, CTA 2009 s.53/s.61, CAA 2001 s.12, s.25, s.33A, s.33B, and the BIM35430/35445/35450 and BIM46901/46905/46910/46935/46945 chains. States no rates — those belong in Rulebook I.</p><p><b>Law Shipping and Odeon are reduced to an operative test the engine can run:</b> the default is revenue if the repairs would have been revenue absent the change of ownership, displaced to capital only where the asset was unusable (or only short-term usable) without repair, or the price was substantially reduced for the dilapidation. A price reduction for ordinary wear and tear does <i>not</i> displace it. HMRC's four worked examples are tabulated against our fact patterns. Pre-use expenditure is separated into three rules that are commonly conflated — s.57/s.61 (7-year limit, revenue only, does not convert capital), s.12 (no time limit, moves the date only), and s.25 (alterations incidental to installing plant).</p><p><b>Two findings worth your attention.</b> First, <b>s.33B(4) is a claim-creating rule we should be hunting</b>: phased works on the same integral feature within a rolling 12 months aggregate, and if the total exceeds 50% of replacement cost measured at the <i>initial</i> spend date, both tranches become capital special-rate expenditure — even where the accountant has already deducted them as repairs. Second, a trap: <b>s.12 is ignored when testing first-year allowance windows</b> (CA23110/23164/23195A), so a pre-commencement fit-out deemed to fall on day one of trading is not thereby brought into an FYA window. Six CTA questions logged, the sharpest being G-Q2 on distressed care home acquisitions where the price reflects a poor CQC rating rather than physical dilapidation — I have taken a view but it is judgement and it affects a large share of that pipeline.</p>

### 15 September 2026, 10:22:36 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5548150408

Phase 132, 14 September 2026 — the repairs-into-a-replacement rule is built, and switched off.

This rulebook identifies a claim-creating rule nothing implemented: small pieces of work on one integral feature — the lighting, the heating, the hot and cold water system — can add up to a replacement. Spend of more than half the feature's replacement cost is a replacement on its own; otherwise spend on the same feature within twelve months of the first spend is added together, and if the total passes half the replacement cost at the date of that first spend, all of it is treated as a replacement.

* Built in the engine as its own module, with nine questions that stay hidden while the switch is off. Caught spend goes whole into the special-rate pool, and a flag is raised where any of it was already deducted as a repair.
* Unknowns never relieve. A replacement cost not known for a date means no window measured from that date can pass; a date or amount not known leaves that piece of work out; later work not known to be on the same system is never added in. "Not sure" and no answer behave identically throughout.
* Tests: off, all five sectors are byte-identical; on, two 30% pieces of work eight months apart are caught, thirteen months apart are not, exactly half is not, and a single piece over half is caught. Every check was shown failing against the site from before.
On, it makes claims bigger, so it stays off until the tax adviser answers this rulebook's questions on it. Status unchanged: Built - awaiting sign-off.

## Rulebook H — land remediation relief

`12830043662` · 4 comments

### 24 August 2026, 12:57:16 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5485546591

<p><b>Rulebook H drafted</b> — v1, ready for CTA review: <a href="https://seveneightsixmediagroup.monday.com/docs/18427873476">Rulebook H — Land Remediation Relief</a>. Built from CTA 2009 Part 14 read in its entirety (ss.1143–1179) plus the CIRD60000 chain.</p><p><b>On the unresolved question — my conclusion is that the Supported Living flow is right, and for a stronger reason than it gives.</b> The dwelling-house restriction is a CAA 2001 rule; LRR is not a capital allowance. Four grounds: (1) the words "dwelling", "dwelling-house" and "residential" appear <i>nowhere</i> in Part 14 — I checked the whole Part; (2) the only cross-reference to the capital allowances code is s.1147(8), which runs the other way; (3) s.1147(8) blocks LRR only where an allowance "has been, or may be" made, so where the dwelling-house rules <i>deny</i> P&M allowances the block is not engaged at all — the restriction widens the LRR field rather than narrowing it; and (4) HMRC's own CIRD60055 worked example applies LRR to a company building a housing estate. <b>I have flagged this as H-13 requiring CTA confirmation before client-facing use</b> — I found no authority deciding the point either way, so it is reasoned from statute, not sourced, and it is the sector's main pivot.</p><p><b>But the proposition is a weak load-bearing member and the flow should be reframed.</b> Four other constraints bite far harder in supported living: LRR is company-only (no partnerships, no sole traders); s.1177 subsidises out grant-funded spend, which is most of SAHP; s.1150 polluter-pays now also catches a third-party polluter's connected person holding any interest, option or overage; and a major interest of 7+ years is required, so short-lease occupiers get nothing. As drafted the flow invites clients to expect relief those rules will usually remove. Also flagged: the s.1148 two-year election deadline is the binding constraint on any LRR engagement, shorter than the CTSA limit for the 50% uplift. Six CTA questions, the most commercially significant being H-Q5 on whether asbestos removal satisfies the s.1145(4)(d) relevant-harm test — that single answer probably determines the size of the LRR opportunity across care homes and supported living.</p>

### 14 September 2026, 07:17:06 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5543986155

Phase 131, 14 September 2026 — Rulebook H corrected where it described land remediation relief more generously than the law allows

What was wrong. The claim that the wording overstated relief was checked against the rulebook before anything changed, and it held. The rulebook was re-read against Part 14 of the Corporation Tax Act 2009, the Corporation Tax (Land Remediation Relief) Order 2009 and the claims rules in Schedule 18 to the Finance Act 1998, all on legislation.gov.uk. It was also re-read against HMRC's Corporate Intangibles Research and Development Manual on gov.uk. All of these were read on 13 September 2026. Six passages said more than the law does:

* The cash tax credit. The rulebook said a loss-making company can surrender "the LRR-attributable part" of its loss. In fact the credit is 16 per cent of the lower of the unrelieved loss and 150 per cent of the spend. Loss that could have been set against other profits of the same period counts as relieved, whether or not that claim is made. The credit must be claimed within one year of the return's filing date. HMRC can hold it back during an enquiry or while PAYE is unpaid.
* Partnerships with a company member. The rulebook said such a partnership "can get relief". Only the company member can, for its own share, and only if it meets the conditions itself.
* Natural contaminants. The Order lifts the non-industrial exclusion for arsenic, radon and Japanese knotweed. It does so only for the part of the land affected and the spend on dealing with them. Knotweed taken to landfill does not qualify at all.
* Work a council notice requires. Remediation required by a local authority notice does not qualify. That covers contaminated land remediation notices, statutory nuisance, dangerous buildings and planning maintenance notices. The rulebook did not say so.
* Supported living conversions. The rulebook listed redundant foundations, machinery bases and buried services "on a formerly industrial or institutional site" as realistic eligible spend. Those items only qualify on land that has stood derelict since 1998 and cannot be used without removing structures, which a conversion keeping the building will rarely meet. It also listed asbestos removal without saying the asbestos must be causing, or seriously likely to cause, harm.
* The dwelling-house point. The same passage stated as fact that the relief reaches spend capital allowances cannot. That rests on the rulebook's own unconfirmed conclusion, so it is now conditional on the tax adviser confirming it.
What changed and where. Sections 1, 2.1, 2.3, 2.4, 2.5, 4 and 5.3 are corrected in place, each with a dated line quoting the old wording. Findings H-1, H-7 and H-14 are amended. Four new findings are added: the limits on natural contaminants, the council-notice exclusion, the derelict-land test for conversions, and the tax credit's time limit and payment rules. A note is added to the asbestos question. The version line now reads v1.1, and a corrections note at the top lists every source. Every change narrows the relief and none widens it, so the corrections are made on our own reading. The tax adviser can still overturn any of them. The dwelling-house conclusion and all six open questions for the adviser are unchanged.

Files. Both attached copies were replaced: the monday export and the statutory rules register copy. Each was compared byte for byte with the disk file after upload and is identical. The previous versions are kept on disk as backups.

## Rulebook I — the rates and reliefs table

`12830060773` · 4 comments

### 24 August 2026, 13:01:04 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5485560814

<p><b>Rulebook I drafted</b> — v1, ready for CTA review: <a href="https://seveneightsixmediagroup.monday.com/docs/18427874000">Rulebook I — Rates and Reliefs Table with Basis Dates</a>. Every figure was fetched from a live primary source today and cited to it; nothing is asserted from training data, per the item's instruction.</p><p><b>Web-verification was not a formality — the rates have moved and our existing material is wrong.</b> Finance Act 2026, following Budget 2025, cut the <b>main pool WDA from 18% to 14%</b> for chargeable periods beginning on or after 1 April 2026 (CT) / 6 April 2026 (IT), and introduced a new <b>40% first-year allowance</b> (CAA 2001 s.45U) for new, unused, main-rate plant incurred on or after 1 January 2026. Crucially the 40% FYA is available to <b>unincorporated businesses as well as companies</b>, including mixed partnerships for both corporate and non-corporate members — the opposite of the full expensing position, and directly relevant to our GP and dental pipeline. The special rate pool is unchanged at 6%.</p><p><b>Two consequences the engines have to absorb.</b> First, <b>the main pool WDA is no longer a constant</b>: any period straddling the change date needs the CA23222 day-count hybrid (HMRC's own example gives 14.99% for a calendar-year 2026 period), so the rate must become a function of period start and end dates. Second, the drifted MARGINAL_RATE copies should be replaced with <b>26.5%</b> for corporates in the £50k–£250k band — derived from the 25% main rate and the 3/200 standard fraction, and not stated directly anywhere on gov.uk — and the income tax model needs the <b>60% effective band</b> between £100k and £125,140 caused by personal allowance taper, which is the highest-value band for a partner claim and should not be rounded to 45%. Thirteen findings and six CTA questions in the doc.</p>

## Rulebook I addendum — Scottish income tax rates

`12889350666` · 4 comments

### 25 August 2026, 07:52:11 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5488637655

Raised by Phase 2 (Opus) while doing LEG-E1. Consolidating the five drifted MARGINAL_RATE copies into one table exposed this — it was invisible while the same unsourced numbers sat in five places.

The gap. Rulebook I §6.2 covers income tax for 2026–27 (20 / 40 / 45%, personal allowance £12,570 tapering to nil at £125,140) and then says only that "Scottish taxpayers have different bands and rates and must be handled separately." It does not give them.

The engine has been asserting 21% to 48% for uninc_scot — inherited from the pre-consolidation modules, with no verified source. Rulebook I rule 7.1 is that no engine, model, report template or marketing asset may state a rate that is not in the table. On a strict reading these should not be stated at all.

What I did instead of deleting them. Deleting would have silently broken the Scottish flow, so they are retained and marked: recorded in LS_RATES.UNVERIFIED with the reason; LS_RATES.describe("uninc_scot") raises a flag at the point of use; and the client-facing reveal says the rates "are not yet verified against the rate table and should be confirmed". Documented in Module-00 §3c.

What this item needs. Fetch the current Scottish income tax bands and rates from a live primary source (gov.scot / Scottish Government Budget, cross-checked against gov.uk), for the current year and for the retrospective years a claim can reach back into — Rulebook I rule 7.2 requires the rate in force for each period, not today's rate. Note Scotland has more bands than rUK, so a two-value [lo, hi] range may not be the right shape. Then issue as a Rulebook I addendum and clear the unverified flag in LS_RATES.

Why it matters commercially: the top Scottish rate is higher than the rUK 45%, so this is a live figure on any Scottish partnership or sole-trader claim — not a rounding point.

Related: LEG-E1 (12804368579), Rulebook I (12830060773).

### 25 August 2026, 08:00:43 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5488657638

Done — verified against two independent primary sources (gov.uk and gov.scot, cross-checked, they agree exactly), five tax years, 25 August 2026. Full addendum: Rulebook I — Addendum 1: Scottish income tax

The engine was asserting [0.21, 0.48]. Both ends were wrong.

1. The floor is 19%, not 21%. Scotland's 21% is its third band (intermediate), not its lowest marginal rate — the starter rate is 19%. Every Scottish range was understated at the bottom.

2. 48% is right only from 2024-25. It was 47% in 2023-24 and 46% in 2022-23 — so any claim valued against an amended earlier year was overstated at the top. Rule 7.2 (use the rate in force for each period) is not optional for Scotland: the rates moved in three of the last five years, and the band count changed too when the Advanced rate arrived in 2024-25.

3. The finding worth your attention: the effective taper band is 67.5%. The personal allowance is reserved, so the £100k–£125,140 withdrawal is UK-wide — but that income is taxed at the Scottish marginal rate. From 2024-25 the zone sits entirely in the Advanced rate, so by the same method Rulebook I uses for rUK's 60%: 45% × 1.5 = 67.5%. That is the highest effective marginal rate anywhere in the UK, and it lands exactly on a Scottish GP partner or dental principal drawing six figures. Not modelled (consistent with open question I-Q2 being unanswered) but now disclosed in the client reveal.

Engine: SCOTLAND_BY_YEAR with all five years and full band structures, rangeForYear() for rule 7.2, taperBandRate(). UNVERIFIED is now empty. Module-00 §3c rewritten. Harness 193 pass / 0 fail / 3 xfail (12 new assertions).

⚠️ One thing I found that needs its own item. Being a Scottish taxpayer turns on where the person's main home is, not where the property is. A Scottish property does not make the claimant a Scottish taxpayer, and an English property owned by a Scottish taxpayer is valued at Scottish rates. The engine currently infers the rate key from the business's registered address — a proxy that will be wrong in real cases. Out of scope here; flagged in §6 of the addendum.

Status set to Awaiting CTA review rather than Done, to match Rulebook I itself — four CTA questions are logged in §5.

<p><b>CA14400 has now been read as a full page</b> (item 12852270243, Done) — write-up: <a href="https://seveneightsixmediagroup.monday.com/docs/18427871629">OPEN GAP — HMRC CA14400 full page</a>.</p><p><b>Your reading is right, but the citation in Rulebook F needs correcting.</b> There is <i>no</i> PropCo–OpCo worked example on CA14400 — the page carries one example only, Johnny's restaurant and June's market garden, whose connected variant is a married couple. Also note s.536(3)(b) requires the contribution not to be deductible in computing the contributor's profits, so the characterisation of the intra-group payment (capital contribution vs rent premium vs service charge) is load-bearing and must be evidenced.</p><p><b>Status set to Blocked</b> (was "Not started") to match the item's own "do not code on Claude's reading" instruction and the plan doc, which lists F-6 among the CTA-gated items. ## Disposal note — the election the client signs on a future sale

`12830181411` · 3 comments

### 25 August 2026, 13:26:24 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5489369910

Done. Full draft: Disposal Note — the s.198 election on the client's future sale. Sourced from Module C (Rulebook C v1) plus a fresh read of CAA 2001 ss.198, 200, 201, 203 and 187A(5)–(9) on legislation.gov.uk, 25 August 2026.

⚠️ This needs a human CTA sanity-check before it reaches a client. The board has no formal review gate for group 06 reports — unlike the Rulebooks, which sit at "Awaiting CTA review" — so nothing else will stop this going out. It is the one deliverable in the pack that a client could sign and be permanently bound by, and there is no correction route if the figure is wrong. Please do not release it without a CTA reading Part B and Part D.

What it contains. Four parts: (A) a client-facing note on what happens to the pools on disposal and why the elected figure decides how much relief is kept; (B) a pro-forma election with all six s.201(3) contents laid out clause by clause, split schedules for special-rate and main-rate fixtures, and drafting notes against each clause; (C) a 12-line completion checklist; (D) the six open CTA questions carried across from Module C §10, each with what the draft currently assumes pending an answer.

Three things I'd flag as the substance.

1. The number is fixed by the sale contract, not by the election. Sale contracts routinely carry a capital allowances clause obliging the seller to elect at a stated figure, at £1, or at "such figure as the buyer shall reasonably require". By the time anyone counts the two-year window, the tax outcome has already been decided by whoever drafted that clause. Part A §3 names the three clause forms to refuse. This moves our intervention point to heads of terms, which is months earlier than the "second touchpoint" framing on this item assumes — worth reflecting in the engagement letter and the pipeline.

2. Irrevocability is worse than "you can't change your mind". s.200(3) makes it irrevocable, there is no variation mechanism, and s.201(5) expressly disapplies TMA 1970 s.42 and Sch 1A and FA 1998 Sch 18 paras 54–60 — which switches off the s.42(9) supplementary claim that normally lets a taxpayer correct an error in an election. A transposed digit has no statutory cure. The declaration at Part B §6(d) makes the parties acknowledge this on the face of the document, which is as much protective drafting for us as it is for them.

3. A live client obligation nobody has costed. s.203(2)(d) and (e) make the making of an election, or a s.200(4) reduction, a trigger for the three-month duty to notify HMRC that a filed return has become incorrect (penalties under TMA s.98). This is Module C's C-7 defect — absent from every deliverable in the pack. It is now in Part A §8, but §10 Q8 (report statement vs separate written notification vs engagement-letter condition) is a professional conduct question and is still open.

Assumptions, stated visibly in the document rather than chosen silently. ## Defence pack — generated at claim close, and verifiable by an outsider

`12804317757` · 6 comments

### 26 August 2026, 13:49:55 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5493112626

Drafted — O4 — The defence pack (specification + pack template v1)

Specification at §2–§9, the pack template drafted in full at §10, including the VERIFY.txt that ships inside every pack.

Contents: twelve sections. The seven named on the board — signed valuation, every source with its retrieval timestamp, the reconciliation result, the surveyor's overrides and reasoning, the CTA sign-off, the s.203 position, and the client's declarations — plus five the Phase 3 data layer already produces and it would be negligent to omit: the anchor quarantine log, the conflict register (inside §3), the document extraction and egress record, the rate basis with any hybrid calculation, and the issued client-facing documents byte for byte. The quarantine log earns its place: the strongest attack on a valuation-led claim is that the valuation was reverse-engineered from a target, and a log showing the surveyor's figures were committed and hashed before the estimate was released answers that with a record rather than an assurance.

Generated automatically at close, and close is defined — at issue for a positive claim, at issue for a reasoned negative (same pack, same template), and at abandonment for an abandoned file, sealed and marked incomplete. Generation cannot be waived or deferred; a missing section blocks the close, in the same posture the reconciliation assertion takes at signature.

On immutability, the specification says plainly what it does not claim. Nothing makes bytes unchangeable; what is achievable is that any change is detectable, attributable and dated by someone who does not trust us. Five mechanisms: content addressing, a manifest whose digest is the pack digest, a hash-chained append-only ledger (the anchor-quarantine construction reused, so one verification routine covers both), external anchoring by three independent routes, and write-once storage with separated duties. The anchoring is the load-bearing part, and its strength is not cryptographic — it is that the pack digest is printed on the client report and the accountant cover and countersigned by the reviewing CTA, so the corroborating copies sit with parties we cannot reach.

Verification is designed against one test: can a competent third party who does not trust us and has no access to our systems establish whether the pack is what it says it is. Six steps, standard tools, no software of ours, procedure shipped inside the pack. Three outcomes — VERIFIED, ALTERED, INCOMPLETE — and the third is deliberately not the second: a tool that collapses "an anchor is unreachable" into "this was tampered with" will eventually accuse us of tampering with our own honest files.

Corrections supersede, never edit: new sealed version, errata record, ledger entry linking the digests, original still verifiable. A correction that leaves no trace is indistinguishable from a cover-up and will be treated as one.

Draft — requires CTA review. Six open items in §9. The highest-priority one is not technical: the retention period, and how a retention lock that cannot be shortened is reconciled with erasure rights in the privacy notice. That is a DPO and CTA decision and it must be settled before the first pack is sealed, because the lock cannot be shortened afterwards. Also recommends anchoring to two independent timestamping authorities from the outset — small marginal cost, otherwise unrecoverable failure mode.

Item 12819676756 (the surveyor's valuation report template) was not touched. §4.1 and §4.4 should be re-read against it once a signing surveyor is appointed — particularly whether capturing override reasoning at the point of entry is workable in their actual field process, which is a question only they can answer.

<p><b>Opened by Phase 113b on 9 September 2026.</b> The full question, with the worked example and an answer box, is in CAPREBATE QUESTIONS, section two, under <i>Three that are judgement rather than law</i> — quoted by its title: <b>"Is 'roughly break-even' enough profit for the relief to bite on?"</b></p>
<p><b>In one line.</b> The six-screen assessment offers four answers on the current year — profitable, loss-making, roughly break-even, not sure. The engine's own profit question has three, and bundles break-even in with loss-making. Which of the three is a break-even answer?</p>
<p><b>Nothing stops without it, and the build is in the safe state meanwhile.</b> A break-even answer is treated as not given at all, which behaves exactly as "not sure" does: no gate opens, nothing is asserted, and our own missing-facts panel goes on asking. So the cost of the question staying open is that we pester a client who has already answered — not a wrong figure.</p>
<p><b>Why it was not simply decided.</b> The engine's own wording points at "no". Against that, the short form deliberately offers break-even as a separate option beside loss-making, so a client who picked it was distinguishing itself from a loss — and reading it as "no" makes us print "insufficient taxable profit confirmed", which is more than a break-even business has confirmed. That is a judgement about a business, not a reading of a statute.</p>

Covers all five subitems: pricing (12552667427), core values (12552667428), vision (12552667430), mission (12552667431), budget and forecasts (12552667432).

FIRST — the two decisions this depends on are still open, and I checked rather than assumed.
• Fee basis (12804368154) — no decision recorded. Modelled BOTH branches, fork marked throughout.
• Minimum fee (12830205390) — no decision recorded. Carried as a recommendation, not an input.
• Advise vs support (12804327781) — your 25 Aug steer is on the item but the options paper's request to confirm what you meant has not been answered. Treated the hybrid as base case and flagged what changes under pure advice.

SECOND — no surveyor or CTA quotes exist. Items 12818132946, 12818112998, 12830181616 and 12830205392 are all unstarted. The estimates carry forward and that is stated on the face of the plan, in the opening section, because every threshold and margin in the document moves with them.

THE HEADLINE, and it is not the one the options papers imply.
Those papers concluded Option B plus a sector minimum makes the unit economics work. I re-derived that independently and it holds. But neither paper carried a founder salary or a working-capital lag, and both change the picture:

• 24-month net WITHOUT a founder salary: +£115,575.
• 24-month net WITH a £60,000 founder salary: −£4,425, and cumulative break-even is not reached inside 24 months.
• Add a two-month gap between paying the surveyor and collecting the fee and the deepest cash trough is −£147,183 at month 17. That is the funding requirement — nearly five times the £30,865 a model without those two items shows. It is the single most important number in the document and neither paper contains it, because neither was asked to.
• 50.9 jobs a year — 4.2 a month — just to cover overhead plus a founder salary. The ramp does not reach that until around month 14.

THREE FINDINGS THAT CORRECT OR EXTEND THE PAPERS

1. Supported living is not a purchase-route business at all. The estimate engine spec §6 gives it NO purchase yield band — refurb/fit-out only, at 10–25% of the COMMUNAL base after the common-parts fraction, and a single dwelling stops the assessment. It is named as one of five sectors and it is not a fifth of the business. I have attributed zero revenue to it and recommended planning it as a credibility and referral-protection line. This is the first place I would challenge the current sector framing.

2. In our favour — the minimum-fee paper says a floor cannot see a loss-making middle band, and gives a £1.5m company-held care home as the example. Tested against that paper's own recommended minimums at 100 jobs/yr, that band does not exist: the £1.5m care home's 5% fee is £5,625, below the £7,500 minimum, so the minimum applies and it makes £1,250. I checked all four sectors and both claimant types — the minimums cover loaded cost in every case.

3. Not in our favour — that reverses entirely at year-one volume. At 25 jobs/yr the recommended minimums are SHORT of loaded cost in every sector: dental by £390, GP by £1,630, care home by £550, private hospital by £1,010. At the 16 jobs my ramp gives in year one the overhead alone is £3,750 a job against the £600 the papers assume. The minimums are right for the business at scale and wrong for it in year one. Two options set out; I would set them at £5,000/£7,500 and fund the ~£10–20k year-one shortfall deliberately as a cost of market entry — but it should be a recorded decision, not a discovery.

One more worth flagging: once the minimum fee is in, claimant type stops mattering. ## Tax Implication Summary — SOLE TRADER variant (personal-allowance restriction + payments-on-account recalculation). Company variant drafted 16 Sep 2026, unsigned, attached here

`12830183379` · 5 comments

### 25 August 2026, 13:35:15 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5489405657

Done. Full draft: Tax Implication Summary — SOLE TRADER variant. Built to the house structure in Build-Prep-Report-Pack-and-Hand-off-Specification §4.2 (part two of the accountant report), with the mandatory s.203 section per §4.3.

⚠️ This needs a human CTA sanity-check before it reaches a client or an accountant. The board has no formal review gate for group 06 reports — unlike the Rulebooks, which sit at "Awaiting CTA review" — so nothing else will catch it. It is a document an accountant would file from.

What makes the sole-trader variant genuinely different from the company version, and it is not cosmetic. Five of the most valuable reliefs in the code are corporation tax only and must not carry over from the company template: full expensing (100% FYA), the 50% special-rate FYA, the super-deduction, the Freeport/Investment Zone ECA, and Land Remediation Relief. §5.2 tables them with authority. A company template reused for a sole trader overstates the claim. Going the other way, the new 40% FYA under CAA 2001 s.45U (FA 2026, expenditure on or after 1 January 2026) is expressly available to unincorporated businesses — the opposite of the full expensing position — so it is the sole trader's main accelerator alongside AIA.

The personal-allowance restriction works in two opposite directions, and §7 covers both because the item names only one. Upward: the £100k–£125,140 taper makes income there worth 60p in the pound, not 45p — Rulebook I I-12 says in terms it must be modelled, not rounded, and on a dental principal's income the claim very often lands there. (67.5% for a Scottish taxpayer, and note Scottish status turns on where the person lives, not where the property is.) Downward: allowances that push income below £12,570 are relieved at 0% and the allowance is use-it-or-lose-it. The fix is statutory and clean — CAA 2001 s.56(5): "a person claiming a writing-down allowance may require the allowance to be reduced to a specified amount" — so the claim is restricted and the balance stays in the pool. I've left I-Q2 open by stating both the conservative 45% figure and the taper effect rather than silently picking one.

Payments on account (§8) — three separate effects, and a conflict with our own D4 decision. The amendment re-bases the prior year's POA under s.59A(4A); next year's POA fall automatically; and a s.59A(3)/(4) reduction claim can cut them now. The trap: if the reduction proves excessive, interest runs from the original due dates as if they had never been reduced — so do not reduce on the strength of an unfiled claim. The conflict: D4 excludes Class 4 NIC from client-facing figures, but the s.59A relevant amount includes Class 4, so a reduction claim computed on income tax alone is wrong and under-reduces. I have not verified the Class 4 limb from primary source — flagged as ST-Q3 and the document tells the preparer to have the accountant compute POA on their own figures until it is settled.

Losses (§9) branch on trade vs property business and getting it backwards reverses the advice. Trade: ITA 2007 s.64/s.72/s.83. Property business: the default is carry-forward, but s.120 gives relief against general income where the loss has a "capital allowances connection", capped by s.122 at the net capital allowances — which is exactly a Ledgerstone-generated loss. A preparer assuming property losses always carry forward will defer relief that is available now. Both routes are capped by ITA 2007 s.24A at the greater of £50,000 or 25% of adjusted total income.

Two gaps in Rulebook I this surfaced (ST-Q4). Rule 7.1 forbids stating a figure that is not in the rate table, but this document needs the s.24A cap and the Class 4 NIC rates, and Rulebook I carries neither. I cited s.24A direct to legislation.gov.uk and flagged it rather than either breaching rule 7.1 silently or omitting a limit the accountant must apply. Rulebook I should absorb both.

A contradiction between two of our own artefacts, flagged not papered over (§4.3, ST-Q1). The s.12ABA write-up §5.2 reads as saying never-pooled expenditure is dead once the window closes; Rulebook A §3 says it can be pooled now in a current open return. Both are right about different things — Sch 1AB Case A(c) blocks forcing an allocation into a closed year via overpayment relief; CAA s.58(3) permits allocation into an open current year, which is a fresh claim and not an overpayment relief claim at all. Stated explicitly because the two documents read as contradictory and a preparer could take the wrong one.

Assumptions stated in the document rather than chosen silently: seven of them tabled at the top, the load-bearing ones being that this is an individual not a partnership (ST-A1), that we have determined trade vs property business (ST-A2 — the largest branch in the document), rest-of-UK not Scottish (ST-A3), still-owns-the-property (ST-A4 — a hard gate, not a detail), not a dwelling-house under s.35 with no FHL route after 6 April 2025 (ST-A5), and Class 4 excluded per D4 so the figures are conservative, not neutral (ST-A6). Also open: ST-Q2, whether the CA23222 hybrid WDA rate bites at 6 April 2026 for a claimant with a non-5-April accounting date after basis period reform — I did not resolve it and the document warns the preparer not to assume it never applies.

Windows. TMA s.9ZA gives 12 months after the filing date, so as at today the only year a sole trader can still amend is 2024-25, closing 31 January 2027 — the same runway as the partnership. Overpayment relief is not a four-year fallback (Sch 1AB Case A(2)(b),(c)); any material offering sole traders a four-year horizon is an over-promise.

Phase 131, 14 September 2026 — sole trader tax summary: Class 4 in payments on account verified, the loss cap made precise, and a new section on when relief becomes cash

What was wrong. Checked against the attached file before changing anything, and all four points were still there:

* The summary said it had not verified whether payments on account include Class 4 National Insurance.
* It said the rates table did not carry the Class 4 rates or the cap on sideways loss relief, so it had cited them outside the table.
* It described the interest on an over-reduced payment on account as running "as if the payments had never been reduced". It also said a claim made "carelessly or deliberately" attracts a penalty. Neither is what the statute says.
* It said nothing about when a claim actually turns into cash.
What changed and where. Every source below was read on 13 September 2026 on legislation.gov.uk or gov.uk.

* Section 8.4. Now verified from primary law. The Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992, section 16(1)(b), applies the payments-on-account rules to Class 4 as if it were income tax. gov.uk's payments-on-account page says the same. So a reduction claim worked out on income tax alone under-reduces. The advice that the accountant computes payments on account on their own figures stays until the tax adviser has reviewed the summary.
* Section 8. Adds when no payments on account are due at all: a previous bill under £1,000, or more than 80 per cent paid at source.
* Section 8.3. Interest and penalty wording now follows the Taxes Management Act 1970. Interest runs on what each payment should have been: the lower of the original payment and the reduced payment plus half the balancing amount. A penalty applies only where the statement was made fraudulently or negligently.
* New section 8.5, when the relief turns into cash. Amending 2024-25 before 31 January 2027 repays that year's tax and re-bases the 2025-26 payments on account. Pooling in a return not yet filed shows up at that year's 31 January balancing payment and in the next year's payments on account. A reduction claim brings the effect forward to the payment dates, at an interest risk. It notes, without settling, that a reduced payment on account puts money back even on a route the document calls "not a refund".
* Section 9.3. Now says which reliefs the Income Tax Act 2007 section 24A cap reaches: trade loss relief, early trade losses relief and property loss relief. It does not reach the capital allowances themselves or losses carried forward. One carve-out in that section would take relief set against profits of the same trade outside the cap. It would make relief bigger, so it is not applied, and it is logged as a new question for the adviser, ST-Q5.
* Cross-references. The Class 4 rates and the cap are now cited to the rates table, which gained them the same day. The assumptions, the rate-basis table, open questions ST-Q3 and ST-Q4, the sources and the version line (now 1.1) are updated to match.
Already right, not changed. Section 4.2 already says overpayment relief is not a four-year fallback. Any material offering a sole trader a four-year horizon is an over-promise. The website still carries such a promise; that has been reported for whoever owns the site file. Nothing in the benefit figures changes: Class 4 stays out of them, as the board decided.

### 15 September 2026, 12:37:05 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5548459245

Phase 132a, 15 September 2026 - section 4.1 no longer calls 2024-25 the only year a sole trader can amend.

What was wrong. It said that, as at 25 August 2026, "the only year a sole trader can still amend is 2024-25". That is the earliest year still open, not the only one.

What changed. The sentence now says "earliest". A dated note explains the rule from the Taxes Management Act 1970, section 9ZA, read on legislation.gov.uk today:

* An amendment can be made up to twelve months after the filing date.

* The filing date is set by the year, not by when the return went in, so a 2025-26 return already filed can be amended until 31 January 2028.

* A year whose return is not yet filed needs no amendment: the claim goes into the return.

* A late notice to file moves the filing date, and the window with it.

So which years are open on a given day depends on each year's filing date and on whether its return has been filed. Nothing else in the summary changed.

## Tax Implication Summary — PARTNERSHIP variant (claim in the partnership return; the benefit reaches partners through the profit share)

`12830205673` · 7 comments

### 24 August 2026, 13:34:26 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5485696809

<p><b>The s.12ABA read this was waiting on is done</b> (item 12851600794, Done) — write-up: <a href="https://seveneightsixmediagroup.monday.com/docs/18427872378">OPEN GAP CLOSED — TMA 1970 s.12ABA</a>. This variant can now be written in full.</p><p><b>What the summary must say.</b> The amendment window is 12 months after the <i>filing date</i>, not after delivery, so filing late does not extend it — for a partnership of individuals that is 31 January of Year 2 plus 12 months. <b>As at today, the only open year for an ordinary GP or dental partnership is 2024-25, closing 31 January 2027.</b> A partnership with any corporate member runs on a different basis entirely (s.12AA(5B)/(5C)), so the report must not print the 31 January date for a mixed partnership. Only the nominated partner who made and delivered the return may amend it. Under s.12ABA(3) the officer <i>must</i> amend each partner's own return, so partners do not file their own amendments and their personal windows are irrelevant — and <b>former partners for the amended period receive adjustments too</b>, in the profit-sharing ratios for that year, which the report and engagement letter should both say plainly.</p><p><b>The commercially important finding:</b> overpayment relief does <i>not</i> provide a four-year fallback. TMA Sch 1AB para 2 Case A(2)(b) and (c) exclude a mistake consisting of failing to make a claim or election, and — in terms — failing to allocate expenditure to a capital allowances pool. So the 12-month s.12ABA window is the only deadline for a partnership. If any client-facing material offers partnerships a four-year retrospective horizon, that is an over-promise and should be treated as a defect.</p>
