Done. Full draft: Tax Implication Summary — PARTNERSHIP variant. Built on Rulebook A v2 §4a as the item specifies, plus the s.12ABA write-up (item 12851600794, confirmed Done before I started), Rulebook I v1 + Addendum 1, and the report pack spec §4.2/§4.3 for structure. Companion to the SOLE TRADER variant (12830183379), also delivered today.

⚠️ This needs a human CTA sanity-check before it reaches a client or an accountant. No formal review gate exists for group 06 reports, unlike the Rulebooks — nothing else will catch it, and this is a document an accountant would file an SA800 from.

The organising idea. A partnership claim happens at two levels, and almost every error here comes from collapsing them: the claim, the pools and the decision how much to claim are partnership-level; the benefit, the rates, the personal allowance, payments on account and losses are all partner-level. That split runs from §7 to §10.

The finding I'd most want you to see (§5.2) — it isn't in Rulebook A or the s.12ABA note. CAA 2001 s.38A(3) defines a "qualifying person" for AIA as an individual, a partnership of which all the members are individuals, or a company. A partnership with a corporate member is none of those three, so it gets no AIA at all — not reduced, not shared. That removes up to £1m of immediate relief. Combined with §4.2, a corporate member changes two things at once: the amendment deadline basis and the availability of AIA. It hits exactly our structures — a GP partnership with a PropCo partner, a dental partnership inside a body corporate group, an LLP with a corporate member. It should be a mandatory intake field, not an assumption. The counterweight is that the new 40% FYA (s.45U) is available to mixed partnerships for both member types, and a corporate partner can access Land Remediation Relief for its share (CIRD60050) — so a mixed partnership is differently placed, not uniformly worse off.

The windows are in, exactly as the s.12ABA note establishes them. 12 months after the filing date, so filing late does not extend it; as at today the only open year for an ordinary GP or dental partnership is 2024-25, closing 31 January 2027. The mixed-partnership branch runs on s.12AA(5B)/(5C) instead and the report must not print a 31 January date for it. Only the nominated partner who made and delivered the return may amend. Under s.12ABA(3) HMRC must amend each partner's own return, so partners do not file their own amendments and their personal s.9ZA windows are irrelevant — the partnership window is the binding constraint. Overpayment relief is not a four-year fallback (Sch 1AB Case A(2)(b),(c)).

Former partners (§8) are given their own section, not a footnote. s.12ABA(3) reaches "each of the partners" for the amended period, and profit-sharing changes since then do not redirect the money — so a 2024-25 claim pays someone who left in 2025, in their 2024-25 share, and the continuing partners have no tax-system route to recover it. Two things follow that belong in the engagement letter: the partnership should see the PSR table at proposal stage so it knows how much benefit will leave the practice and to whom; and on a contingent fee the partnership pays a fee on money going to ex-partners. PT-Q4 carries A-10-Q4 forward.

The hardest thing in the document, and it's genuinely new (§9.2). CAA s.56(5) lets the claim be restricted so relief isn't wasted below the personal allowance. For a sole trader that's a clean optimisation. For a partnership it is a compromise: the person claiming is the partnership, but a restriction calibrated to preserve one partner's allowance can take relief from another sitting in the 60% taper zone, where the same pound is worth three times as much — and there is no mechanism to give different partners different allowance treatment on the same pool. I've modelled it as options with the per-partner outcome shown, to be put to the partnership rather than optimised silently for the average. PT-Q8 asks whose decision that is and how it should be recorded — it's a governance question as much as a technical one.

On rates: partners are not on one rate. A partnership with one partner in the taper zone and one below the higher-rate threshold has identical profit shares worth 60% and 20%. And Scottish taxpayer status turns on where each partner lives, not where the practice is, so one partnership can contain both bases and the Scottish taper band is 67.5%. A blended practice rate isn't a simplification, it's wrong for every partner.

Also carried in: s.42(7)(c) lists CAA s.183 as well as s.3, so the incoming-lessee election goes in the partnership return too — load-bearing because GP practices reach the fixtures rules through leases far more than freeholds, and s.183 is the gateway to s.199 rather than s.198. But the s.198/199 election itself is outside s.42 (s.201(5)(a)), so there is no s.42(9) correction route — cross-referenced to today's Disposal Note.

Eight open questions logged (§14), and three things I did not verify and said so: the Class 4 NIC limb of the s.59A relevant amount (PT-Q5 — it conflicts with D4, since benefit figures exclude Class 4 but payments on account cannot); the ITA 2007 s.103C non-active partner cap (PT-Q6 — s.110/s.111 are stated accurately, s.103C is flagged); and the basis-period-reform interaction with the CA23222 hybrid WDA rate (PT-Q3). PT-Q2 flags the same Rulebook A / s.12ABA §5.2 tension I raised on the sole trader item — Case A(c) blocks forcing an allocation into a closed year via overpayment relief, but s.58(3) still permits allocation into an open current year; both artefacts are right about different things and a preparer could take the wrong one. PT-Q7 is the same Rulebook I gap: rule 7.1 forbids stating figures not in the rate table, but this document needs the s.24A cap and the NIC rates and Rulebook I carries neither.

What was wrong. It said that, as at 25 August 2026, "the only open year for an ordinary unincorporated GP or dental partnership is 2024-25". That is the earliest open year, not the only one.

What changed. The sentence now says "earliest". A dated note explains the rule from the Taxes Management Act 1970, section 12ABA, read on legislation.gov.uk today:

* A partnership return can be amended up to twelve months after the filing date.

* A year whose return is not yet filed needs no amendment: the claim goes into the return.

* A late notice to file moves the filing date, and the window with it.

* A partnership with a company partner is on a different filing date, as section 4.2 already says.

## Caprebate BLD-T3 — BUILD: four-document request to the ACCOUNTANT at engagement, in parallel with survey

`12804375390` · 3 comments

### 26 August 2026, 13:40:23 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5493074810

Drafted — T3 — The four-document request to the client's accountant (letter + internal note)

Three parts: the decision on which four documents and why (§2–§4), the sendable letter (§5), and the internal note on what each document sets and what happens when it does not arrive (§6–§10).

The four: (1) the client's own capital allowances computations and fixed asset register; (2) the CPSE replies; (3) the sale contract with every schedule; (4) the filed return and computation for the acquisition period. Non-overlapping by design — each answers a question none of the others can.

Two findings worth the read. Documents 1 and 2 are not the same question. The CPSE tells us about the seller's pooling, which is the s.187A condition and decides whether a claim exists; the client's own computations tell us about our client's claim history, which decides double-claim risk, gives the pool opening balances the forward schedule is built on, and is the only evidence base for the mandatory s.203 section. A file without document 1 is a file that cannot complete a section that may not be issued blank. And we ask for the contract, not for "the election" — the drafted £1 election case found it at schedule 6, and an accountant asked for a free-standing election will correctly reply that there was none, which is the most expensive wrong answer available on the file.

The letter is built to be finished in under fifteen minutes: four asks, a per-item "if you don't hold it" route, a paste-back reply block, an explicit "we are not asking you to review anything", and the paragraph that makes the referral channel work — we do not file and we do not compete. It states no rate and uses no refund language, neither being appropriate at engagement before the route is known.

Non-arrival is handled as UNKNOWN, never nil (invariant I-1), with a day-0-to-day-25 ladder, a forwardable script for the client, and a named consequence per document — including that a missing contract blocks signature via assertion AS-3, which is correct behaviour and not a system fault.

Draft — requires CTA review. Five open items in §10, chiefly the treatment of a "never pooled" CPSE reply as sufficient evidence where the sum is material, and what may be stated in the s.203 section when the client's own claim history cannot be established. Also recommends making the associated company count a mandatory field here, which would close Rulebook I question I-Q3 for corporate claimants.

`12818978746` · 3 comments

### 26 August 2026, 13:53:28 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5493127867

Drafted — Stage 2 client document upload screen (specification + drafted screen copy v1)

The ten subitems turned into the actual screen: the client-facing copy for every row (§3), the conditional display rules (§4), the funding question in its strong form (§5), the "I don't have this" control (§6), and the internal note on what each document yields and what happens when it does not arrive (§7–§10).

Ordered by evidential value per minute of client effort, which is not the same as evidential value. The fire risk assessment and the O&M manuals lead — richest fixture evidence in the set, on site, findable in ten minutes, and no third party involved. The purchase contract and CPSE replies sit third: they are the highest-stakes documents in the system and a client usually cannot produce them without a phone call they can't make until Monday. That ordering is only safe because T3 pursues them through the accountant and solicitor in parallel — if T3 is ever dropped, this must be revisited. Flagged in the doc.

Two design points worth noting. The "I don't have this" button is schema §0.3 surfaced as UI — it writes UNKNOWN with a reason, where doing nothing leaves no cell at all. "Asked and not known" and "never asked" are different states and the screen is what makes them different in practice: a client who told us they have no asbestos register is never chased again; one who closed the tab is. And the footer says outright which documents are optional — three can change whether there is a claim at all, the rest only improve accuracy. Telling a client that seven of ten are optional is what gets the three that matter uploaded.

Row 10 is conditional on the funding question, so the question does the work: it is asked in the long form covering grants, NHS premises funding, landlord contributions and connected-party payments, because the short form misses exactly the two that arise most in this sector. A missing funding agreement is the one place a gap must not be worked around — it is the only over-claim direction on the screen.

One finding worth raising separately. The document pipeline carries extraction specs for seven types; six are on this screen. Four documents here have no spec at all — the sale contract and election, the CPSE replies, the grant agreement, and the building regs completion certificate — and three of those four are the highest-consequence documents in the set. Human reading is the right answer for now (these are legal instruments where the question is whether the document does a legal thing, and an extraction error on an election is a wrong claim, not a confidence score), but it must be a recorded decision with a route: a HUMAN_READ_ONLY flag so an upload cannot silently go unprocessed, structured capture forms producing the same fields at the same grade, and reviewer identity into the defence pack. Recommend this is raised on the board as a build item in its own right rather than left inside this document.

Draft — requires CTA review. Five open items in §10, including CTA sight of the wording on rows 7, 8 and 10, which are correct and blunt in equal measure.

## Accountant cover note — show the work without embarrassing them

`12804375491` · 4 comments

### 26 August 2026, 13:44:50 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5493090912

Drafted — O3 — Accountant partner cover (specification + drafted cover v1)

Specification (§2–§6, §8–§11) plus the cover drafted in full (§7) on the care-home W2 company case, so it reads against the same worked example as the client report.

The governing design rule is that the cover must be forwardable. Every sentence is written as though the client will read it, because sooner or later one will. That rule is what keeps §G usable: a defence the client can see through is worse than none.

Nine mandatory sections. §C (what we did not do) sits deliberately before §D (what to file) — an accountant checks a specialist's edges before reading their checklist, and answering that first is what makes the checklist readable. §D and §E may not be blank; §E is the s.203 position, completed here as "no notification appears to be required" with the issue date on its face, and the note that the evidence for that answer is the capital allowances history requested at engagement in T3.

§G is the section this item exists for. Four factual reasons — the split does not exist in the accounting records; creating it is a chartered valuation, not an accounting exercise; two of the four determinative documents sit on the conveyancing file; and nothing was lost except acceleration, which would have required commissioning a survey at the time and is a client spending decision. Then three sentences drafted in the accountant's own voice, the verbatim line we will use if the client asks us the same question (so there is no daylight), and an explicit list of what we will never say — starting with "most accountants miss this", which buys one sale at the cost of the channel and is banned in this document, in the client report and in conversation.

One rule worth CTA attention: where the honest answer is uncomfortable, §G states the facts and offers no manufactured defence. There will be files where the accountant could reasonably have flagged it. Supplying an excuse they cannot support puts them in a worse position than silence, because they may repeat it.

Also carries: the no-claim variant (§6 — the cover that matters most, because it confirms the accountant's judgement rather than testing it), claimant-type variants of the filing block with the personal-allowance restriction and payments-on-account for individuals and the profit-share dependency for partnerships, the hard Scottish-rate gate, and the hybrid-rate note where a period straddles the WDA change.

Draft — requires CTA review. Five open items in §11, chiefly the acceleration paragraph in §G and the open-ended free enquiry support offered at §H, which is the right commercial promise and needs a defined boundary before it is made in writing.

## Build a room-by-room list of what equipment sits in each type of room

`12819698557` · 5 comments

### 26 August 2026, 07:17:46 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5492259720

What this is
A missing piece of the model. It needs a surveyor's input, which is why it is not Claude work.

In plain English
Our system currently thinks in totals — so much electrical work, so much heating. Surveyors do not work that way. They walk a building room by room and record what is in each one: this bedroom has a call point and an emergency light; this bathroom has an assisted bath and a hoist; this plant room has the boiler.

We need a list of room types for each sector, and what equipment is typically found in each.

Where the information can come from without a visit
• The regulator tells us the number of beds
• Planning drawings show the layout
• The fire risk assessment lists alarms, emergency lighting and fire doors room by room — every care home has one and it is kept up to date
• The energy certificate reveals what the heating and ventilation systems are

Why it matters
Without this, a surveyor cannot check our work in the way they naturally think, and we cannot turn a floor area into countable quantities. A related task on this board depends entirely on this one.

Original wording: "S8 — ROOM SCHEDULE MODEL: schedule of accommodation with fixtures per room type. Derive from bed count (regulator) + planning drawings + fire risk assessment + EPC servicing. Surveyors work room by room, not by element total."

### 29 August 2026, 08:23:54 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5502098543

The straw man is now attached to this item as a file (strawman-room-equipment-schedule.md) — it previously existed on one machine's disk only. Fixed 29 Aug.

Phase 10 populated the Dental section of this schedule for a specific (fictional) property (item 12818132946, Document 3) and closed three of its blanks without needing a surveyor.

F-11 — the decontamination room is not a client assertion. HTM 01-05 defines two compliance tiers, Essential Quality Requirements and Best Practice, and a dedicated, zoned decontamination room used for that purpose only, with restricted access, is the Best Practice design expectation for primary dental care. A CQC-registered practice fitted out in 2024 with no separate decontamination area is the exception requiring evidence, not the default. The residual question is which tier, not whether the room exists. The same move should be attempted per sector.

F-12 — the amalgam separator is a legal test, answerable from one client question. Retained Regulation (EU) 2017/852 Article 10(4) (read at source) requires separators, from 1 January 2019, in dental facilities "in which dental amalgam is used or dental amalgam fillings or teeth containing such fillings are removed", at 95% retention. A practice that places no amalgam but removes existing restorations is still caught. That moves LS-DEN-010 from surveyor-blank to gate-answerable. (Separately confirmed: SI 2025/1189 applies to Northern Ireland only — there is no Great Britain amalgam-use ban.)

The wider point about absent rows. Two rows on the worked case were marked present_flag = FALSE with a stated basis rather than left blank — sedation piping and sprinklers. A row correctly determined absent is worth as much to a surveyor as one correctly determined present, and costs them nothing to confirm. Most of the taxonomy is not present at any given property, so this is a large part of what "closer to one-click" actually looks like. ## Turn floor area and a room list into countable quantities

`12819686328` · 5 comments

### 27 August 2026, 09:47:56 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5496127633

Phase 9 — a STRAW MAN is attached for the surveyor. NOT Done.

File: phase9/strawman-s9-quantity-derivation.md

Why it could be drafted now

This item was blocked only behind the room-equipment schedule (item 12819698557), which was drafted in the same pass. The two documents are built to fit together — this one consumes that one. The mechanism is mine to design; the numbers are the surveyor's to supply, and they are left blank.

What it sets out

An 8-stage derivation chain from gross internal floor area + room schedule to countable quantities, in the common real-world case where the client has no fire plan and no O&M manual: floor area → room schedule → corroboration → sector room-count aggregation → per-row resolution → grading → UNKNOWN handling → output. Stated so a developer could implement it.

The honest part, which is the useful part

It classifies what is genuinely automatable versus what is not. Only two inputs are truly API-derivable today (the ODS dispensing flag and regulator registration, both grade A). Every density coefficient and every per-item quantity is irreducibly client-asserted or surveyor-only.

It works the schema's grade-inheritance rule through explicitly and reaches an uncomfortable conclusion worth stating plainly: the schema already fixes quantity at grade D regardless of derivation path, so this model can never make a quantity engine-ready. What it can do is give the surveyor something to confirm rather than nothing. That is a smaller claim than the item title implies, and it is the true one.

The UNKNOWN rule, applied to quantities

Never impute a plausible count — imputing inflates the claim. Missing data must produce an under-count, not a guess. This is the quantity analogue of the schema's rule that UNKNOWN never routes to the branch producing the larger claim.

What is left blank for the surveyor

14 named-but-empty coefficients, RD-01 to RD-14 — each with its name, its unit, and what it multiplies, and an empty value cell. For example "fire-detection points per 100m² GIA, no fire plan". I did not invent any of them.

Also included

7 failure modes with guards, and 7 explicit stop-and-hand-to-survey conditions — where the model must stop rather than push through.

Next step

Goes to the surveyor with the room schedule. The 14 coefficients are on the agenda for the free 45-minute call (item 12830181616).

<p><b>Deliverable:</b> <code>04-phase-work/phase9/s9-quantity-derivation-v2.md</code> (authoritative). Completion record and surveyor brief in the Document column.</p>
<p><b>The finding. RD-01 was not wrong in value — it was wrong in shape, and that is worse.</b> A wrong value gets corrected by the first surveyor who looks at it. A wrong shape gets <i>filled in</i> by them: they supply a number for the question we asked, not the question we should have asked.</p>
<p>RD-01 counted fire-detection points per m² of floor area. Tested on a real 268 m² dental fit-out, the area method gives <b>2.4–4.8 points</b>; a room-by-room count gives <b>15–19</b>. That is not a factor-of-two disagreement a better coefficient would close. It is four to six times, the same way every time, because <b>detection follows compartmentation, not floor area</b> — a 14 m² surgery needs its own detector whether the building is 268 m² or 2,680. An area density derived from spacing implicitly assumes an open floor plate; healthcare buildings are heavily cellularised.</p>
<p><b>And it generalises.</b> Any device whose real driver is "one per enclosed space" has the same defect if modelled per m² — emergency lighting, thermostats, door contacts, extract grilles, call points.</p>
<p><b>What v2 does.</b> Room-driven is now the primary method. Area-density is <b>demoted to a labelled sanity floor</b> — a lower bound that says "fewer than this would be surprising" — and the model refuses to emit one as a result: <code>resolution_path</code> has no <code>area_density</code> value at all. The type system enforces the demotion; a comment would not have. The readings are kept, not deleted — deleting them loses a genuine check.</p>
<ul>
<li>RD-01 split into <b>RD-01a</b> (room-driven, primary) and <b>RD-01b</b> (area-density, floor only). RD-13 demoted the same way — supported-living common parts are cellular too.</li>
<li>New <b>Stage 6 sanity-floor check</b>: a room count <i>below</i> the area floor means the room schedule is incomplete. Flagged — never silently replaced by the floor figure.</li>
<li>Stage 2 gains <code>enclosed</code> and <code>typical_area_m2</code>. <code>enclosed</code> is what makes the room-driven method work and it did not exist at v1.</li>
<li><code>bed count</code> with an unknown room schedule now resolves to <b>UNRESOLVED</b>, where v1 sent it to area-density. <b>Fewer rows now resolve. That is the point.</b></li>
<li>RD-15 added (emergency lighting) — blocked behind the taxonomy gap: the row has no home yet.</li>
<li>14 coefficients become 15. <b>No value supplied for any of them.</b> What changed is which question each blank asks.</li>
</ul>
<p><b>RD-04 stays open, and it is open by purchase, not by judgement.</b> Data-outlet density lives in structured-cabling standards we do not hold. We are deliberately not modelling around it: data outlets genuinely are partly area-driven and partly room-driven and we do not know the mix, and reasoning our way to a number when a published answer exists is how a repo acquires an invented figure that later looks sourced. ## Build the surveyor's valuation report template, with the surveyor

`12819676756` · 8 comments

### 26 August 2026, 07:18:03 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5492260069

What this is
The surveyor's own report template. The instruction here is important: build it with the signing surveyor, not for them.

In plain English
This is the document the surveyor signs. It sets out how the purchase price was split between land, building and claimable equipment, and it is the foundation everything else rests on — the accountant's pack quotes it, the client report summarises it, and if HMRC ever asks questions, this is what gets produced.

How the work splits
Roughly 80% of it fills itself in from data we already hold — the address, the price, the floor area, the cost build-up. The remaining 20% is the surveyor's professional judgement and their signed declaration. That part is theirs and must not be pre-written for them.

Why it must come before the other reports
Everything downstream cites this document. Building the summaries first and this one afterwards means rewriting the summaries.

Why it is blocked
There is no appointed surveyor yet. A template built without one would be a guess at what a professional is prepared to put their name to.

Original wording: "S11 — CAVR template: build WITH the signing surveyor, not for them. ~80% auto-populates; narrative and declaration are theirs. Everything downstream cites it — build before the other reports."

### 27 August 2026, 09:48:34 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5496128405

Phase 9 — a STRAW MAN is attached for the surveyor. NOT Done, and this item stays owned by the Surveyor.

File: phase9/strawman-surveyor-valuation-report-template.md

Built to the board's instruction: WITH the surveyor, not for them

The board says roughly 80% auto-populates. I built that 80% — the data-driven sections that fill themselves from what we already hold — and left the rest genuinely empty: the narrative, the qualifying percentages, the element splits, and the signed declaration, each with a note saying it is the surveyor's call.

That distinction is the whole task. A pre-populated skeleton with judgement left blank honours the instruction. A completed template with guessed qualifying percentages would violate it — it would invite a surveyor to rubber-stamp numbers nobody stands behind, and put their PII signature on our arithmetic.

Structure: 23 sections, each marked one of three states.

• [AUTO] — 5 sections. Every field names the exact Consolidated Schema field_id, its provenance code and its confidence grade.

• [MIXED] — 11 sections. Auto-populated inputs presented for the surveyor to accept, adjust or reject, with the adjustment mechanism shown and the decision itself blank.

• [SURVEYOR] — 7 sections. Genuinely empty, with the question they are answering stated.

37 surveyor-blank markers in total. The fixture schedule (schema §1.G) has its columns auto-populated and the qualifying-percentage column empty for every row.

═══ On the 80% claim — I checked it rather than asserting it, and it needs qualifying ═══

Two honest numbers, both in the document:

• Section-level: ~46% (AUTO=1.0, MIXED=0.5, SURVEYOR=0). Well short of 80%.

• Field-level: ~74% across all 85 shared-core schema fields, counting grades A+B+C as auto-populatable.

Both are true and they reconcile: the 80% holds at the level of individual data points — identity, dates, addresses, base amounts, taxonomy metadata, and there is a lot of it. But the report's professional weight concentrates in a handful of sections — qualifying %, element splits, pool allocation, dwelling apportionment, the declaration — which are exactly the ones that must stay empty. So the section-level share is much lower. Worth knowing before the 80% figure is used to set an expectation about how much surveyor time this saves.

Four places it was tempting to fill something in, and did not

1. The taxonomy's own "100% statutory" qualifying percentages. The easiest cheat, since the CSV already asserts them. Left blank anyway: matching the item found on inspection to the taxonomy row is itself a judgement.

2. A pre-survey land-value band (25–35% of price). This exists as a working assumption in the current sign-off brief. Deliberately not repeated — a band still anchors, and register finding R-B9 records that similar bands may be fitted to one non-independent case rather than derived.

3. A headline qualifying-expenditure figure in the executive summary. The client-facing sample report has one. Left with inputs only — it cannot be computed honestly before the judgement sections are done.

4. Pool tags for the contested taxonomy rows (care-home underfloor heating, dental chair services, private-hospital theatre ventilation). Surfaced by name as needing extra scrutiny; no default assigned.

The R-B10 lesson is designed in

The register records that our existing sign-off brief presents figures to signatories without disclosing their provenance. This template does not repeat that: every AUTO and MIXED line carries field_id · provenance · grade inline, on the face of the document, so the signing surveyor can see where each number came from and how far it can be trusted. E-grade (CTA-only) fields that surfaced — grant_quantification, contribution_payer_class, s198_election_validity, lrr_polluter_status — are explicitly marked "not this document / CTA report", so the surveyor's report never quietly absorbs the tax adviser's calls.

Next step

Goes to the surveyor to correct and complete. Not Done — they have not seen it.

## Agree when a site visit can be replaced by a video walkthrough

`12819697866` · 6 comments

### 26 August 2026, 07:17:56 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5492259942

What this is
A policy that has to be agreed with the surveyor. It is the biggest single cost lever in the business.

In plain English
Visiting a property takes about a third of a surveyor's time on a job. If we can give them enough evidence that they are willing to sign without attending, our cost per job drops sharply and we can handle far more work.

What we need to write down is: exactly what evidence is enough, and at what point a visit becomes unavoidable. Probably it varies — a straightforward £600,000 dental practice might never need a visit, while a £4m hospital always would.

The substitute
Where no visit happens, a structured video walkthrough takes its place. There is already a video capture protocol drafted; this task decides when it is sufficient on its own.

Do the free call first
There is a separate item on this board for a free 45-minute call with a surveyor asking precisely this question. That call should happen before anyone writes this policy.

Original wording: "S12 — Desktop-first policy: define the evidence threshold at which a site visit is NOT required, and the video capture protocol that substitutes. Site visit is ~33% of surveyor time — the single biggest lever."

What this is

Not a takeover of the item. A first draft so the appointed surveyor corrects a document rather than starting from nothing. It opens with an unmissable notice saying it is a draft for a surveyor to correct, is not professional advice, and is not a settled policy.

I designed the STRUCTURE. The surveyor supplies the NUMBERS.

The threshold values are the whole professional judgement here, so all of them are left as explicit [SURVEYOR'S CALL] markers — about 20 of them. A finished-looking policy with invented thresholds would be worse than nothing, because it invites rubber-stamping of numbers nobody stands behind.

The two axes

• Job value — four bands (V1 small → V4 major), boundaries blank.

• Complexity — a scored composite across seven named factors: trigger type (purchase apportionment vs invoice-based fit-out), sector and acuity, property age, documentary evidence available (O&M manual / fire plan / M&E drawings), deal and entitlement structure, s.198 election status, HMRC enquiry risk, scale and fixture density. Banded C1–C4, with both the per-factor weightings and the band cut-offs blank.

A 4×4 value × complexity grid maps to four evidence tiers (T1 desktop-only → T4 physical inspection required), flagged explicitly as a structural hypothesis, not an agreed threshold set.

═══ The framing I think is the useful contribution here ═══

The desktop-vs-visit question is really a question about which schema fields can reach an acceptable confidence grade without an on-site SV provenance. §4 names them concretely rather than talking in generalities: gross_internal_area_m2, construction_type, residential_split_m2, room_counts, pool_tag, present_flag, quantity, cost_basis, fixture_vs_chattel — nine fields carrying grade D or E. Those nine are the entire argument. Everything else already clears on documents alone.

Also covered: what each tier requires and what its residual risk is, the escalation triggers that force a visit regardless of tier (the safety valve — a real list), and the audit trail needed so a decision not to visit is defensible to HMRC later.

The 45-minute call agenda, built to close these blanks

Timeboxed and ruthlessly prioritised — intro 3 min, core question 8, the grid 15, escalation 8, other open questions 6, commercials 5 — with an explicit drop order if it runs late, because 45 minutes is short and the temptation is to over-pack it. 11 questions in priority order, each with why we are asking and what a good answer looks like, so the asker can tell a real answer from a polite deflection. Plus a one-page pre-read to send beforehand and a capture template for writing answers down live.

The four decisions the call is aimed at closing:

1. Whether this surveyor would ever sign off from video at all.

2. First-cut job-value bands.

3. Which of the nine hard-to-verify fields they would accept from video versus insist on seeing themselves.

4. Whether and how they would take the engagement on.

Lower-priority if time allows: the valuation-basis question (now built and defaulted to depreciated — item 12804374838) and the room-schedule / quantity-derivation coefficients (items 12819698557 and 12819686328).

### 31 August 2026, 16:22:36 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5506303576

<h3>Phase 52 — the capture script now exists, written for a client with a phone</h3>
<p><b>Deliverable:</b> <code>04-phase-work/phase9/video-walkthrough-capture-script-v1.md</code> (authoritative). Completion record and surveyor brief in the Document column.</p>
<p><b>The gap this closes.</b> Two documents already existed and neither was a script anyone could follow. The Build-Prep protocol specifies <i>how the system generates a brief</i>; the desktop-first policy sets out <i>when a video may stand in for a visit</i>. This is the script itself — written to be handed to a practice manager or care-home manager who has never seen a survey brief, and followed on their own phone.</p>
<p><b>Shooting order</b> — building-wide services first while the operator is fresh, fiddly void shots last: outside → plant room → electrical intake → comms/data → water → every clinical room → circulation and life safety → kitchen and laundry → ceiling and floor voids → <i>everything you skipped, said out loud</i>.</p>
<p><b>§A.3 states plainly what a video CANNOT establish</b> — eleven items, written as a position rather than a question, so the surveyor is correcting a boundary rather than inventing one. Behind panels and walls. Above suspended ceilings beyond the one tile we ask them to lift. Below raised floors — where dental's highest-value missed item lives. Anything requiring <b>touch</b>, and the fixture-vs-chattel call very often turns on whether something is physically fixed. Measurement. Age and condition with any precision. A passenger lift from a through-floor lift — different pools, 6% and 14%. Whether an item is already on the accountant's register. Any contested pool allocation, where perfect footage does not move it one inch. What serves what in a mixed building, which in supported living decides whether the largest item on site is excluded in full. And <b>anything the operator did not point the camera at — the failure mode we are most worried about, because it looks like completeness</b>.</p>
<p><b>The honest summary:</b> a video tells you what is there and roughly where. It does not tell you how much of it there is, how old it is, whether it is fixed, or which pool it belongs in. Three of those four are what a claim actually turns on.</p>
<p><b>Three things in the script worth flagging.</b> We ask the client to <b>open</b> a distribution board cover (only if hinged, never if it needs a screwdriver), a comms cabinet, and one ceiling tile — each a small risk. We ask them to <b>count out loud</b> detectors, emergency lights, CCTV and access readers as they walk, which is the most tedious instruction in the script and may be worthless if a surveyor would disregard a layperson's count. And <b>data protection comes first, not last</b>: empty rooms, out of hours, no patients, no residents, no screens or notes — Health Tax Partners becomes the controller for this footage.</p>
<p><b>The coverage score, stated honestly:</b> it measures capture-compliance against this script, not the accuracy of the claim. A 100% score means the surveyor has been handed good eyes. <b>It does not mean the figure is settled and must never be shown to a client as if it does.</b></p>
<p><b>What the surveyor is being asked to decide:</b></p>
<ol>
<li><b>Is §A.3 right?</b> Which of the eleven is wrong, and what have we missed? We would rather you struck one out than added one — a boundary we have overstated costs us jobs, one we have understated costs us a claim.</li>
<li>Which of the things we ask the client to open would you drop?</li>
<li><b>What is a passing video?</b> Coverage threshold, how many re-shoots, what forces a visit. We have deliberately set no numbers — it is a judgement about evidential sufficiency.</li>
<li><b>Would you sign a valuation resting partly on this footage, with what caveat, and is there a size or complexity above which the answer is simply no?</b></li>
<li>Is the shooting order right, or should clinical rooms come first?</li>
<li>Is a client's own count worth having, or would you disregard it? If disregarded we take it out.</li>
</ol>
<p><b>Question 4 changes the business, not just the document.</b> If a video works, a job costs an hour and we can serve clients anywhere. If it does not, every job carries a travel day and the smallest jobs stop being worth doing.</p>
<p>Machine claim cleared. Status is "Waiting on someone else" — the board has no "Awaiting review" label and the only near-match is CTA-specific.</p>

### 26 August 2026, 07:17:29 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5492259371

What this is
A purchase decision — roughly £330 — plus a test worth doing once the books arrive.

In plain English
Spon's are the standard UK building price books. Surveyors use them to work out what it would cost to rebuild a property today. We currently estimate those costs from other sources; buying the real books lets us check whether our estimates are any good.

The test that matters
Once we have them, re-run one of our worked example cases — the Cardiff care home — using the real Spon's rates, without looking at what our engine produced. Then compare. If the two land close together, our cost assumptions are sound. If they are far apart, we have found a serious problem before a client did.

That kind of blind re-run is the only honest way to test our own figures.

Worth noting
Two volumes are needed: Architectural & Building Works, and Mechanical & Electrical. The M&E one matters most to us, because most claimable equipment is mechanical or electrical.

Phase 10 — a blind re-run protocol is now attached as a doc on this item. It specifies how "blind" is enforced rather than promised: the engine's GC-01 outputs are sealed before anything else happens, the pricer receives §3 (a self-contained brief with the property, the schedule and the method, and no output figure, percentage or yield band anywhere in it) and nothing else, and their figures are committed in writing before the envelope opens. It names who may hold the pen — best is the surveyor once appointed; not acceptable is you, having already seen A and B, trying not to think about them. Tolerances are set in advance and the primary statistic is the plant share A/(A+B), not the qualifying figure: because A sits in both numerator and denominator of the apportionment, a same-direction error in A and B is largely absorbed by m, so the mix matters far more than the level — green is ±3pp on plant share and ±20% on total, red is >7pp or >35%. §6 says what to do if the gap is wide (find the misclassified elements before touching any number; and note that GC-01 derives from a competitor deliverable, so a low Spon's figure may mean their claim was aggressive). §9 states what the test does not cover: it cannot test the land figure at 31% of price, and it tests the specified residual model rather than the shipped yield-band engine. §8 flags that the same purchase clears LEG-E4, which should be moved out of the VOA queue. The books have not been bought and no re-run has been done. Status, owner and group unchanged.

31 August 2026 — answering Lakhbir's question: "which books and from what year specifically are needed?"

Buy one book: Spon's Mechanical and Electrical Services Price Book 2026.

There are two volumes in the set. The mechanical and electrical one is what matters to us, because almost everything we claim on is mechanical or electrical — boilers, air handling, medical gas, lighting, alarms, specialist drainage. The architectural and building volume matters much less.

What is already on the Desktop, and why it does not solve this:
• Mechanical & Electrical 2021 — five years old. Too old to rely on.
• Mechanical & Electrical 2022 (two copies of the same file, one is a duplicate) — four years old. Same problem.
• Architects & Builders 2024 — two years old, probably fine for a sanity check.

Why the year is the whole point. The books exist to check our own figures against an independent published source. Checking a 2026 figure against a 2021 book tells you very little: if the two disagree, you cannot tell whether we made a mistake or whether building costs simply rose. Mechanical and electrical costs in particular moved sharply over that period. A test whose failure you cannot attribute is not a test.

Recommendation: buy the M&E 2026 volume only — roughly half the £330, since you are not buying the pair.

But ask the surveyor first. On the call from Tuesday 1 September, ask what cost data they already subscribe to. Most cost surveyors hold this or the equivalent service, and the blind re-run protocol on this item already says the surveyor is the better person to hold the pen — because you have already seen our engine's figures and cannot un-see them. ## Decide whether to buy the two British Standards behind the quantity model

`12927091743` · 4 comments

### 29 August 2026, 08:22:40 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5502098273

A decision for you, not research. Two British Standards sit behind the quantity model. Both are paywalled BSI documents. Neither has been read, and the Phase 10 pack says so explicitly rather than citing them second-hand — standing rule 5 on the plan doc forbids citing guidance we have not actually read.

BS EN 50173-2 (generic cabling, office spaces). This is the named source that would close coefficient RD-04 — data and comms outlets per m² where no M&E schedule exists. Searching found the standard but not the outlet-density figure, so RD-04 stays blank. This is the only one of the fourteen coefficients that a purchase closes outright.

BS 5839-1 (fire detection and alarm systems). This one is subtler. Reputable published guides disagree on how to turn the standard's 7.5 m rule into a coverage area: read as a radius it gives an inscribed square of 10.6 m × 10.6 m ≈ 112 m² per smoke detector; read as a maximum spacing it gives 7.5 m × 7.5 m ≈ 56 m². Both readings appear in BS 5839-1 pocket guides from established manufacturers. The Phase 10 pack reports the conflict rather than picking a side.

Important — buying BS 5839-1 is optional, and here is why. The worked example showed that the area-density model is the wrong shape for this business regardless of which reading is correct: a room-by-room count for a 268 m² dental fit-out gives 15–19 detection points against 2.4 or 4.8 on the two area-density readings. Detector count is driven by compartmentation, not floor area — a 14 m² surgery needs its own detector whether the building is 268 m² or 2,680 m². So the standard settles a number we should probably stop using. Buy it only if you want the lower-bound sanity check stated precisely.

What this is not. Separate from the £330 Spon's price books (item 12804374406) and from a BCIS subscription. Those two are the price of doing purchase-apportionment work at all — see finding F-2. These two standards are about the quantity side, and are much smaller sums.

31 August 2026 — answering Lakhbir's question: "tell me specifically what the purchase is for".

Two published British Standards. The answer is: buy one, not both.

BS EN 50173-2 — worth buying. It tells us how many data and communications outlets to expect per square metre of office-type space. We have fourteen rules of this kind that convert floor area into countable items, and we worked thirteen of them out ourselves. This is the only one where buying a document closes the gap outright.

BS 5839-1 — not worth buying. It covers fire detector spacing, and it would settle a genuine disagreement between published guides about how to read a "7.5 metre" rule — one reading gives roughly one detector per 112 square metres, the other one per 56.

But we tested it against reality and the whole calculation is the wrong shape. On a real 268 square metre dental fit-out, counting room by room gives fifteen to nineteen detection points. The area-based readings give between two and five. Detectors follow compartmentation, not floor area — a 14 square metre surgery needs its own detector whether the building is 268 square metres or 2,680.

So buying it would settle a number we should stop using. Buy it only if you specifically want the lower-bound sanity check written down precisely. Otherwise the money is better spent on the M&E price book.

Cause and effect: buying the cabling standard closes one of fourteen coefficients outright. Not buying the fire standard costs nothing, provided we replace the area-based detector rule with a room-driven count — which is scheduled as part of Phase 52 in the build plan.

<h3>Phase 52 — both depreciation methods built behind one switch, defaulting to today's behaviour</h3>
<p><b>Deliverable:</b> <code>04-phase-work/phase9/depreciation-both-methods-v1.md</code>; code in <code>phase9/ledgerstone-cost-model.cjs</code>. Completion record in Document 2. <b>Document 1 (the F-3 prepared patch) is extended, not superseded</b> — the crosswalk-completeness gate is still required and still unshipped.</p>
<p><b>What was built.</b> A <code>depreciation_method</code> switch with three positions — <code>none</code>, <code>per_element</code> (LEG-E5), <code>whole_building</code> (new, LEG-E5b). It defaults to <code>none</code>, which is exactly today's behaviour. <b>No number anywhere changes.</b></p>
<p><b>Why a second method was needed.</b> E5's argument for per-element is sound as far as it goes — plant lives differ by an order of magnitude and depreciating at one rate moves value between pools attracting 14%, 6% and 3%. But three things weigh the other way and <b>not one of them is ours to settle</b>: E5 applies PAFOAS, a whole-<i>building</i> scale, per plant <i>element</i> over a CIBSE life — an invention nobody has ruled on, which is F-3's own finding; whole-building depreciation is the stock contractor's-basis treatment an HMRC valuer is likeliest to recognise; and E5 needs a 95-row crosswalk that does not exist while E5b needs none, because a building has no plant life to look up.</p>
<p><b>The consequence, stated plainly.</b> If a surveyor rules that PAFOAS may not be applied per plant element, LEG-E5 does not ship in its current form — and until today <b>there was no second method to fall back to</b>. The fallback is now a switch position rather than a rebuild.</p>
<p><b>Why the default is <code>none</code> and not <code>per_element</code>.</b> Both gates are off with empty tables, so today every method gives factor 1 whatever the default. But a default is not neutral — it is what runs when nobody decides, and on the day a table lands the default is what silently starts applying. Defaulting to a <i>method</i> would be choosing between them by inaction, and that choice is the thing this item exists to hand to a surveyor. Same discipline as the Phase 51 CTA switches.</p>
<p><b>The one back-compatibility rule runs one way only.</b> E5's gate on with no method stated still resolves to per-element — exactly the pre-Phase-52 behaviour, no number changes. E5b's gate on <b>never</b> self-selects, because nothing was behaving that way before, so falling into it would not preserve behaviour, it would be choosing. And <b>both gates on with no method stated resolves to <code>none</code></b> — that is the configuration where a genuine choice exists, and the one place inaction must not become a decision.</p>
<p><b>Alternatives, not layers.</b> Applying an element's own age allowance and the building's depreciates the same asset twice. There is no configuration where stacking is right, so it is an error, not a flag. On a worked case (30-year building, 30-year lift on a 20-year life, 30-year shell on a 60-year life, invented fixtures) the two methods give qualifying figures <b>more than 5% apart</b>. We deliberately do not assert which is higher — it depends on the age profile of the plant against the age of the building, and that dependence is exactly why a surveyor chooses rather than us.</p>
<p><b>Guards are identical on both sides:</b> gate off is flagged; a gate on over an empty stub refuses rather than guessing; a missing age refuses rather than assuming nought; an unlisted scale refuses rather than falling back; past the end of a scale it <b>clamps to the last band and never extrapolates</b>, because extrapolating a scale beyond its last band is inventing data; and a working asset never depreciates to zero — the residual floor is read from the scale, never assumed. One knock-on fix: the DRC-without-depreciation warning now considers both methods, not just E5.</p>
<p><b>Tests:</b> group H1–H22. Cost model suite 51 → <b>73 pass / 0 fail</b>; phase9 total 137/0. Site harness <b>363/0/4, unchanged</b> — nothing shipped. No real figure entered either table; <code>LS_VOA_BUILDING_OBSOLESCENCE</code> ships empty with its licence note like the other five, and every test fixture is invented and says so.</p>
<p><b>What the surveyor is being asked to decide.</b> (1) <b>May a whole-building obsolescence scale be applied per plant element at all?</b> F-3's real gate, upstream of both licences — a cheap question against an expensive assumption, and it should be asked <i>before</i> buying either. (2) <b>Per element or whole building, and does it depend on the case?</b> More accurate and much more work versus quick and cruder — we do not know whether the extra accuracy is worth having or is false precision. (3) Where expected plant lives should come from at all. (4) Whether a residual floor is the right instrument past a scale's end. (5) Whether the pool split legitimately bears on the choice, or is a tax consideration with no business influencing a valuation judgement — we suspect the latter and would rather be told. All five are in plain English on 12933605005.</p>
<p><b>Unchanged from F-3:</b> CIBSE Guide M terms still have no board item at all; the VOA obsolescence licence is 12818978633; the crosswalk is a professional deliverable, not a licence; the pool reallocation remains mandatory CTA sign-off.</p>
<p>Owner type changed Developer → Surveyor: the developer work here is done and the remaining gate is a professional ruling. Machine claim cleared. Status is "Waiting on someone else" — the board has no "Awaiting review" label and the only near-match is CTA-specific.</p>

### 27 August 2026, 09:46:10 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5496125330

Phase 9 — the mechanism is prepared and is NOT shipped. This item stays Blocked.

Where the code is

phase9/ledgerstone-cost-model.cjs — gate leg_e4_location_and_contract_size, shipped false.

LS_LOCATION_FACTORS.factors = {} and LS_CONTRACT_SIZE_ADJUSTMENT.bands = [] — empty, labelled stubs.

Tests: 51 assertions passing. Harness 216 pass / 0 fail / 14 xfail. Shipped site unchanged.

═══ Worth flagging: this is not a licence problem, and it is much cheaper to clear ═══

LEG-E4 sits in the same queue as E2, E3 and E5, but it is a completely different kind of block. E2/E3/E5 wait on a VOA licence — a counterparty, a negotiation, a solicitor, and no guarantee of the answer. LEG-E4 waits on a purchase: Spon's or BCIS, item 12804374406, about £330.

No solicitor. No clearance. No counterparty. Someone buys a book. It can be cleared this week by anyone with a card, whereas the VOA items cannot be cleared by us at all. It may be worth separating on the board so it stops sitting behind things we cannot move — of the four engine fixes this is the one that is entirely within your control today.

The defect

Rates are applied nationally. A national mean rate applied to a property in a cheaper region overstates replacement cost; in a dearer region it understates it. Your worked example: Cardiff at 94 against a mean of 100, so a national rate overstates Cardiff replacement cost by about 6%. Contract size bites the same way — price books quote at an assumed contract value, and a much larger or smaller job does not carry those unit rates.

What the mechanism does

• Regional factor ÷ the table's mean, times a contract-size factor banded on contract value. Test D2 asserts the Cardiff 94/100 → 0.94 case; test D3 asserts a dearer region raises the factor, so the adjustment cuts both ways.

• An unlisted region refuses (E_LOCATION_NOT_IN_TABLE). It does not fall back to 1.0. An unlisted region is a question, not a national mean.

• Gate on with no location raises E_LOCATION_KEY_REQUIRED; gate on over an empty table raises E_TABLE_NOT_LOADED.

• Contract size is optional but its absence is flagged rather than silent (LEG_E4_NO_CONTRACT_SIZE).

Order of operations — asserted, so a later refactor cannot transpose it

Location and contract size are multiplicative on the base rate, applied before indexation and before prelims and fees. Applying them after an uplift would compound the uplift by a regional factor, which is not what either adjustment means. Test D7 pins this against an explicit arithmetic expectation rather than trusting the reading order of the code.

What has to happen to ship

Buy the book (12804374406) → load the real factors and bands with a verified_at date → flip the gate. The mechanism is done and tested; only the data is missing, and the data costs £330.

The code does not differentiate this threshold by field (all ten fields — five APPORTIONMENT-consequence, e.g. qualifying_pct_sanitary, and the others TAXONOMY-consequence — share one MIN_N_FOR_RATE); that simplification is unchanged by this pass and is worth a future item if the APPORTIONMENT-consequence fields, which move a client's actual claim figure, are judged to warrant a stricter (higher-n) bar than a taxonomy-classification field would.

MIN_N_FOR_RATE=5 does not still hold — raised to 7. Ad-hoc pooling adds a between-surveyor variance component a same-surveyor repeat panel never had to absorb, so more observations are needed before the median is trustworthy.

ADOPTION_GOOD lowered 0.6→0.5; BIAS_THRESHOLD widened 0.03→0.05. Reasoning in full on item 12927112944 and in the code comments. Net effect: a slightly harder bar to clear before a field is trusted (more observations required) but a slightly more forgiving read of what those observations mean once gathered (both the "good" bar and the bias band relaxed) — consistent with treating ad-hoc, first-encounter data as noisier but not worthless.

Also named the previously-inline per-surveyor divergence floor as MIN_SURVEYOR_OBS_FOR_DIVERGENCE = 3 (unchanged value, now documented as load-bearing under ad-hoc engagement) and flagged that selfConsistency() will mostly report null under ad-hoc — a documented limitation, not something the threshold change was meant to fix.

This item remains Blocked on real job data to test any of this against — these are reasoned starting points for the ad-hoc model, not findings.

### 31 August 2026, 16:23:35 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5506307164

<h3>Phase 52 — the instrument is built and empty. The item stays blocked on real jobs</h3>
<p><b>The 28 August confirmation on this item stands and is not withdrawn.</b> No document, research pass, model or analysis can produce calibration data. The input is a chartered surveyor's decision to accept or override a pre-fill, on a real property, on a real job.</p>
<p><b>What that note got wrong was the conclusion drawn from it</b> — that because the <i>data</i> cannot be produced, nothing could be built. The instrument can be built, and <b>three of its parts cannot be retrofitted</b>:</p>
<ul>
<li><b>The blank-field control</b> needs an unanchored comparison arm. Every job run before it starts has already seen a pre-fill and can serve as neither arm. Start it at job 20 and the first 19 are unusable.</li>
<li><b>Acceptance versus never-looked</b> has to be captured at the moment, from a positive confirmation in the surveyor's flow. It cannot be inferred afterwards from data that records both as "the value did not change".</li>
<li><b>Which meaning of adoption is being measured</b> — within-surveyor trust or cross-surveyor consensus — produces an identical-looking number, and afterwards it is not recoverable which one a given figure was.</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Deliverables:</b> <code>04-phase-work/phase9/calibration-instrument-v1.md</code>; code in <code>03-app/phase3/ledgerstone-surveyor-crm.ts</code> §8–§10; two headers-only registers and a README at <code>phase9/calibration/</code>. Completion record in Document 2.</p>
<p><b>What was added.</b> <code>NOT_REVIEWED</code> as a distinct outcome — an UNTOUCHED pre-fill and one nobody opened produce identical data and mean opposite things, so a 90% adoption rate could mean the pre-fills are excellent or that nobody is checking. Unreviewed events are counted and reported but kept out of n, and "not reviewed plus a changed value" is refused as a contradiction. <code>drift()</code> over ordered cohorts of four, because a pooled median hides a crossover: a field running 8% high early and 8% low late reports a median near zero and looks perfectly calibrated. The blank-field control at one job in ten per field, <b>deterministically assigned</b> so the arm is reconstructable at audit — an unreconstructable control arm is not a control — with an anchored control observation refused outright. And the mode stamped: <code>CROSS_SURVEYOR</code>, recorded now because it cannot be recovered later.</p>
<p><b>What the control detects that adoption cannot.</b> A high adoption rate is consistent with two opposite worlds — our pre-fill is accurate, or our pre-fill is an anchor surveyors drift toward. <code>adoption()</code> cannot separate them because both produce the same data. The control can.</p>
<p><b>A unit problem stated rather than papered over.</b> The protocol's three-percentage-point retirement threshold transfers directly to six of the ten tracked fields. Two are GBP/m², where "percentage points" is meaningless and nobody has set an equivalent — a relative 3% and an absolute £3/m² differ by two orders of magnitude. Those fields return <code>THRESHOLD_NOT_DEFINED_FOR_UNIT</code> with both medians and the gap still reported: the comparison stays visible, only the pass/fail call is withheld. <b>Escalated to the surveyor pack on 12933605005 (Question 16).</b></p>
<p><b>Also recorded so nobody rebuilds it:</b> the CRM already implements far more than the 28 August note implied — outcome classification on materiality, reason discipline, origin stratification, anchor-quarantine exclusion that is counted rather than dropped, median signed delta, four verdicts, divergence, self-consistency. And <code>MIN_N_FOR_RATE = 7</code> already answers §4.2 of that note, which recorded the sample size as undecided.</p>
<p><b>Tests:</b> D1–D24, all passing. Suite 25 → 49; phase3 total <b>311 pass / 0 fail</b>. The one worth naming is D8: a field whose pooled median is exactly zero — perfectly calibrated on the snapshot — caught by the cohort series as DRIFTING_LOW.</p>
<p><b>Every reading says INSUFFICIENT_DATA and the instrument reports <code>empty: true</code>, not "healthy".</b> That is the correct output of a correctly built instrument with nothing in it.</p>
<p><b>Two things now need a developer, not Claude:</b> the positive-confirmation step in the surveyor's UI (without it <code>reviewed</code> is always true and NOT_REVIEWED never fires — the type exists, the capture does not), and actually serving the blank field on one job in ten. <b>Two need the surveyor:</b> the GBP/m² threshold, and whether the ten tracked rate fields are the right ten.</p>
<p><b>Owner type left as Claude, deliberately, and flagged rather than edited</b> — the 28 August note's observation was right about the data and is now wrong about the instrument, and re-typing the item is Lakhbir's call.</p>
<p>Machine claim cleared. Status is "Waiting on someone else" — the board has no "Awaiting review" label and the only near-match is CTA-specific.</p>

## Rebuild-cost cross-check restated at £2,841,400 — surveyor to say what must be made like-for-like, and how far apart is too far

`12991293063` · 4 comments

### 7 September 2026, 19:54:11 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5525632652

Found by Phase 97, 7 September 2026, while correcting where the location factor is applied. Deliberately not patched, because the fix is a judgement and not arithmetic.

The full specification's worked example states the same quantity twice and the two do not agree.

§10 builds the replacement cost element by element and sums to A + B = £2,841,400.
§7, the independent rebuild cost cross-check, gives "Our A + B, before land" as £2,567,720.

They differ by 9.6%. That gap is not the location factor — 0.94 applied to §10 would give £2,670,916 — and it is not any other step in the build-up. Nothing in the document explains it.

Why it matters more than a typo. §7 compares our figure against a surveyor-prepared insurance reinstatement valuation of £2,610,000 and reports a 1.6% divergence, which it calls corroboration — and the pack says that if it had come back far apart it would be "the single most important line". That corroboration is computed off the smaller figure. Against §10's own total the divergence is 8.9%, which is a materially weaker claim than the one the document makes.

The question for the surveyor. Which build-up is right — the §10 element sum, or the £2,567,720 in §7? Whichever it is, the other one has to move, and the corroboration paragraph has to be re-worded to match.

A caveat has been added to §7 in the specification so nobody reads the 1.6% as settled while this is open.

THREE THINGS THAT WILL COST MONEY IF THEY ARE MISSED
----------------------------------------------------

1. WordPress changes where a statutory duty attaches, and three control questions are OPEN. The data protection controls were designed against object storage. Brief §3.0 sets out three questions for Lakhbir and the DPO: Q51 (do client documents avoid the Media Library entirely?), Q52 (can a directory be excluded from the host's backups? a file deleted from disk and alive in a 30-day snapshot has not been deleted), Q53 (where does the immutable audit log live? a log every Administrator can edit is not an audit log). 2. Board-Done does not mean DPO-approved. Thirteen data protection documents are marked Done here on the instruction to treat the DPO appointment as signed. It is not signed, and all thirteen still say "DRAFT — NOT APPROVED" in their own headers. That gap closes with a signature, not by editing headers.

3. Eight of the ten adviser switches make claims BIGGER, and all ten are OFF. Flipping one fails its branch-B assertion in the harness. That failure is the harness telling you a tax position has been taken. Answer it by updating the harness deliberately — never by muting it.

## The upload strip runs after the file is already stored — fix the boundary

`12928214881` · 4 comments

### 29 August 2026, 19:06:51 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5502455821

Found by Phase 42 (sweep & stress-test), 29 Aug 2026.

The claim. phase3/ledgerstone-client-doc-ingestion.ts describes applyReceiptPolicy as "THE STRIP. Runs on receipt, before anything is written to durable storage", says it "drops them out of the document", and RECEIPT_CONTRACT step 3 states it "REMOVES on receipt, before the first write", with step 4 "write ONLY result.retained to durable storage; result.removed is never written anywhere".

The architecture that contradicts it — recorded in the same file. STORAGE_POSITION.intended_store is "AWS S3, eu-west-2 (London), SSE, pre-signed URLs", lifted from Developer Brief §3. A pre-signed URL upload writes the file to S3 directly from the client's browser. Ledgerstone's server never holds the bytes before they are in durable storage. So at the moment applyReceiptPolicy runs, the unredacted original is already stored.

What the strip actually strips. applyReceiptPolicy takes Segment[] and returns Segment[] — extracted text. It never touches the file. result.removed is correctly kept out of the text written onward; it remains in the stored original for the whole retention period.

Why this matters more than a wording fix. Phase 40 §5.4 establishes that Ledgerstone's structured records contain no third-party name at all, so the entire third-party personal data holding lives in the raw file. Phase 40 found every control sat at the model boundary while the Article 14 duty attaches at the door. Phase 41 moved the control to "receipt" — but "receipt" here means after text extraction, and the architecture of record puts durable storage before it. The control moved one step and the door moved with it. Condition D4 (planning representations "removed on receipt, not merely kept out of the model") is the one that suffers most: it is stated as absolute and, under this architecture, is not.

What to do.
1. Decide where the true ingestion boundary is: server-mediated upload (bytes reach Ledgerstone before S3), or accept that durable storage precedes the strip and say so plainly everywhere that currently says otherwise.
2. If pre-signed URLs stay, add a documented quarantine step — upload to a short-lived quarantine prefix, strip/redact, write to the durable prefix, delete the quarantine object — and make that the first steps of RECEIPT_CONTRACT.
3. Correct the language in applyReceiptPolicy, ReceiptResult.removed and RECEIPT_CONTRACT so it says what it does: it filters the extracted text, not the file.
4. Re-check Phase 40 condition D4 against whichever answer lands.

Written up as Phase 44 in the build plan (item 12878920167). Related: 12928215019 (the redaction option that has no producer), 12928031577, 12928074627.

## Record that a transparency notice was sent to the people we hold names for

`12927936989` · 2 comments

### 29 August 2026, 17:27:06 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5502412889

<p><b>Why this exists.</b> On 28 August 2026 Item 5 §8.5 adopted <b>Route 2</b> as a decision, not a recommendation: publish under Article 14(5)(e) with Article 14(7) as the baseline, <b>and notify the individual directly wherever a route to them exists</b>. Phase 39 has now drafted that notice (template T6 on board item 12927894775).</p>

<p><b>There is nowhere to record that it was sent.</b> The breach register records breaches. The rights-request register records requests. The two exception stores — E1 (Companies House person with significant control: name, birth month and year, nationality) and E2 (HM Land Registry individual proprietor: name) — hold the records but have no transparency field. Item 5 condition C7 requires those stores to be separately held, name-searchable, markable as restricted and deletable. <b>It says nothing about recording that the person was told.</b></p>

<p><b>Three concrete consequences of the gap:</b></p>
<ol>
<li>Ledgerstone <b>cannot demonstrate compliance with Article 14</b> for any individual. Article 5(2) accountability means being able to show it, not just having done it.</li>
<li>Ledgerstone <b>cannot avoid sending a second notice</b> to someone already notified, which is its own small intrusion on a stranger.</li>
<li>Ledgerstone <b>cannot say which individuals the Article 14(5)(e) exemption is actually being relied on for</b>. That is the one that matters most: it is the difference between "we notified everyone we could reach and published for the rest" and an assertion nobody can evidence. Article 14(6) makes the number of data subjects relevant, and Ledgerstone's numbers are small — which is exactly where the exemption is weakest.</li>
</ol>

<p><b>What to build.</b> Add to each record in the E1 and E2 stores:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>art14_notice_sent</code> — date, or explicitly NOT SENT</li>
<li><code>art14_notice_route</code> — DIRECT / VIA CLIENT / NOT SENT — NO ROUTE. (Whether the client route is permitted at all is open question <b>Q31</b>; the field is needed either way)</li>
<li><code>art14_basis</code> — NOTIFIED (Art 14 met directly) / EXEMPTION RELIED ON (Art 14(5)(e) with 14(7) publication). <b>This is the field that answers question Q32.</b></li>
<li><code>art14_notice_version</code> — which version of the notice was sent, so a later amendment is traceable</li>
</ul>

<p><b>A blank is not an answer</b> — the same rule the breach register applies at its §2.5. NOT SENT with a reason is an answer; empty is not.</p>

<p>Sits alongside Item 5 conditions C5 and C7. Closes §7.10 of the Phase 39 pack and the "Recorded in: Nowhere" row in its §0.5 table.</p>

<p><i>Created by Claude, Phase 39, 29 August 2026. Owner type: Developer.</i></p>

### 8 September 2026, 07:54:40 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5527420232

BUILT 8 September 2026, Phase 98. Four fields, and the cross-field rules that make them a record rather than four boxes.

Where it went. phase3/caprebate-name-exclusion.ts, new section 6 — the file that already decides which records retain a natural person's name. The predicate that decides whether a notice is owed is derived from the name policy, so a record cannot retain a name under an exception and separately claim it owes nobody a notice. 17 new tests; phase3 went 362 to 379.

FIRST, A CORRECTION TO THIS PHASE'S OWN PREMISE. The prompt said art14_notice_sent appears nowhere in 04-phase-work, and that grep was correct. The conclusion drawn from it was not. A full Article 14 transparency record already existed for the uploaded-document population — per-person notices, 14(5)(e) exemption reasons, a completeness assertion. Its own header even says that population was "worse off than the register population because it has no store at all to add a field to", implying the register population had one. It did not. So the gap was real; it was just not the gap the grep described, and the fix is a mirror of an existing mechanism rather than a new invention. (This is the second time in three phases that a correct grep produced a wrong conclusion.)

The four fields are as specified on this item and were not re-derived. What was added is the part that makes them evidence:

Each field is plausible on its own. It is the combinations that are either evidence or nonsense, and a half-completed form produces exactly the incoherent ones. So: a notice sent on a date cannot sit beside a route of NOT SENT — NO ROUTE; a basis of NOTIFIED cannot be claimed when nothing was sent, because Article 14 is not met by intending to meet it; and the 14(5)(e) exemption cannot be relied on for somebody we actually reached — the exemption is for people we cannot reach. A notice sent must name its version, or a later amendment cannot be traced to the people who got the earlier wording. A record against a person who is owed nothing is refused too: a notice recorded against nobody is not evidence of compliance, it is a record that will later be cited as one.

A BLANK IS NOT AN ANSWER, asserted on every required field, and NOT_SENT is an explicit value distinct from empty — exactly as this item asked. A free-text near-miss in the date ("sent last week") is refused too: an unqueryable field cannot answer which individuals are we relying on the exemption for, which is the question that matters most.

Two things done deliberately. A corporate proprietor owes no Article 14 duty, so Exception 2 only triggers the requirement where proprietorType is individual — getting that wrong would generate obligations to companies which would then be "discharged" and look like compliance. And ingestion is NOT gated on the record: Article 14(3)(a) gives a month from obtaining, so requiring the notice at ingestion would make lawful ingestion impossible. Same split the document population uses. art14DeadlineFor() computes that month.

VIA CLIENT is recordable but findable. Whether Article 14 may be discharged by asking our client to pass a notice to a person named on their own title is open with the DPO — the field was needed either way, which is why this was buildable now. art14PendingDpoDecision() exists so those records can be found when the answer arrives, rather than the answer arriving and nothing changing.

The open question did not exist in writing. This item cites it as Q31, but the questions document — restructured since — contained no Article 14 question at all. It has now been written up for the data protection officer, which is the same failure this board hit before: an item blocked on a question nobody had written down.

Proved rather than asserted: two mutations were run. Removing the exemption-versus-sent coherence check fails exactly one test; making the duty predicate always return false fails six. Both restored.

Suites: site harness 632 / 0 / 4 xfail, phase3 379 / 0, phase9 189 / 0. Drift green. 1,200 passing assertions.

phase9/ledgerstone-cost-model.md — the write-up.

Regression harness: 216 pass / 0 fail / 14 xfail (was 207/0/11). Nothing in the shipped site changed.

One thing you should know before anything else

There was no code to patch. LEG-E2 to E5 are fixes to the residual replacement-cost model in the Care Homes Estimate Engine Specification §4.1–4.3, and that model had never been built — the shipped engine values a claim from sector yield bands and contains no prelims, no fees and no A+B+C at all. The 18% and the 15% live only in the specification and in the remediation register at R-B9. So Phase 9 built the model with all four corrections designed in and held behind gates. Same result, arrived at from the other end.

═══ QUESTION FOR YOU: is this item actually blocked? ═══

This is marked blocked on VOA licence clearance. Looking at what the change actually does, I think that may be over-blocked, and I'd like you to decide.

The case that it is not licence-gated. Turning this gate on sets a multiplier to 1.0 and deletes a parameter. It reproduces no VOA table, quotes no VOA figure and needs no VOA data to compute — test B2 forces the gate on with no tables supplied at all and the fix still works. The only VOA-derived thing involved is the knowledge that on-costs already sit inside estimated replacement cost, and that knowledge is what tells us our own arithmetic counts them twice. Knowing a double count exists is not the same as republishing the data that revealed it. On that reading this is the one fix of the four that could ship on its own.

The case that it is. Two arguments, which is why this is a question and not a conclusion:

1. If the licence restricts derived works rather than reproduction, a model shaped by VOA methodology may be caught even where no VOA number appears in it. That is a question for whoever reads the licence, not for me.

2. E2 and E3 touch the same expression. Ship E2 alone and A and B carry a corrected prelims term next to an uncorrected flat 15% fee term. Defensible as an interim — but a state someone has to be told about rather than discover.

I have not unblocked it. The gate ships false like the other three. Your call.

The defect, and how big it actually is

§4.2 multiplies both replacement-cost components by (1 + prelims), prelims defaulting to 0.18. VOA guidance is that on-costs — site set-up, scaffolding, plant hire, site management, insurances — are already inside the ERC. The further 1.18 counts them twice.

But the error is not 18%. The model divides: m = PC / (A + B + C). A common uplift on A and B partly cancels in m × A. It does not cancel completely, because C — bare-site land value — is not uplifted. So the double count shifts value out of land and into buildings and plant. It always moves in the direction of overstating the claim, and it moves most on properties with the highest land fraction. Overstatement is the direction that loses an enquiry. Test B6 asserts both facts.

⚠ A trap for whoever ships this — please read

This is not a contradiction of JD Wetherspoon plc v HMRC [2012] UKUT 42, and it must not be "tidied" into looking like one.

Wetherspoon holds that preliminaries and professional fees do apportion to qualifying P&M, pro rata, and are routinely missed — which understates claims. Both are true at once because they are about different paths:

• Invoice / fit-out path — prelims are real lines in a cost package. Apportion them to qualifying P&M. ADD. (Wetherspoon)

• Residual / valuation path — the price-book rate already contains on-costs. A further uplift double counts. DO NOT ADD. (VOA)

Same words, opposite treatment. LEG-E2 changes the residual path only. Anyone applying it to the invoice path would understate every fit-out claim and would be reversing Wetherspoon. The model enforces this structurally: cost_basis must be stated and is never defaulted, and test B3 asserts that forcing the E2 gate on leaves the invoice path untouched at 1.18.

What has to happen to ship

Your decision on whether the block is real. Then flip one boolean. No table to load — that is the whole point of the argument above.
