## Replace the flat 15% professional fees with a proper scale

`12804380489` · 5 comments

### 27 August 2026, 09:45:57 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5496125045

Phase 9 — the mechanism is prepared and is NOT shipped. This item stays Blocked.

Where the code is

phase9/ledgerstone-cost-model.cjs — gate leg_e3_voa_fee_scale, shipped false.

The band table LS_VOA_FEE_SCALE.bands is [] — an empty, labelled stub. It stays empty.

Tests: 51 assertions passing. Harness 216 pass / 0 fail / 14 xfail (was 207/0/11). Shipped site unchanged.

This one IS genuinely licence-gated — unlike LEG-E2

I queried the block on E2 because that fix removes a multiplier and needs no VOA data. This is the opposite case. The band table IS the VOA data. There is no version of this fix that does not reproduce a VOA schedule, because the schedule is the entire content of the change. So what is built is the mechanism that applies a banded fee scale, with the bands left empty and clearly labelled.

The defect

§4.2 applies a flat 15% professional fee uplift to every line regardless of contract size. Remediation register R-B9 records that the 0.15 carries no cited source and may have been back-solved to reproduce the GC-01 golden case.

A flat rate is wrong in shape as well as in level. Fee scales are regressive — the percentage falls as the contract grows — so a flat 15% understates fees on small jobs and overstates them on large ones. The error is signed by job size and does not wash out across a portfolio. Test C4 asserts both directions against an invented fixture scale.

What the mechanism does

• Bands are half-open [floor, ceiling) so a value on a boundary lands in exactly one band and nothing is double counted (test C3).

• A value outside every band raises E_BAND_NOT_FOUND rather than falling through to a default.

• Gate on with the table still empty raises E_TABLE_NOT_LOADED, naming the gate and the licence — it does not quietly fall back to 15%. Silence is how a stub becomes a fabricated figure.

• Gate on without a construction cost raises E_CONSTRUCTION_COST_REQUIRED, because the scale is banded on it.

The JD Wetherspoon citation, and why it is not in tension with this fix

JD Wetherspoon plc v HMRC [2012] UKUT 42 is the authority that professional fees reach qualifying plant and machinery at all — they apportion to qualifying P&M pro rata and are routinely missed, which understates claims.

Wetherspoon settles whether fees qualify. It says nothing about how much the fees were. LEG-E3 changes only the quantum, and only on the residual path where the figure is modelled rather than invoiced. On the invoice path the fee quantum comes off the invoice and no scale is involved at all — test C6 asserts that the invoice path ignores the scale even with the gate forced on.

The citation is carried in the authority string the function returns, so it reaches the report rather than living only in a comment. Test C7 asserts it survives the fix.

What has to happen to ship

VOA licence cleared → load the real bands into LS_VOA_FEE_SCALE with a verified_at date → flip the gate. The mechanism is done and tested; only the data is missing.

## Pull in the government valuation database (waiting on the licence)

### 26 August 2026, 07:18:46 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5492261004

What this is
A developer build that is blocked on a licence. Do not start it until the clearance comes through.

In plain English
The Valuation Office publishes a large database describing commercial properties — floor areas, how each property has been valued, what category it falls into. That would give us floor area and property type for a great many of our target properties without asking the client for anything.

The data is published as bulk files rather than a live lookup, so the build is a nightly job that downloads new and changed files and keeps our copy current. There are four separate valuation years to handle.

Why it is stopped
The Valuation Office has said the standard open-government licence does not cover their data. Until a solicitor confirms we may use it in a commercial product, nothing should be built. There is a separate item on this board tracking that clearance.

Worth knowing: this is the only source in our whole pipeline with this restriction. Everything else is standard open data.

Original wording: "VOA bulk ingestion via Azure blob REST — nightly watcher, epoch + change files, four list years. GATED ON LICENCE CLEARANCE."

### 27 August 2026, 09:47:10 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5496126692

Phase 9 — connector written and tested. NOT SHIPPED, and no live data was ever pulled. This item stays Blocked.

Files (all in phase9/)

ledgerstone-voa-import.ts — connector, parser, incremental-update logic

ledgerstone-voa-import.test.ts — 29 tests, 29 pass, 0 fail

ledgerstone-voa-import.md — the specification, including every unverified assumption

═══ NOT ONE NETWORK CALL WAS MADE ═══

No fetch, no HTTP client, no test call, not even to check the file format. I audited the finished file for network primitives afterwards and it is clean. Every test fixture is a hand-written literal string invented for the test.

The module is structurally incapable of touching the network today: the injected fetcher defaults to voaFetchNotCleared, which throws E_LICENCE_NOT_CLEARED before any DNS lookup, socket or filesystem activity. Supplying a real fetcher is a deliberate, separate future act.

What it does

• Four list years kept apart. A closed union type; every method takes an explicit year; there is no "operate on everything" method. Crossing years throws E_LIST_YEAR_MISMATCH. The one legitimate cross-year query returns a Map keyed by year — never a merged object, which is asserted in a test.

• Epoch + change-file ordering. A change applies only at last_applied + 1. A gap throws E_SEQUENCE_GAP rather than silently skipping. Re-applying the same file is a no-op, so the nightly run is idempotent.

• Malformed rows are quarantined with a reason, never dropped silently and never allowed to poison the batch — bad column counts, bad values, duplicates, unknown change types, and ADD-onto-existing / AMEND-missing / DELETE-missing all recorded individually while the rest of the batch still applies.

• The nightly watcher is pure. planNightlyFetch() decides what should be fetched and returns that as data. It never fetches. A blocked fetch on one list does not stop the other three plans.

• Reference tables are empty stubs returning {loaded: false, reason} until a real epoch load succeeds.

• Output maps to the voa_* field ids the Phase 3 source register already whitelists, provenance API, grade A per Consolidated Schema §0.5.

⚠ The format assumptions are guesses, and they are labelled as guesses

Because nothing was fetched, the documented file format the code parses is my description of it, not a verified one. §8 of the spec lists every assumption for verification when the licence lands. The largest:

• A-2 — the pipe-delimited layout with #LIST_YEAR/#SEQ pragma lines is this connector's own invented shape, not a confirmed VOA format. Likely wrong; needs revalidating against a real sample.

• A-6 — voa_total_area_m2 may not exist in the real bulk product at all; floor area more plausibly comes from elsewhere. Modelled as present: false with a note, never silently defaulted.

• A-3/4/5/7/8 — key field (BA reference vs UARN), rateable-value and date encoding, the sequencing mechanism, and the ADD/AMEND/DELETE vocabulary are all unverified, and each is isolated so it is a contained change once real data is seen.

Being explicitly wrong and labelled is the right outcome here; being accidentally right by fetching unlicensed data would not be.

What has to happen to ship

Licence cleared → validate the format assumptions in §8 against a real sample → correct the parser → supply a real fetcher. The connector, the ordering logic, the quarantine handling and the tests are already done.

## Land boundary maps for site size - fetcher built and switched off 24 Sep 2026. Fetching waits only on the DPO: can we make a few small, logged test lookups?

`12830205914` · 14 comments

### 26 August 2026, 07:18:50 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5492261102

What this is
A developer build waiting on a licence answer. Small job, but do not start it yet.

In plain English
There is a public dataset of land boundaries — the outline of each property's plot. Pulling it in would tell us two useful things automatically: the total site area, and how much of that site the building actually covers.

That matters because the land under a property never qualifies for any relief, so knowing how much land there is helps us sanity-check a valuation before a surveyor sees it.

Why it is stopped
Although the dataset is free to reuse, it was prepared from Ordnance Survey mapping, and reproducing it in a document we hand to a client or surveyor may need permission beyond our current account. There is a separate item on this board for getting that checked.

A likely middle path: we may be cleared to use the boundaries internally for calculation while not reproducing the map itself in any outgoing report. If so, most of the value survives.

Original wording: "INSPIRE polygon ingestion — site area + coverage ratio. GATED ON OS LICENCE CLEARANCE."

### 27 August 2026, 09:47:28 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5496127063

Phase 9 — connector written and tested. NOT SHIPPED, and no live data was ever pulled. This item stays Blocked.

Files (all in phase9/)

ledgerstone-boundary-import.ts — connector and geometry logic

ledgerstone-boundary-import.test.ts — 35 tests, 35 pass, 0 fail

ledgerstone-boundary-import.md — the specification and the assumptions

═══ NOT ONE NETWORK CALL WAS MADE ═══

No fetch, no HTTP client, no test call. Audited afterwards for network primitives — clean. Every fixture is a hand-invented polygon (a 100m square, a 20×20 courtyard hole, a 40×30 footprint, two disjoint 50×50 parcels). The default fetcher throws E_LICENCE_NOT_CLEARED before any I/O.

═══ Built for the MIDDLE licensing outcome, which is the likely one ═══

Three outcomes are possible and only the middle one is probable:

(a) never cleared; (b) cleared for internal calculation only — we may use the geometry to compute site area and coverage and feed those into a claim, but may not reproduce the map in an outgoing client report; (c) cleared for full reproduction.

The code defaults to (b), and moving to (a) or (c) requires changing one constant — CURRENT_LICENCE_PERMISSION, currently INTERNAL_CALCULATION_ONLY. No other line changes. Tests cover all three settings.

The split is enforced at the type level, not by convention — this was the part I most wanted to get right:

• DerivedScalar<T> — what the compute functions return. It structurally cannot hold a coordinate, so it is safe in any report whatever the licence says.

• CartographicArtefact — an opaque handle. Its coordinates live in a module-private WeakMap, not on the object. A caller can pass the handle into a calculation but has no way to read a coordinate off it.

• releaseGeometryForReport() is the single choke point that turns an artefact back into readable rings, and it is the only place the permission is checked. It refuses with E_LICENCE_NOT_CLEARED_FOR_REPRODUCTION.

Leaking geometry into a report by accident is therefore not a discipline problem — it is a compile-and-runtime error. A second independent net: flipping the licence switch alone never enables a network call, because the fetcher is a separate default.

The CRS trap, handled

British National Grid (EPSG:27700) is metres, so area works. A lat/long CRS is degrees and area cannot be computed from it naively — a classic way to get a confidently wrong number. The code refuses with E_CRS_NOT_PROJECTED / E_UNKNOWN_CRS rather than computing, and never silently reprojects. Shoelace area with winding-order handling and holes subtracted; coverage ratio guarded against footprint-larger-than-site and zero-area.

A grading point worth your attention

site_area_m2 is deliberately not graded A despite the arithmetic being deterministic. Schema §0.5 warns against exactly that. It is capped at B for register sources because of the Land Registration Act 2002 s.60 "general boundaries" rule — title plan boundaries are indicative, not exact. A register lookup here is closer to document-extraction-with-a-threshold than to a bare deterministic fact. Surveyor-measured sources cap at D, matching gross_internal_area_m2. building_coverage_ratio inherits the worst of its two inputs.

This matters commercially: it means a boundary-derived site area can never on its own carry a figure to sign-off.

Assumptions flagged (§6 of the spec): delivery shape, the explicit per-feature CRS string, EPSG:27700-only units, the parcel identifier joining to title_number, and whether the building footprint is a distinct geometry under a distinct licence.

What has to happen to ship

Licence position established → set CURRENT_LICENCE_PERMISSION to the real outcome → validate the format assumptions → supply a real fetcher.

## DPO: allow company names on conveyancing uploads, strip individuals?

`12927233336` · 3 comments

### 4 September 2026, 17:54:49 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5521469667

Why this item exists, recorded here before the name was shortened (Phase 83, 4 September 2026).

A narrower interim option for the DPO to rule on.

CPSE replies and the sale contract are the two document types that remain gated: both name the parties to a transaction, and who sold the property to whom is exactly the fact the tax rules need. The pipeline currently refuses to send anything resembling a person's name to the extraction model, so the one fact these documents exist to supply is the one thing it cannot read.

The narrower option: permit corporate party identifiers on those two upload types — company names and numbers — and strip individuals. That would unblock the common case (company to company) without ever sending a natural person's name.

This is offered as an option with its cost, not as a recommendation. It is the DPO's call.

### 5 September 2026, 18:19:28 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5522874960

<b>Phase 89, 5 September 2026 — the question this item is blocked on now exists.</b> It did not before, anywhere.<br><br>

The third of the four blockers Phase 86 found pointing at a question nobody had written. It is now in CAPREBATE QUESTIONS, section five, in the standard six-part shape, titled <b>"May company names stay on conveyancing uploads if we strip the individuals?"</b><br><br>

<b>The difficulty the question makes explicit, rather than assuming away.</b> A company name is not personal data, so keeping it should need no basis. But in this sector the party very often IS a person — a sole trader's practice, a family property company, a proprietor holding personally — and the parties clause is the fact entitlement turns on. So "keep companies, strip individuals" is easy to write and hard to apply, because the document does not always say which it is looking at. The worked example is a contract naming a company as seller and a named dentist as freehold proprietor on the next line.<br><br>

<b>Our recommendation, stated as a recommendation.</b> Permit company names and registered numbers on these two document types; strip named individuals by default; and where an individual IS the party to the transaction, keep the name but as a party to our client's own transaction and recorded as such, rather than as an incidental name that slipped through. <b>And if the answer is no, say so plainly</b> — that decides we cannot process these two document types at all, and the two extraction specifications behind them should be abandoned rather than left gated indefinitely.<br><br>

<b>It should be answered alongside the document-pipeline impact assessment</b> (item 12910861459), which carries this as one of its own conditions. Both are now listed for the DPO in the new register FOR THE SOLICITOR, THE DPO AND THE DEVELOPER (item 12983537653).<br><br>

### 12 September 2026, 18:34:18 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5542865783

Phase 129, 12 September 2026 — the strip this item asks about is built, and switched off.

What it does when switched on. On the pre-contract enquiry replies and the sale contract, a party to the transaction that is a company or an LLP keeps its name and its Companies House number. Every individual is replaced by a role token such as [SELLER], [WITNESS] or [FEE EARNER]: a proprietor holding personally, a witness, a signatory, the fee earner. A sole trader, a partnership and a public body are stripped too. So is any party whose legal form is not known, and "not known" and "never recorded" behave the same. A company name that reads like a person's name is stripped rather than kept.

Off is exactly today. While switched off, every party is captured as its role token and nothing else, and a test compares the two byte for byte. It is tested both ways, and each test was seen to fail when its rule was deliberately undone.

What it does not do. It does not keep an individual who is the party — the question's own example of a dentist holding the freehold personally. That wider permission waits on the answer. It does not change either document's receipt policy, and no screen uses it yet.

Files: 09-app/backend/src/web/conveyancing-strip.ts (new), 09-app/backend/src/web/upload-handler-port.ts and 09-app/backend/test/phase129.test.ts (new). Recorded in the Developer Spec, section 4, and in the CRM disposition, row E156 and Part S.

What it contains. Ten events and nine parameters, both as closed lists, with permitted value sets for every enum. An explicit never-send list of parameter names that are hard-blocked even if a future call site passes them. Two design decisions worth your eye. First, GA4 is not loaded on post-engagement pages at all — stage 4 of the funnel only exists after engagement, and everything behind engagement handles a named client and a named property, so the clean control is not loading the tag rather than policing its parameters. Second, every event goes through one wrapper that validates against the allow-list, drops anything unrecognised in production and errors in development, with a build-time test over every call site. The real failure mode here is not malice; it is somebody adding a helpful debug parameter eighteen months from now. A list enforced in one place survives that. A convention in a document does not.

One caution I have flagged rather than buried. `nation` and `sector` are safe as counts and unsafe as a drill-down: private hospitals + Northern Ireland may well be one real business, because the sector with the highest value per job also has the fewest instances. The rule attached is behavioural — report on counts, never open a single session's detail view. If that feels fragile, drop `nation` and take the Scotland suppression count from the internal record instead; the analytical loss is small. For the same reason floor area, GIA, room count and every money field are on the never-send list even though none is an identifier on its own.

The question I would actually put to the DPO first (§5.9). Does GA4 need to be in the picture at all? Five counts grouped by four enums could be produced from our own server logs — no third-party recipient, no international transfer, no privacy-notice entry, no consent dependency, and none of this section's failure surface. The cost is losing GA4's ready-made reporting, which section 4 already says not to build a dashboard around at pilot volume. Worth an explicit decision rather than defaulting to GA4 because it is what everyone uses.

## Resolve a property's postcode to its billing authority from the ONS postcode lookup — the free route is confirmed available

`12991298199` · 3 comments

### 7 September 2026, 19:54:11 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5525632625

Phase 97, 7 September 2026 — this was described as blocked and it is not.

Nothing in the system resolves a property to its billing authority. Re-verified today: location_key is an input the cost model consumes and nothing produces it, which is the real reason the location factor could not ship even with the price book on the desk.

The item had been recorded as blocked on the VOA rating list, which is licence-gated. The free alternative was never checked. It has now been checked and it works.

Publisher. Office for National Statistics, Open Geography Portal.
Product. National Statistics Postcode Lookup (August 2026) — also the ONS Postcode Directory (August 2026), same licence, same cadence.
Licence. Open Government Licence v3.0. No negotiation, no counterparty, no fee. Three attribution lines must be displayed: "Contains OS data © Crown copyright and database right [year]", "Contains Royal Mail data © Royal Mail copyright and database right [year]", and "Source: Office for National Statistics licensed under the Open Government Licence v.3.0".
Bulk file. NSPL_AUG_2026.zip, 176.5 MB (185,109,467 bytes), CSV, downloadable with no key and no account.
Cadence. Quarterly — February, May, August, November.
Coverage. 2,726,477 postcodes.
The field we need. LAD25CD, the local authority district code — which at England and Wales level is the billing authority for non-domestic rates.

Proved, not assumed. The ONS's own live service was queried today and returned: CF10 3NB → W06000015 (Cardiff); SW1A 1AA → E09000033 (Westminster); M1 1AE → E08000003 (Manchester). So there are two build routes — ingest the quarterly file, or query the live service per postcode — and the choice is an engineering one, not a licensing one.

One carve-out, and it does not bite us. Northern Ireland postcodes (BT) need a separate commercial licence from Land and Property Services. We serve England and Wales, so this is out of scope — but it must not be quietly ignored if that ever changes.

Two things to get right when this is built. A postcode unit can straddle a boundary and ONS assigns it by mean grid reference, so the answer is a best fit rather than a certainty — immaterial for a regional cost factor, but it should be recorded as derived and not asserted as fact. And under the standing rule on when a call may fire, this is a free lookup: it fires once the client has given permission, behind the published privacy notice, not after signature.

Also fix this when you build it. The full specification's evidence table already prints "Billing authority — Cardiff — Derived". Nothing derives it. That row is currently a claim the engine cannot support.

Two empty tables — and they are empty for different reasons, which the licence strings say in terms: the postcode table waits on an ingest anybody could run this afternoon, the price-book key map waits on a £330 purchase. resolveLocationKey fails with a different error code at each link so the message names which of the two is missing.

## Make the postcode resolver actually run — where the 292MB table lives, and who refreshes it quarterly

`12993800139` · 3 comments

### 8 September 2026, 07:38:40 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5527391578

Created 8 September 2026. Nothing is in the way — this is a build, and it is written up as Phase 110 in the action plan.

The postcode-to-billing-authority resolver was built and proven end to end against the real 2.7 million-row ONS file. What it has not got is anywhere to live and anyone to refresh it, and nothing calls it.

Three jobs, and the first decides the other two.

1. Where does a 292 MB table live at runtime? A real architectural choice: JSON in memory (simplest, ~292 MB resident per process), a keyed store such as SQLite or the back end's own database, or trimmed to what we serve. Trimming is not consequence-free — we serve England and Wales and the table holds Scotland too, so a trimmed table must make a Scottish postcode refuse as outside the served jurisdiction rather than as not in table. The adapter goes behind an interface so the choice can change without touching the resolver.

2. Wire it to the location factor, and leave the gate off. Connect postcode to location key and stop there — the last link, council area to the price book's own regional key, stays empty until the book is bought. The chain must keep failing at that link and naming which half is missing; that behaviour is built and tested, and a wiring change must not turn a refusal into a silent 1.0.

3. Who refreshes it, and what a stale table does. ONS publishes quarterly, tableIsStale() reports at 120 days, and nothing reads it. The refresh belongs in an operational document, not a code comment — a quarterly duty that lives only in a comment is a duty nobody performs. The procedure must also say to check the local-authority column name, because ONS renames it every release.

Not to be decided in this work: whether the lookup needs the published-notice gate. That is open with the data protection officer, with our recommendation written up. Build so either answer is a one-line change, and do not build a second gate.

## The amendment window is read from the latest accounting year end only — check which period's return a claim belongs in

`13034238993` · 1 comment

### 13 September 2026, 11:02:21 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5543197019

Built — Phase 129b, 13 September 2026, on the Mac copy of the tree. One half is live; the other half is a tax-adviser switch, off.

What Rulebook A says. Section 4 settles it: the annual investment allowance and first-year allowances are made for the chargeable period in which the money was spent, so the amendment window that counts is the return for that period — not the latest one the client gives.

Live. The engine now finds the accounting year the money was spent in — the first year end on or after the completion date, on the day and month of the year end given — and uses it wherever that year ends before the year end given. That can only close a window, never open one. Example: year end given 31 March 2026, purchase completed 1 June 2021. The return for the year to 31 March 2022 closed on 31 March 2024, so the client is now shown writing-down allowances and no refund, where until today they were told the return was still open. The client is told which year the window was worked out for, and that it assumes twelve-month accounting years that kept the same year end.

Switched off. Where the money was spent after the year end given, the year end given still decides. Rolling it forward there could open a window, so it sits behind a new tax-adviser switch that ships off. The question is in CAPREBATE QUESTIONS, section two, among the questions that change money, and the entry is A15 in FOR THE ACCOUNTANT.

Evidence. Suite W, W4 to W7, in both engine modes (912 pass, 0 fail, 4 expected failures), and the cash route proof's R17 and R18 — red against the copy taken before the change. The back end already reads the recorded accounting period that contains the acquisition date, so it needed no change.

What this is. The whole of it is written as a phase in the action plan, under the heading "taking back a pick". It closes a one-way door that the phase before it built: when a person chooses, from a ranked list, which register entry is the client's building, the choice is stored and there is no way back. Saying "none of them" can be undone; saying "this one" cannot.

## A person's word that a name on a client document belongs to an organisation — built, and waiting on the data protection officer (Word question 210)

`13118508369` · 1 comment

### 23 September 2026, 18:09:02 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5573077176

Built on 23 September 2026 by Phase 146i. Nothing is waiting on a build; it is waiting on one decision.

When we read a client's document, two of the things it can tell us are names: who paid a grant, and who signed the building work off. We keep either one only if it is an organisation — a funding body, or a council — and never if it is a person. Nothing in the system can tell the two apart, because the control checks the name of the field and never the value in it.

So somebody has to say. Until this phase nobody could, and the consequence was worse than it sounds: the refusal covers the whole set of claims, so the entire document was discarded, not only that one line. A grant funding agreement and a building regulations completion certificate were document types that could never be captured at all.

What now exists. The question is on the document's own page, for Admin and Sales: "Is the name of whoever paid the grant an organisation, not a person?", with yes, no and not sure. ## OPEN GAP — TMA 1970 s.12ABA partnership return amendment window, and how a partnership amendment flows to partners' individual returns. Named as unclosed in Module A v2 §10 Q2 and §11. GP and dental are partnership-heavy

`12851600794` · 2 comments

### 24 August 2026, 12:49:21 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5485521858

<p><b>Gap closed.</b> Read TMA 1970 s.12ABA, s.12AA, s.12ABB, s.12AC, s.30B, Schedule 1AB and CAA 2001 s.3 in full on legislation.gov.uk. Write-up: <a href="https://seveneightsixmediagroup.monday.com/docs/18427872378">OPEN GAP CLOSED — TMA 1970 s.12ABA</a>.</p><p><b>Window:</b> 12 months after the <i>filing date</i>, not after delivery — so filing late does not extend it. For a partnership of individuals that is 31 January of Year 2 plus 12 months. <b>As at today the only open year for an ordinary GP or dental partnership is 2024-25, closing 31 January 2027.</b> A partnership with any corporate member runs on a different basis entirely (s.12AA(5B)/(5C), broadly two years from period end), so the engine must not apply the 31 January date to a mixed partnership. <b>Flow-through:</b> s.12ABA(3) makes it HMRC's job — the officer <i>shall</i> amend each partner's s.8/8A or company tax return. Partners do not amend their own returns and their own windows are irrelevant, which answers §10 Q2. Former partners for the period are in scope and will receive repayments.</p><p><b>The commercially important finding, which I did not expect going in:</b> overpayment relief will <i>not</i> rescue a missed capital allowances claim. TMA Sch 1AB para 2 Case A(2)(b) and (c) exclude, in terms, a mistake consisting of failing to make a claim or election and "a mistake consisting of making, or failing to make" an allocation of expenditure to a capital allowances pool; Case C reinforces it. So there is no four-year fallback for partnerships — the 12-month s.12ABA window is the only deadline. If the funnel currently offers partnership clients a four-year retrospective horizon, that is an over-promise and should be treated as a defect. Ten findings and four CTA questions in the doc, the first being confirmation of that Case A reading since the partnership commercial model rests on it.</p>

The question is now a document request with a stated consequence — "Do you have the election notice?" not "was there an election?" — followed by a checklist running the six s.201 content requirements against the document. ## C-5 — Nominal (£1) elections have no handling. Valid, irrevocable, bind all future owners. Need early-exit reasoned negative

`12840979280` · 1 comment

### 24 August 2026, 14:49:58 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5486063382

The reasoned negative says the three things that matter: it's valid (no floor in s.198(3)/s.199(3), only a ceiling); it's irrevocable (s.200(3), and TMA 1970 s.42 is expressly disapplied by s.201(5)); and it binds every future owner because it fixes the disposal value for s.185. Closing line: "We would rather tell you that now than bill you to reach the same conclusion."

The "still worth knowing" panel is doing real work, not softening the blow. Two things genuinely survive a nominal election and both are live money — fixtures outside its scope (asset-by-asset, CA26850 → C-6) and the client's own s.25 installation spend, which sits on top of the elected figure under s.185(3) (→ D-4/C-4).

Flagging one judgement for review: the de minimis threshold is commercial, not statutory — there is no de minimis in the legislation. I used ≤£1,000 or <0.5% of price paid, as named exported constants with a comment saying they decide only whether we stop early, decide nothing about entitlement, and are meant to be tuned against real pipeline data. Dressing a routing heuristic as a legal test is exactly what these reviews exist to catch, so it's labelled in both the code and the spec.

Also: applyCap returns [value, value], not [0,0] — a nominal election is not nil, and £1 of qualifying expenditure is £1.

## C-7 — s.203 three-month obligation to notify HMRC of a return made incorrect by an election is absent from every deliverable

`12840953135` · 2 comments

### 24 August 2026, 14:56:18 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5486099437

C-7 fixed. s.203 is now a named, mandatory section in both reports (Report Pack §4.3), a subsection in Module-00, a client-facing row in the sample report, and LS_ELECTION.s203Position() in all five engines.

Why this one is different from the rest of Module C: every other defect is about getting a number right. This is a duty that runs against our own client, and our work is what triggers it. A client who has never heard of s.203 can acquire an affirmative obligation because of diligence we performed — and the three-month clock starts when they become aware, which in practice is when our report is issued. That's why it can't sit in the small print.

Three positions: no_election_identified · return_being_amended · notification_may_be_required. Two rules attached — the issue date must appear on the face of the section so the accountant can diary it, and where no obligation arises the section still appears and says so, because recording that the question was asked is worth as much as raising the duty.

One branch flagged for CTA rather than assumed: I treat "return still open → amend rather than notify" as the correction route. That's sensible but s.203 doesn't carve out in-date returns in terms, and it could be wrong where an earlier closed period is also affected. The branch prompts for that, and I added a release check asking the CTA to confirm it.

Also: required is null, not true — the engine establishes that the question arises and who must answer it, not that a notification is due. And every artefact says Ledgerstone does not make the notification; the client does, through their own accountant.

Full record: C-7 — s.203 three-month notification: fix record

LS_ELECTION.rateSplit() captures the split from the document, and where the election states one it feeds D-2's pool model at the measured basis — the one basis D-2 permits to drive a client-facing pool figure. Verified end to end: a £400k election with £150k on integral features produces main [250000,250000] / special [150000,150000]. A document the client already holds now sizes the tax-timing layer, which is the state D-2 couldn't reach alone.

One restriction that matters: the election's split feeds the whole-property pool only where the election covers the fixtures generally. Scoped to a schedule (C-6), the split describes the elected items alone and extrapolating it would be unevidenced. Enforced and tested.

⚠️ Flagging a deliberate deviation for review. Rulebook C row E-B10 labels a single-figure election LIVE. In this engine LIVE also means "do not cap" — and those come apart here, because a missing split doesn't defeat the FVR. The election can be perfectly good as to quantum in total; what's unsafe is the split, and therefore the timing. Un-capping would overstate the claim on the strength of a defect that doesn't touch the total. So a single-figure election still caps at its stated amount and carries splitRisk plus a window-dependent action (re-elect while open; surveyor/CTA allocation once closed). This is the only Module C row I haven't implemented as written — I think the row and the code agree on substance and only the label differs, but it should be checked.

Also: "I can't tell from the document" resolves to null, not single_figure — not being able to read a document isn't evidence it lacks a split.

## F-1 — BLOCKER, over-claim (GP): Stage 1(a) strips the grant PRO-RATA, directly beneath a comment stating the rule is per-element, not pro-rata. NHS grants target integral features, so % of works understates % of QUALIFYING spend met

`12852269901` · 2 comments

### 24 August 2026, 13:33:44 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5485693643

<p><b>The Phase 1 read this depended on is done.</b> Cyril Lord Carpets Ltd v Schofield 42 TC 637 has been read from the official Tax Cases report (item 12852267431, Done) — write-up: <a href="https://seveneightsixmediagroup.monday.com/docs/18427871876">OPEN GAP — Cyril Lord Carpets v Schofield</a>.</p><p><b>It supports the per-element position this item is raising.</b> The Special Commissioners held that grants under the Capital Grants to Industry Acts were payable "in respect of specific items of plant or machinery" and were <i>therefore</i> related to the expenditure caught by the deeming provision. The transferable principle is a <b>method</b>, not a conclusion: read the grant instrument's own quantification machinery to decide what the grant traces to. HMRC states the same test at CA14100 — "The grant should be specifically related to the capital expenditure on the provision of capital assets" — and s.1177(2) CTA 2009 supplies just-and-reasonable apportionment where a grant is <i>not</i> allocated to particular expenditure.</p><p><b>So the pro-rata strip is wrong where the grant instrument itemises, and defensible only where it does not.</b> That makes the fix conditional on a new input — how the grant was quantified (per-item, per-element, per-square-metre, percentage of approved cost, or unallocated block sum) — rather than a straight swap of pro-rata for per-element. The highest-value open question, logged as F-1-Q2, is whether NHS GMS Premises Directions grants actually itemise; that needs a documents review of a real grant offer, not a legal answer.</p>

### 25 August 2026, 09:40:35 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5488815842

Fixed the BLOCKER — Stage 1's code (pro-rata) genuinely contradicted its own comment ("not pro-rata"). Added a new question (G17q) implementing the Cyril Lord Carpets tracing method directly: where the grant names specific elements (the NHS-typical case), the figure is now disclosed as a conservative floor with a specialist-review flag, instead of silently asserting an "in full" treatment the math never actually did. Where the grant is genuinely whole-scheme, pro-rata is now correctly labelled as the right, final treatment. Didn't attempt to fabricate true per-element netting — no reliable SR-pool split exists at this stage, and the case-read itself flags "how are NHS grants actually quantified" as an open documents-review question (F-1-Q2), not something to guess at. This was tagged Lakhbir + Blocked, which appears to have been inherited from the calibration group's licence and purchase gates (VOA restricted licence, Spon's £330). Neither applies here: Bowerswood House Retirement Home Ltd v HMRC [2015] UKFTT 94 (TC) and Glais House Care Ltd v HMRC [2019] UKFTT 59 (TC) are published tribunal decisions, freely available, no purchase or clearance needed.

These two decisions are the only source of genuinely independent, judicially-examined apportionment figures for care homes that costs nothing. They will not replace BCIS or Spon's for rate-level calibration, but they give a defensible outer sanity check on whether a sector band is in the right region.

Caveat to carry into the work. Both are FTT decisions, so no precedent value, and both are old enough that any figure needs indexing before comparison. Bowerswood in particular turned on a pool enclosure and a s.562 apportionment dispute, so the useful output is the apportionment method and the accepted proportions, not the absolute numbers.

Bowerswood House [2015] UKFTT 94 (TC): going-concern purchase £940k (2004); conservatory pool-enclosure disallowed in full (building/structure, not plant); tribunal endorsed a replacement-cost apportionment formula (Q = P × A/(B+C)) over an asset-by-asset approach; swimming pool value itself left unresolved (£45,596 vs £84,000 claimed) pending further agreement.

Glais House [2019] UKFTT 59 (TC): second-hand asset purchase £1.7m (2011) from administrators; established that a buyer's claim on already-claimed fixtures is capped at the PRIOR owner's original incurred cost — not the sale contract's apportionment figure and not the seller's own (understated) disposal value — except for asset classes (cold water, mains electrical) that only became CA-eligible after the prior owner's spend, which get no cap. £236,144 allowed of £318,792 claimed (equipment line left unresolved).

## Source register — publisher, licence and retrieval timestamp on every field written

`12830181420` · 1 comment

### 26 August 2026, 12:37:06 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5492856149

<p><b>Done — spec + working code attached.</b> Doc: <a href="https://seveneightsixmediagroup.monday.com/docs/18428253325">Source register — publisher, licence and retrieval timestamp on every field</a> (also on the Document column).</p>

<p><b>What was built.</b> Provenance is not stored alongside the value, it is part of the value. The unit of storage is a <code>Cell</code> — the number plus its publisher, licence and retrieval timestamp, hashed together. <code>Cell</code> is a branded type whose brand is exported nowhere, so the store's only write method cannot accept a bare value: <code>store.put(1200)</code> is a type error, not a validation failure.</p>

<p><b>Enforcement sits in three layers</b> — branded types at compile time, runtime validation at the repository, and NOT NULL/CHECK/append-only rules in Postgres. Options and the reasoning for taking all three are in §3. Each catches a class the others structurally cannot; the SQL layer is the only one that survives someone connecting with a psql client.</p>

<p><b>The name exclusion register (12818313893) is now executable.</b> All twelve subitems are encoded as per-source field whitelists. §7 sets out whitelist vs blacklist as a real choice and recommends whitelist-primary, because a control that fails open does not serve a register whose purpose is that a third party's name never arrives. PLANNING — the highest-risk source — has a six-field whitelist containing no free-text field capable of carrying a name. Test T8 asserts that exactly two sources in the whole register declare a personal-name exception (Companies House PSC, HMLR personal proprietor) and fails the build if a third is ever added. That is the automated assertion asked for in subitem 12818333519.</p>

<p><b>Two things the tests found, not review.</b> (1) A derived figure's licence is our own, and our own licence caps nothing — so a figure computed from a 30-day CQC field would have become immortal. The cache window now inherits the strictest cap in the input chain exactly as the grade inherits the worst grade (I-2). (2) UNKNOWN now has no in-cell representation for "not yet asked" — that state is the absence of a row — so there is nothing for a <code>|| 0</code> to catch hold of. That is the direct fix for the five-sector <code>grant_fraction || 0</code> defect.</p>

<p><b>Flagged, not assumed — needs the solicitor/DPO (§9).</b> Three licences are coded at the restrictive reading and pinned by a test until cleared: HMLR official-copy redistribution to the accountant report; the CQC syndication cache window; and whether a derived £/m² printed in the CAVR counts as reproduction of the BCIS rate table. The BCIS one may be a real constraint on what the CAVR can show, so it wants answering rather than living in a flag. Retention periods for the two personal-name exceptions also need stating in the LIA.</p>

<p><b>Tests:</b> 30 tests, <code>node --test</code> on Node 24, no build step and no dependencies. <b>30 pass, 0 fail.</b> Source files on the build machine at <code>Desktop\Ledgestone all\ledgerstone all\phase3\</code>.</p>

## Reconciliation engine — conflict register, confidence grading, capture list

`12830181808` · 1 comment

### 26 August 2026, 12:47:30 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5492883307

<p><b>Done — spec + working code attached.</b> Doc: <a href="https://seveneightsixmediagroup.monday.com/docs/18428254853">Reconciliation engine — conflict register, confidence grading, capture list</a> (also on the Document column). Builds on 12830181420, so every claim arrives carrying its publisher, licence and retrieval timestamp.</p>

<p><b>Three outputs, as specified.</b> A conflict register holding every claim including the ones that lost; a confidence per field; and a capture list of questions in the words you would actually put to a person. On the worked example — EPC 1,200 m², VOA 1,340, client 1,400 — the engine registers a 200 m² / 16.67% spread across three positions, chooses <b>nothing</b>, and produces one question: "What is the gross internal area? Sources disagree: 1200 m2 (MHCLG) vs 1340 m2 (Valuation Office Agency) vs 1400 m2 (Client). Which figure is correct, and on what basis?"</p>

<p><b>The first test run failed, and the failure mattered.</b> The item-1 whitelist rejected writing <code>gia_m2</code> from the EPC — correctly, since the EPC publishes <code>epc_total_floor_area_m2</code> and the VOA <code>voa_total_area_m2</code>. Three publishers, three names, one quantity. Without a mapping the three numbers would never have met and <b>no conflict would ever have been detected</b> — the most dangerous failure available to a reconciliation engine, and one that looks exactly like everything working. <code>FieldSpec.claims_from</code> and <code>gatherClaims()</code> close it; test R26 pins it. This is now open item O-2: the mappings need building out across the shared core and all five sectors, because the gap recurs silently per field.</p>

<p><b>Two design choices worth your attention (§4 and §7).</b> First, when may the engine pick? Never picking floods the capture list with 0.1 m² differences and trains people to skim it, which is worse than a shorter list they read. So: rounding-level differences settle on best evidence, material ones go to a human. Second, the "confidence grade per field" does <b>not</b> rewrite the schema grade — §0.5 says the grade belongs to the field, not the job. The grade travels through untouched and the job-level judgement is a separate <code>gate_ready</code> flag stating I-17 directly.</p>

<p><b>Corroboration requires independence.</b> The client answering 1,400 on the form and 1,400 in an uploaded lease is one source saying it twice, not two sources agreeing. Same for HMLR Price Paid and HMLR Title — one publisher. Without this a C-grade assertion could promote itself through a gate simply by being repeated.</p>

<p><b>The null never gets guessed.</b> Absent, UNKNOWN and contested are three distinct capture reasons carrying no value at all, and they route to different people: UNKNOWN escalates with "Do not re-ask — establish it from a document or on site", because asking the client again gets the same answer. Stale evidence routes to SYSTEM as a re-fetch rather than becoming noise in front of a person.</p>

<p><b>Tests:</b> 26 tests, <code>node --test</code> on Node 24, no dependencies. <b>26 pass, 0 fail.</b> Files at <code>Desktop\Ledgestone all\ledgerstone all\phase3\</code>.</p>

<p><b>Open — needs a human decision, not an engineering one (§12).</b> Tolerances are set for three worked-example fields only; the rest need a pass, and the 2%/5 m² on gross internal area is a surveying judgement about measuring conventions. Schema gap G-1 (<code>contribution_payer_class</code> inferred rather than established) now surfaces as UNCORROBORATED_GATE instead of passing silently — visible, but not closed.</p>

AS-2 is the one that would have been missed: <b>the base is not the price paid</b>. GC-03 in the Report Pack has a purchase of £317,000 and an apportioned base of £332,850 — a 5% difference that flows straight into the qualifying figure. Build only AS-1 and that £15,850 sails through, because nothing ever compares those two numbers. AS-2 requires every pound of it to be a named, evidenced adjustment. AS-3 enforces I-15: where a valid evidenced s.198 election exists it governs A; an asserted one does not engage.</p>

<p><b>Tolerance: zero.</b> "Rounding only" is implemented as <i>rounding is allocated, not tolerated</i>. All money is integer pence — no floating-point currency anywhere, because a gate that fails on 0.30000000000000004 is a gate people learn to route around. One penny out blocks. Presentation rounding to whole pounds is a separate later step, and the residual is allocated to the largest component and <b>printed in a footnote on the face of the CAVR</b>. A "residual" over £1.50 is refused rather than allocated, because it is not rounding.</p>

<p><b>Where it runs:</b> five times. Advisory at DRAFT_RECOMPUTE and PRE_REVIEWER — a half-built apportionment obviously does not sum yet, and blocking there teaches people the block is noise. Hard block at PRE_SIGNATURE, REPORT_RENDER and RELEASE_CHECK. The gate is <b>inside</b> signCAVR(), not beside it: SignedCAVR is a branded type with one producer, so there is no code path from an apportionment to a signature that skips the check. Every blocked attempt is recorded with who, when and by how much.</p>

<p><b>What the surveyor sees</b> (§6 has the full rendering): "SIGNATURE BLOCKED… A + B + C comes to £331,100.00. The apportionment base is £332,850.00… under by £1,750.00", then every component with its own publisher, locator and retrieval timestamp, then five ranked likely causes drawn from how these figures actually get built wrong, then: "change the figures — do not absorb the difference."</p>

<p><b>Override: none, as recommended.</b> Not a flag defaulted to false — none, with the rationale sitting in the code beside it so a future reader looking for the override finds the reasoning instead of adding one. The short version: A+B+C=base is arithmetic, not judgement, so no correct apportionment fails it. An override would be used at 6pm on a £4 discrepancy, and the same control is then available for £40,000 — the mechanism cannot tell them apart. A chartered surveyor signing over a known arithmetic failure is making a false professional statement with PI cover and RICS registration behind it. And <b>an override log is disclosable</b>: "the system flagged that it did not add up and someone clicked past it" is the worst document to produce in an enquiry. The legitimate escape already exists and is not an override — change the figures. If this is ever revisited, the question to put is not "should there be an override" but "who signs it, and does their PI policy cover it".</p>

<p><b>Tests:</b> 25 tests, <code>node --test</code> on Node 24. <b>25 pass, 0 fail</b> (first run). GC-03 is the worked case throughout.</p>

<p><b>Needs the tax adviser, not a developer (§11).</b> Five of the nine adjustment kinds are CTA-flagged: whether SDLT, acquisition legal fees and agent fees are capitalised into the apportionment base, and the VAT recoverable/irrecoverable treatment. The code carries them as itemised sourced lines; it does not assert the treatment is right. Also: the Report Pack gives GC-03's £317,000 and £332,850 but not the breakdown — the £9,510/£6,340 split in the tests is a plausible reconstruction for exercising the arithmetic, <b>not</b> a statement about that job, and needs confirming before GC-03 is used as an acceptance case.</p>

## Anchor quarantine — client estimate withheld from surveyor; release logged with timestamp

`12830183464` · 1 comment

### 26 August 2026, 13:05:12 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5492937067

<p><b>Done — spec + working code attached.</b> Doc: <a href="https://seveneightsixmediagroup.monday.com/docs/18428257590">Anchor quarantine — estimate withheld from the surveyor, release logged</a> (also on the Document column).</p>

<p><b>The design does a second job the item did not ask for and which turns out to matter more.</b> By freezing the surveyor's pre-release figures, the quarantine does not merely <i>prevent</i> anchoring — it <b>measures</b> it. Every post-release amendment is compared against the estimate they were then exposed to, so "did they move toward our number, and by how much of the gap" becomes answerable per surveyor, per field, across every job. Worked example in the tests: committed £68,000 against our £73,740, amended to £71,000 after release — 52% of the gap closed. That measurement is the input to 12830166861 and it is not obtainable any other way.</p>

<p><b>Outputs are quarantined; inputs flow freely.</b> The qualifying £, the qualifying %, the pool split, the land value, the multiplier and the saving are withheld — the percentage especially, because it is the same anchor in a different unit. The client's answers, documents, register data, floor areas, room schedule and the capture list are <b>never</b> withheld: holding those back would degrade the survey without protecting anything.</p>

<p><b>Only the surveyor is quarantined, and that is what removes the need for an exception path.</b> The estimate is not a secret — it is simply not shown to that one person until they commit. If the client rings mid-survey wanting to discuss the number, someone who is not the surveyor answers. So there is no legitimate early-access case, and no early-release path exists.</p>

<p><b>Release is automatic on commitment.</b> There is deliberately no separate release action — a control someone can be persuaded to exercise early is not a control, it is an etiquette. Commitment requires the surveyor's own A/B/C figures plus a <b>mandatory method note</b>; a checkbox would prove nothing. Figures are content-hashed at commitment. Amendment afterwards is permitted — it must be, if the estimate reveals a genuine error — but requires a stated reason, because an unexplained change after seeing our number is indistinguishable from drift.</p>

<p><b>The log is hash-chained</b> — edits, deletions and reorderings all detectable, verified from a copy read back out of storage rather than through the object that wrote it. Two details worth flagging: <b>the log records the estimate's hash and never its figures</b>, because a log that stored them would hand the anchor to anyone with audit access, including the surveyor; and <b>denied access attempts are logged</b> — a surveyor who tries three times to peek before committing has told you something.</p>

<p><b>What the system honestly cannot do:</b> stop the client telling the surveyor. It can record it — self-report marks the job EXPOSED rather than CLEAN, so it is excluded from the calibration set instead of quietly polluting it. The matching process control (an engagement-letter clause asking the client not to discuss the estimate with the surveyor) is open item O-3 and needs you plus the solicitor.</p>

<p><b>Tests:</b> 27 tests, <code>node --test</code> on Node 24. <b>27 pass, 0 fail.</b> One test initially passed <i>vacuously</i> — a private field meant the tamper it attempted never happened, so it asserted nothing. Fixing it produced a better design: <code>verifyChain()</code> as a free function over an entries array, which is the shape the real audit use actually needs.</p>

<p><b>Also open (§11):</b> clock provenance — the log is only as good as its timestamps, so server-side time is the minimum and attested time is better; log storage, which should be the same append-only store as the blocked-signature log from 12830173668; and the surveyor-facing wording, which reads as distrust unless it is framed as protecting the value of their signature — worth writing with the surveyor rather than at them.</p>

## AI document pipeline — planning, FRA, O&M, asbestos, reinstatement, lease, contractor breakdown. NEVER pass planning comment text to a model

`12830166311` · 2 comments

### 26 August 2026, 13:15:48 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5492977948

<p><b>Done — spec + working code attached.</b> Doc: <a href="https://seveneightsixmediagroup.monday.com/docs/18428259243">AI document pipeline — extraction per type, thresholds, and the planning-comment rule</a> (also on the Document column).</p>

<p><b>The rule is enforced in four layers, and the two that matter are the first two.</b> <b>L1 NOT ACQUIRED</b> — the fetcher never calls a comments endpoint, and item 12830181420 already refuses to store those fields. You cannot leak what you do not hold. <b>L2 DISCARDED</b> — uploaded planning PDFs <i>do</i> carry representations inline, so the document is segmented and every forbidden segment is dropped <b>before the payload object is constructed</b>. Dropped, not redacted: the text is never a property of the payload, so there is nothing to accidentally serialise, log, cache or forward. <b>L3 UNTYPEABLE</b> — the model client accepts only a branded ModelPayload whose sole producer is sanitise(), so callModel(rawText) is a compile error rather than a code-review question. <b>L4 RE-ASSERTED</b> — pattern scan at the boundary, for plain-JS callers.</p>

<p><b>The test that matters.</b> A spy model records everything it is handed, and the fixture is a realistic officer report with two named objectors at named addresses. P4 asserts that "Brookfield", "Alan", "Chapel Lane", "Raman", "Priya", "objects", the consultee response and the correspondence are <b>all absent</b> from what left. P5 asserts the converse — "two-storey extension", "extract ventilation" and "acoustically enclosed" all arrive, because a control that blocks the useful content too is a broken pipeline rather than a safe one.</p>

<p><b>Two things I want to flag as deliberate.</b> First, <b>the audit trail must not become the leak</b>: the drop record and the egress log carry segment kind, page and reason, never the text they withheld — tests assert the objector's name appears in neither. Second, <b>the spec is honest about the limit of pattern matching</b>: P26 demonstrates that a bare name in running text ("Alan Brookfield objects to the plant") is <b>not</b> caught by any regex. It is caught because the section it sits in is headed "Representations received" and that whole section is dropped. Segment-level dropping is the control; the scrubber is the last line, not the first. Unclassifiable sections fail closed for the same reason.</p>

<p><b>This closes schema gap G-3.</b> Thresholds are set <b>per field by consequence</b>, not one global number: 0.95 for anything entering the apportionment or driving a gate, 0.85 for taxonomy selection, 0.70 for narrative. Above threshold the field stands at grade B; below it drops to C — which means the reconciliation engine then refuses to let it drive a gate uncorroborated (I-17). The threshold plugs into the machinery from item 2 rather than being a quality score nobody acts on. Review tasks route by consequence: apportionment to the surveyor, gate to the CTA, the rest to an analyst, each naming the page and quote reference.</p>

<p><b>Seven document types, each with a stated reason for being in the pipeline.</b> Worth noting three: the <b>O&M plant schedule</b> is a fixture inventory somebody else already built, and is the most direct answer available to gap G-6; the <b>insurance reinstatement valuation</b> is the only genuinely independent cross-check on the rebuild cost in the s.562 residual, so it enters reconciliation as a separate claim on B; and the <b>lease</b> carries the landlord contribution as a pence amount graded APPORTIONMENT, per I-4 — which records that it was a note in four of five sectors and a number in none.</p>

<p><b>The model decides nothing.</b> Extraction produces claims that enter the source register as CLIENT_DOC cells and are then reconciled against every other claim. A value with no locator in the document is refused; an out-of-range confidence is refused rather than clamped; a missing field is NOT_FOUND and routes to capture, never guessed.</p>

<p><b>Tests:</b> 26 tests, all pass. <b>Full Phase 3 suite: 134 tests, 134 pass, 0 fail</b> on Node 24.</p>

<p><b>Needs the DPO, not a developer (§9).</b> A DPIA for the pipeline — which model, hosted where, what retention, what training-use position — and that answer materially affects whether even the permitted segments may be sent. Also the lease-party nuance: the client's own name is theirs and they instructed us, but the counterparty individual is a third party. The pipeline currently drops both, which is safe but may be over-broad and could cost us the entitlement chain. It should not be relaxed without a view.</p>

## Caprebate — surveyor CRM: overrides persist as that surveyor's own rate library, proposed back on later jobs. Track adoption rate per field

`12818968809` · 2 comments

### 26 August 2026, 13:24:14 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5493011707

<p><b>Done — spec + working code attached.</b> Doc: <a href="https://seveneightsixmediagroup.monday.com/docs/18428261014">Surveyor CRM — rate library, proposal-back, and the adoption metric</a> (also on the Document column).</p>

<p><b>The line on the item — "the only honest evidence we will ever have" — is right, and it decided the whole design.</b> Nobody grades our pre-fills. But a chartered surveyor, on a real job, with their own signature at the end of it, either leaves our number alone or does not. That is a revealed preference and it is worth more than any internal review, precisely because nobody is performing it for our benefit. Which means the metric has to be built so it cannot flatter us.</p>

<p><b>Two disciplines do most of that work.</b> First, <b>stratify by what was actually shown</b>. If we pre-fill from the surveyor's own library and they accept it, that is not evidence our estimate is good — it is evidence they agree with themselves. The naive version is easy to build by accident: count acceptances, divide by offers, and watch the number climb steadily as the library fills up. It would not be our estimates improving; it would be the library. So only PLATFORM_DEFAULT pre-fills calibrate, and the code <b>throws</b> if you try to learn an untouched platform default as the surveyor's figure — that would launder our number into their library and destroy the stratification a job later.</p>

<p><b>Second, direction beats magnitude.</b> An adoption rate alone cannot tell apart two very different problems. Overrides scattered symmetrically around zero mean our central estimate is right and our precision is poor. Overrides that all go one way mean we are <b>biased</b> — worse, and far more fixable, because the default is simply wrong and should move. So the median signed delta is reported alongside, and the verdict is one of GOOD / UNBIASED_IMPRECISE / BIASED_HIGH / BIASED_LOW.</p>

<p><b>A third discipline worth flagging:</b> below five observations the rate is <code>null</code> and the verdict is INSUFFICIENT_DATA. Not a percentage with a caveat — null. This number will end up in a board pack, and the caveat gets dropped in the retelling while the number does not.</p>

<p><b>It ties back to the anchor quarantine.</b> An override from a job that quarantine marked EXPOSED is not evidence — the surveyor had already seen our estimate before committing, so their agreement with it means nothing. Those jobs are excluded, and the count of exclusions sits on the face of every stats object so a reader can see how much data was set aside. That closes a loop across three items: the quarantine protects independence, records whether it held, and that record then decides admissibility here.</p>

<p><b>The library and proposal-back:</b> keyed on surveyor × field × sector × region, offered after one observation rather than N — withholding a surveyor's own considered figure from them helps nobody — but always <b>labelled with its origin, observation count and age</b>: "Your figure … 1 observation, last confirmed 14 days ago (job J7)" versus "Ledgerstone default … Not your figure — override freely." A pre-fill whose origin is hidden is the anchoring problem in miniature. Also: divergence is surfaced rather than averaged away, with a note that deliberately withholds judgement — on a technical question the one surveyor who keeps disagreeing may well be the one who has looked properly.</p>

<p><b>Tests:</b> 25, all pass. <b>Full Phase 3 suite: 159 tests, 159 pass, 0 fail.</b></p>

<p><b>Needs a decision before the first number exists (§11).</b> This is a <b>performance metric about a named professional</b>. Using it to calibrate our estimates is one thing; using it to rank, price or select surveyors is another and would need a lawful basis and a fairness assessment. The intended use should be stated in the surveyor's contract up front — and they should be told it exists and why, because a metric discovered later reads as surveillance while one explained up front reads as the mechanism by which their expertise improves our defaults. It also changes behaviour, and behaviour is the measurement.</p>

<p><b>Feeds:</b> 12830166861 (calibration set), via <code>calibrationFeed()</code> — which carries its own method note stating both exclusions, because a percentage travels much further than the caveats attached to it in an email.</p>

### 29 August 2026, 12:20:01 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5502223262

## Build both valuation methods behind a switch — the surveyor picks one later

`12804374838` · 2 comments

### 26 August 2026, 07:17:39 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5492259567

What this is
A question for the surveyor once appointed. Importantly, it does not block the build — we can construct both answers and let them pick.

In plain English
To value the equipment in a building you first ask what it would cost to put it there. There are two accepted ways to answer:

• Replacement new — what it would cost to install it brand new today. Simpler, and produces a higher figure.
• Depreciated replacement cost — the same, then reduced to reflect the age and condition of what is actually there. More defensible, and produces a lower figure.

Different surveyors prefer different answers, and it is their professional judgement to make, not ours.

How we are handling it
Build both calculations behind a setting, and let the appointed surveyor choose which one runs. That way nothing waits on this decision — which is why it is marked not blocking.

Original wording: "D5 — DECIDE with surveyor: replacement-new vs depreciated replacement cost. NOT BLOCKING — build both branches behind a config flag, surveyor picks."

### 27 August 2026, 09:46:48 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5496126299

Phase 9 — DONE. Both branches built, tested, and the default set.

Where the code is

phase9/ledgerstone-cost-model.cjs — resolveValuationBasis() and the VALUATION_BASIS switch.

Tests F1–F8 in ledgerstone-cost-model.test.cjs. All 51 assertions passing.

Harness 216 pass / 0 fail / 14 xfail (was 207/0/11).

Why this one is Done when the four LEG-E items around it are not

This item's own text said it: "NOT BLOCKING — build both branches behind a config flag, surveyor picks." It had been tagged to the Surveyor and sat untouched. But a switch does not need a surveyor to exist — it needs a surveyor to be set. Building it was never blocked; only choosing it is. Now built, it is also the thing LEG-E5 was partly waiting on, so that dependency is cleared.

The two branches

• replacement_new — what it would cost to install brand new today. Simpler, higher figure.

• drc (depreciated replacement cost) — the same, then reduced for the age and condition of what is actually there. More defensible, lower figure.

═══ The default is drc, the conservative basis. Three reasons. ═══

1. The asymmetry of being wrong. Default high and the surveyor lowers it, and a client has already been shown a number we then take away — on the residual path that number has usually reached them through the public calculator. Default low and the surveyor raises it, and the client gets better news than promised. Only one of those two costs us a client, and only one of them looks like a bait.

2. It is the harder basis to attack. DRC values what is actually in the building. Replacement-new values a building nobody has — a twelve-year-old boiler valued as new is a figure that invites an enquiry to open by asking what else we rounded up.

3. A default is not neutral, so it should not pretend to be. Whichever way this switch points, most cases will run on it, because defaults are what get accepted. A default that overstates is a commercial choice dressed as a technical one.

And it changes no number today — which is why it could ship immediately

Depreciation is LEG-E5 (item 12804317685), which is gated off with empty tables. With E5 off, DRC applies a factor of 1.0 to every element — arithmetically identical to replacement-new. Test F3 asserts this. So the conservative default is live from today at zero cost, and the day E5's tables land the basis is already pointing the right way.

But it says so, rather than pretending. The output carries DRC_SELECTED_BUT_DEPRECIATION_UNAVAILABLE and depreciation_effective: false. A "DRC" label sitting over undepreciated arithmetic would otherwise be a quiet lie on the face of a report (test F4).

Test F5 proves the switch actually bites once tables are loaded: with an invented fixture scale, DRC produces a materially lower qualifying figure than replacement-new. Test F6 proves replacement-new skips depreciation entirely even with the tables loaded.

The surveyor overrides it, and their choice is attributed

basis_source reads default until someone sets it, then config or surveyor, with basis_set_by recording the name. Whose judgement a figure rests on is part of the figure. Until a named surveyor sets it the output carries VALUATION_BASIS_NOT_SET_BY_SURVEYOR.

The basis is graded D (surveyor judgement) per Consolidated Schema §0.5, and under the sign-off rule an unresolved D blocks the sign-off-ready output. So this being Done does not mean the question is closed — it means the question now has somewhere to be answered. It is on the agenda for the free 45-minute surveyor call (item 12830181616).

One caveat on "Done"

The switch is complete and tested inside the Phase 9 module. Wiring the module into ledgerstone-site.html is a separate act and has not happened — the shipped engine still uses yield bands and has no residual model at all. Suite I of the regression harness carries an xfail that watches for it: the day the site imports this module the harness goes loudly red and tells whoever did it to convert the suite.

## 🔒 MULTI-MACHINE PROTOCOL — read before starting anything. Claim an item (Status='Working on it' + 'Claimed by (machine)') BEFORE you touch it. Monday has no file locking; this column IS the lock. Full rules: Working Conventions v2 §9

`12852095730` · 2 comments

### 20 August 2026, 09:03:12 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5476561524

How to run more than one machine on this board
----------------------------------------------

Monday has no file locking and no merge. Two machines editing the same artefact means one loses its work silently, and neither notices until the wrong version has been attached and treated as current. These rules are what prevent that.

1. Claim before you start
-------------------------

* Open the item. Check Status and Claimed by (machine).
* Status Working on it with a machine name in the claim column means taken. Pick something else.

* If free: set Status to Working on it, put your machine name in Claimed by (machine), and post a one-line update saying what you intend to change.
* Finish with the close-out protocol (Working Conventions v2 §7), then clear the claim column.
* Abandoning a task means resetting it — Status back to Not started, claim column cleared. A stale claim blocks another machine indefinitely and is worse than no claim at all.

2. Parallel-safe versus single-writer
-------------------------------------

The rule of thumb: work that produces NEW files is parallel-safe. Work that EDITS an existing file is single-writer.

Safe to run simultaneously: Rulebooks F, G, H and I (one new file each — four machines could take one each); case-law and legislation research; C2 BAILII extraction; the five report templates; S13 private hospitals question flow; S2–S5 sector uplifts once S1 has completed.

Single-writer only: every engine defect (E-, D-, C-, LEG-) — they all edit the same application file; the E-1/E-2 propagation task, which touches four files at once; and S1, which must finish before S2–S5 start.

3. The file-state problem
-------------------------

Each machine has its own workspace and files are not shared between them. A board attachment is a snapshot from the moment of upload, not the live file. Before editing an existing artefact, get the current version — do not assume the local copy is current and do not reconstruct from an attachment. After editing, attach the new version with a version suffix immediately.

If you find an item marked Done that is not actually done, post an update naming the discrepancy before fixing it. Silent correction destroys the audit trail that makes the board trustworthy. This rule exists because E-1 and E-2 were marked Done while four of five files still carried the wrong copy.

4. The safe split until the shared store exists
-----------------------------------------------

Google Drive is connected to this workspace but is not yet the canonical file store. Until it is:

One machine holds all code and engine work — the application file, the propagation task, the prototypes. Other machines take document work only — rulebooks, research, report templates, schema specs. That split has no overlap and needs no merge.

Setting up the shared folder is logged in group 11 and would remove the constraint entirely. Until then this is the binding limit on how many machines can usefully run at once: one on code, any number on documents.

## Pipeline defect — no extraction spec verifies an uploaded document relates to the subject property. Entity association is asserted at upload, never checked against the document. Add a cross-cutting document_property_match

`12902224596` · 2 comments

### 26 August 2026, 14:14:12 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5493226898

The defect. All seven extraction specifications in the pipeline (item 12830166311) extract fields from an uploaded document and write them as claims against the job's entity. None of them checks that the document is about that property. The entity_id comes from the upload context — which slot on which job the file arrived in — so the association is asserted by us, never verified from the document's own contents.

Why it matters more than it sounds. Care home operators typically run several homes, and a manager asked for "your fire risk assessment" will upload the one they find first. The failure mode is not a bad extraction. It is a clean, high-confidence extraction of correct data about the wrong building. Every existing control passes it:

• Thresholds don't catch it. They measure extraction confidence, not relevance. A legible FRA for the client's other home scores well above 0.95.
• Reconciliation doesn't catch it. The engine compares claims about a field; it has no notion of a claim being about a different entity. A single confident claim raises no conflict.
• Grade doesn't catch it. Client-derived either way.
• It can falsely corroborate. An insurance reinstatement valuation for another property enters as an independent claim on rebuild cost — and then either agrees with our model, which is worse, or creates a spurious conflict that a human spends time resolving.
• And it survives into the defence pack, where it sits looking like evidence, with a retrieval timestamp and a provenance cell.

The fix — cross-cutting, not per-spec. A shared document_property_match applied to every DocType, at GATE consequence (0.95). Extract the property as the document itself states it — address lines, postcode, UPRN where present, site or building name — and compare against the Land Registry title address for the job plus any known alternative names for the site.

Three outcomes, and the third is where the design work is:
• MATCH — proceed normally.
• MISMATCH — the document contributes no claims and routes to review. Not discarded: a mismatch can be legitimate (a group-wide FRA covering six homes, a portfolio insurance schedule), and that is a human call.
• NOT_STATED — the document identifies no property at all. This cannot be collapsed into MATCH, for the same reason UNKNOWN is never coalesced with a value.

The real tension, named. NOT_STATED will be common, and it will be commonest on the most valuable document type: O&M plant schedules frequently carry only a project reference and no address. So this must not be a hard ingestion gate, or it will fail exactly where the richest fixture evidence lives.

Proposed resolution. The check runs per document and its outcome is carried with every claim that document produces, rather than gating ingestion. A claim from a NOT_STATED document is still usable, but it is marked, and it cannot corroborate another claim. That mirrors a principle already in the codebase — a pre-fill the surveyor accepted from their own library is not independent evidence that our estimate was good, and is stratified out of the adoption metric for exactly that reason. Same logic, different place.

Portfolio documents need a second pass. Where a document names several properties and the subject is among them, MATCH is correct only if the extraction is then scoped to the right section. A group FRA that lists six homes will otherwise contribute another home's plant to this claim. Flagging it as a known sub-problem rather than solving it here.

Why now rather than after pilot. Nothing is in production, so there is no back-catalogue of already-ingested documents to re-check. The same fix after launch means retrofitting the check across every stored claim and re-opening closed defence packs — which, given those are sealed and immutable by design (item 12804317757), means superseding packs rather than correcting them. It is cheap this month and expensive later.

Tests. An FRA for a different property in the same client's group → MISMATCH, no claims written, review task raised. An O&M schedule with no address → NOT_STATED, claims written but marked, and asserted not to corroborate. A group FRA naming the subject among six → MATCH, plus the scoping sub-problem flagged. A subject-property document with a formatting variance in the address (abbreviations, missing postcode) → MATCH, because a check that fails on "Rd" versus "Road" will be switched off within a week.

Found while specifying item 12902240772; it is a defect in the shipped seven, not part of that work. Developer to build — no DPO question arises, since a property address is the client's own data and already held.
