Why this exists. The Stage 2 upload screen (12818978746) asks for ten documents; the pipeline (12830166311) has specs for seven types, six of which are on that screen. Four have no spec at all. The record shows this was scoping inheritance, not a considered exclusion: all ten subitems were created 17 Aug 2026, the pipeline item was created 18 Aug already titled with seven types, and the build delivered exactly to that title. No reason for the omission is recorded anywhere.

The four are four different cases, and treating them as one is what produced the gap.

Buildable now, no dependencies:
• BUILDING_REGS_COMPLETION — reference, issuing body (local authority vs approved inspector, which decides whether any other copy exists), works description, completion date. TAXONOMY. A straight omission.
• GRANT_FUNDING_AGREEMENT — funder, amount in pence, date, purpose verbatim with locator, itemised schedule, conditions. APPORTIONMENT. Emits no derived deduction figure: whether funding was payable for specific items is the Rulebook F tracing judgement and goes to a CTA review task.

Designed, gated:
• CPSE_REPLIES — locates the capital allowances enquiries and returns question and reply verbatim with page and quote reference. Emits no seller_pooled field; a person sets the gate from the quoted words. That is the better design, not a compromise — "the Seller has not claimed" and "not so far as the Seller is aware" are different answers, and a conclusion-extraction would flatten the difference. Also captures the form edition, because CPSE.1 renumbers across editions and an enquiry number alone is not a stable identifier.
• SALE_CONTRACT — a recall-tuned finder, never a decider. The failure mode is asymmetric: a false negative lets a file proceed on a full apportionment when it is capped, possibly at £1; a false positive costs five minutes. So it over-flags every schedule, clause or annexe that could be a fixtures value agreement. Emits no election_present, no elected_amount, no s.201(3) validity assessment. Plus contract_schedule_index, returned unconditionally — a finder that silently returns nothing is otherwise indistinguishable from a contract with no election.

One structural addition. A candidate is not a value, so the existing threshold machinery does not fit: candidates emit review tasks directly and never enter the source register as claims — no grade, not reconciled, cannot corroborate. Needs a FinderSpec alongside FieldSpec. That is the only change to the pipeline's shape in this document; nothing else loosens a single existing control.

What gates the last two. Not a new blocker — the one the pipeline already raised. SIGNATORIES and CORRESPONDENCE fail closed, but for a contract or conveyancing replies the parties clause is load-bearing for the entitlement chain: who sold to whom is the s.187A question. The pipeline flagged this exact tension for the lease and left it with the DPO. So these wait on the pipeline DPIA and the lease-party question. §7 offers a narrower interim option for the DPO to consider — permit corporate party identifiers only (company name and number), continue dropping individual names, which covers most healthcare entitlement chains. Offered as an option, not a recommendation.

Also in the doc: the seven tests to write, including the decoy case (an inventory schedule headed "Fixtures and Fittings" must be flagged, not suppressed — over-flagging is the spec and the test has to lock it in), and assertions that no conclusions are emitted for any of the three.

A separate defect this surfaced, worth its own item. None of the seven existing specs verifies that an uploaded document actually relates to the subject property. A fire risk assessment for the client's other home would extract cleanly and be silently wrong. Recommend a shared document_property_match check at GATE consequence across every type, rather than a field bolted onto each spec.

## TAXONOMY DEFECT (Phase 10, F-8) — Dental has no contested-ventilation row. HTM/IHEEM-driven LDU negative-pressure extract will default silently into LS-SR-004 with no flag raised

`12927122790` · 2 comments

### 29 August 2026, 08:21:44 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5502097986

What this is. A defect in Ledgerstone-Fixture-Taxonomy-v1.csv, found while running the Phase 10 worked example (item 12818132946, Document 3, finding F-8). It is a source-file gap, not a judgement call — like B3, it should be fixed before a surveyor sees the schedule rather than put to them as a question.

The evidence. IHEEM's Design Output and Performance Specification Guidance for the Ventilation Strategy / Systems for Dental Care Facilities (VTP/GN/001/V1.0, March 2021 — read at source) sets minimum air-change rates by room for dental facilities: treatment rooms 6–12 ACH at positive pressure (15 ACH in the higher category), instrument cleaning rooms a minimum of 10 ACH at negative pressure, dirty utility 6 ACH extract, clean utility 6 ACH positive. Those rates cannot be met by openable windows, so any HTM-compliant dental fit-out has mechanical ventilation, and the LDU extract in particular is a dedicated, clinically-driven installation rather than comfort ventilation.

Why it matters. That is the same main-pool-vs-special-rate argument the framework already flags as contested in two other sectors — LS-GP-008 (GP treatment-room enhanced/negative-pressure ventilation, judgement/contested) and LS-PH-002/LS-PH-003 (private-hospital UCV and isolation ventilation, "the single biggest pool call"). Dental has neither row. As the taxonomy stands, the LDU extract is absorbed into LS-SR-004 as a special-rate integral feature by default, no flag is raised, and nobody is ever asked the question.

Proposed fix. Add a dental row for clinically-driven mechanical ventilation to the LDU and treatment rooms, tagged APPORTION — open pool call, surveyor and CTA only, never defaulted — consistent with Modules 04 and 05. Claude can draft the row and its authority; the pool call itself stays with the surveyor and CTA.

## RESEARCH (Phase 10, F-10) — Confirm whether a non-domestic EPC's floor-area figure is the same measurement as a surveyor's GIA. Stage 1 of the quantity model rests on this and the convention has never been checked

`12927112165` · 2 comments

### 29 August 2026, 08:22:09 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5502098113

The question, precisely. The Consolidated Schema takes gross_internal_area_m2 from an EPC or the client's plans (provenance CD / SV, grade D). The Phase 10 worked example used exactly that route. But we have never confirmed that the floor-area figure on a non-domestic EPC is measured on the same basis as a chartered surveyor's Gross Internal Area under the RICS code of measuring practice / IPMS. If the two conventions differ — over what is included at stair cores, plant areas, internal walls — then every downstream area-density calculation inherits a systematic error that no amount of care further down the chain will catch.

Why this is worth its own item. Item 12830166757 (three-way floor-area derivation, OS NGD + EA LiDAR + EPC) is marked Done and is about producing a number with a variance flag. This is a different question: whether the numbers being compared are measuring the same thing in the first place. A variance flag between two sources using different conventions reports variance that is definitional, not evidential.

Why it matters more than its size suggests. The Report Pack specification calls the gross internal area "the master input" for the s.562 apportionment and the element cost build-up. It is also one of the nine hard-to-verify fields the desktop-first policy is entirely built around. Getting the convention wrong quietly biases the whole model.

Bounded and closable now. This needs the SBEM / non-domestic EPC conventions document read against the RICS code of measuring practice — desk research, no licence, no purchase, no professional appointment. Raised as finding F-10 in the Phase 10 walkthrough (12818132946, Document 3), where it is flagged rather than answered.

### 29 August 2026, 12:19:22 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5502223078

Answer: not simply interchangeable, though textually anchored to the same definition.

Approved Document Part L defines "Total Useful Floor Area" as "the total area of all enclosed spaces measured to the internal face of the external walls," equivalent to gross floor area per RICS guidance — and the SBEM/NCM conventions actually used by accredited non-domestic energy assessors (Non-Domestic EPC Conventions for England & Wales) are explicit that EPC floor space counts only where it is "a useable floor space in accordance with the definition of GIA from the RICS Code of Measuring Practice." So the EPC methodology does borrow the RICS GIA definition rather than inventing its own — but three things break the equivalence in practice:

1. RICS's own GIA basis has moved and is currently unsettled. Code of Measuring Practice 6th ed. (2015) → RICS Property Measurement 2nd ed. (IPMS for offices from Jan 2016, residential from May 2018) → that 2nd edition archived 9 June 2025, with the current interim position being that a surveyor may adopt either IPMS: All Buildings or the (still unreplaced) Code of Measuring Practice, pending a 7th edition expected later in 2026. A surveyor measuring today and an EPC assessed years ago (EPCs run 10 years) may not share a basis.
2. The EPC figure is GIA filtered through the NCM "activity area" concept, not pure GIA — unheated car parks and other zones without an assessable NCM activity are excluded, whereas a surveyor's GIA is enclosure-based, not conditioning-based. Expect the EPC figure to run smaller than a surveyor's GIA of the same building for this reason alone.
3. Different provenance — an accredited energy assessor working from a software zone model (SBEM), not a chartered surveyor's measurement.

Documented in full, with citations, against Stage 1 of strawman-s9-quantity-derivation.md (item 12819686328) — including the recommended guard (EPC_FLOOR_AREA_NOT_SURVEYOR_GIA flag) rather than a numeric adjustment factor, since none is sourced and none should be invented. Does not change the grade D the schema already assigns an EPC-sourced floor area; confirms it was already the right call.

## Re-derive the surveyor-calibration thresholds against the AD-HOC engagement model — MIN_N_FOR_RATE, ADOPTION_GOOD 0.6 and BIAS_THRESHOLD 0.03 were all set assuming repeat engagements with the same surveyor

`12927112944` · 2 comments

### 29 August 2026, 08:22:54 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5502098332

A consequence of the 28 August decision that nobody has written down. Moving from a single retained surveyor to ad-hoc, one-off engagements was the right commercial call, and this item does not reopen it. But the surveyor CRM (item 12818968809, marked Done) and the calibration set (item 12830166861) were both designed against a repeat-engagement assumption that no longer holds, and their thresholds were set accordingly.

What breaks. The adoption metric in phase3/ledgerstone-surveyor-crm.ts rests on repeat observations:
• MIN_N_FOR_RATE = 5 — below five observations an adoption rate is an anecdote. Under ad-hoc, each surveyor appears once or twice.
• selfConsistency() measures how often a surveyor leaves their own earlier figure untouched. Under ad-hoc it will never have enough data per surveyor to return anything.
• Every adoption statistic becomes cross-surveyor from the first observation — noisier and much slower to reach significance than the design assumes.
• divergences() — disagreement between surveyors — becomes the primary signal rather than a secondary one, because it is the only pattern that will actually accumulate.

What needs re-deriving. ADOPTION_GOOD = 0.6 and BIAS_THRESHOLD = 0.03 are flagged in the code itself as "provisional, reasoned starting points, not findings" (open item O-4). They now need re-deriving against the ad-hoc model, or an explicit note recording that they have been re-confirmed as still appropriate.

The honest consequence. The calibration set will take materially longer to become usable than the original design implied. That does not change the decision; it changes the expectation, and it should be visible before anyone plans around the calibration data arriving.

Full reasoning at item 12818132946, Document 3, Part C section C.3.

### 29 August 2026, 12:19:43 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5502223178

Re-derived and applied in phase3/ledgerstone-surveyor-crm.ts (25/25 tests pass after updating fixtures that hardcoded the old values):

MIN_N_FOR_RATE: 5 → 7. This gates the pooled, cross-surveyor adoption()/divergences() signal, which was never itself repeat-engagement-dependent (adoption() already pools across ALL_SURVEYORS by default). What ad-hoc engagement changes is the composition of the pool: instead of a few repeat observations from one surveyor whose personal calibration is already known, each observation now comes from a different, unfamiliar surveyor, adding a between-surveyor variance component on top of pure estimate error. More observations are needed before the pooled median is signal rather than noise from whichever surveyors happened to be sampled.

New named constant MIN_SURVEYOR_OBS_FOR_DIVERGENCE = 3 (previously an unnamed inline literal inside divergences()). This is the per-surveyor floor for flagging one surveyor as an outlier. Under ad-hoc engagement most surveyors will contribute exactly one job, so divergences() returning nothing most of the time is now documented as the expected behaviour of a correctly-guarded function, not a sign it's broken.

ADOPTION_GOOD: 0.6 → 0.5. A "good" adoption rate under repeat engagement partly reflects accumulated trust a surveyor builds after seeing our pre-fills before; ad-hoc engagement gives every surveyor a first, cold encounter with no such discount available, so ordinary professional due diligence alone predicts more touches even on an accurate pre-fill. Holding strangers to the same 60% bar as a trust-built panel conflates unfamiliarity with inaccuracy.

BIAS_THRESHOLD: 0.03 → 0.05. The same cross-surveyor pooling that motivated raising MIN_N_FOR_RATE also raises the variance of each individual relative_delta observation (style/region/risk-appetite differences mixed in with genuine estimate error). A 3% band was already tight against a stable panel; widened to 5% to avoid reading ordinary cross-sectional heterogeneity as BIASED_HIGH/LOW — material because verdictFor() checks bias before adoption, so a too-tight threshold would misclassify an unbiased-but-noisy field before ADOPTION_GOOD is ever consulted.

selfConsistency() — not re-thresholded, flagged instead. It inherently needs repeat jobs from the same surveyor_id to clear MIN_N_FOR_RATE. Under ad-hoc engagement it will mostly report rate: null — documented as an accepted, structural limitation. Lowering the threshold to make it produce numbers sooner would relabel one or two data points as a "rate", which is exactly the anecdote-vs-rate distinction this whole file exists to prevent.

All values are still provisional (no real ad-hoc job data exists yet) — this is a reasoned adjustment for a changed assumption, not a value fitted to data. Full reasoning is in the code comments at each constant. Cross-posted to items 12830166861 and 12818968809.

A <code>TransparencyRecord</code> keyed to the document (<code>doc_id</code>, <code>doc_type</code>, <code>received_at</code> — the Article 14(3)(a) month runs from <code>received_at</code>), carrying an <code>IdentifiedPerson</code> per natural person identified on receipt: <code>role</code>, <code>route_group</code> (R-A / R-B), <code>address_on_document</code>, and then either a <code>notice</code> (template T7, route, sent_at) <b>or</b> an <code>exemption</code> (article 14(5)(e), reason, recorded_by, recorded_at).<br><br>

<b>Why per person.</b> The Article 14(5) chapeau was substituted on 5 February 2026 to read "do not apply <b>to the extent that</b>", so reliance is a per-person, per-item assertion. <b>A position that cannot be evidenced person by person is not a position.</b><br><br>

<b><code>assertTransparencyRecordComplete()</code> throws in four distinct situations</b>, kept distinct because they are different failures:<br>
• <code>E_TRANSPARENCY_NO_BASIS_ROLE</code> — a planning objector or consultee is in the record <i>at all</i>. There is no lawful basis for them, so there is nothing for a notice to describe and the exemption is not the answer either. The message says the receipt policy did not run, or did not run first. <b>This is what closes the loop between condition D4 and condition D1.</b><br>
• <code>E_TRANSPARENCY_REF_IS_NAME</code> — see the design constraint below.<br>
• <code>E_TRANSPARENCY_PERSON_UNRESOLVED</code> for an <b>R-A</b> person with no notice. <b>The exemption is not available to them and cannot be substituted for the letter</b> (test T3) — Phase 40 §7.5: one letter to an address printed on the document is not a disproportionate effort, it is an argument that fails.<br>
• <code>E_TRANSPARENCY_PERSON_UNRESOLVED</code> for an <b>R-B</b> person with no recorded reason — or an empty one (test T5b: an empty reason is not a reason).<br><br>

<b>THE DESIGN CONSTRAINT THAT SHAPED IT, and it is worth reading on its own.</b> Ledgerstone's structured records contain no third-party name by design (Phase 40 §5.4) and that is the strongest single fact it has. <b>A compliance record keyed by name would destroy it</b> — the store built to prove minimisation would become the name index the minimisation exists to avoid. So <code>person_ref</code> is an <b>opaque per-document reference</b> (<code>LEASE-2026-0007/witness-1</code>) and a name-shaped ref is refused (test T7).<br><br>

<b>8 tests, T1–T8, all passing. 57 pass / 0 fail across the new suite; 262 / 0 across all of phase3.</b><br><br>

<b>RESIDUE 1 — there is no store to deploy it into, and that is not this item's to fix.</b> Board item 12928031577 established that there is no upload handler and no storage adapter anywhere in the codebase. The record type and its completeness assertion exist and are enforced; they run when somebody writes the handler, whose required call order is <code>RECEIPT_CONTRACT</code> in the same module.<br><br>

<b>RESIDUE 2 — one open decision could change the shape of <code>person_ref</code>, and it is now Q37.</b> An opaque ref is not name-searchable, which bears directly on Phase 40's question L5 to the DPO: whether a controller holding full-text documents it <i>could</i> search, but has chosen not to index, can rely on Article 11(2) to disapply Articles 15 to 20. If the DPO says it cannot, the record needs to become name-searchable and the minimisation argument above weakens. <b>That is a DPO decision, not a build decision</b>, and it is asked as Q37 in QUESTIONS TO BE ANSWERED (item 12919337890, Document 2) rather than left as a note here.<br><br>

<b>Note on scope, for whoever reads this next to item 12927936989:</b> that item adds a notice-sent field to Item 5's two <i>exception stores</i> and still needs doing. It does not reach this population and this does not reach that one. Phase 40 §5.7 / condition D6 governs the overlap case — where one individual is in both populations, <b>one</b> notice is sent naming both sources and both bases — and D6 remains open with the DPO.

## GAP (Phase 45) — item RENAME silently no-ops and returns SUCCESS when the new name exceeds 255 chars. This board records outcomes in long item names, so a phase can believe it recorded a decision and not have. Cap names, or record outcomes as item updates

`12929302538` · 3 comments

### 30 August 2026, 09:45:28 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5503586093

<b>Phase 46 sweep, 30 August 2026 — tested for the silent-failure this item warns about. Two findings.</b><br><br><b>1. The cap is enforced honestly on creation and silently on rename. That asymmetry is the whole bug.</b><br><code>create_item</code> with a 261-character name was <b>rejected with an explicit error</b> ("Item name must be 255 characters or fewer", with the maximum stated). The same overlong string passed to a rename returns success and leaves the old name in place. So the platform <i>does</i> know the rule and <i>does</i> surface it — on one path and not the other. Any phase that creates an item gets told; any phase that records an outcome by renaming does not.<br><br><b>2. No historical rename appears to have failed. Recorded so the next sweep does not redo this.</b> All 310 item names were measured. Eleven are 250 characters or more; <b>four are exactly 255</b> — 12929302538, 12830043662, 12830037617, 12852270415. Each was read in full and each ends on a complete clause that reads as deliberately fitted to the limit, not cut off. Nothing on the board shows the signature of a truncated or reverted rename.<br><br><b>That result is weaker evidence than it looks, and the reason matters.</b> A failed rename leaves the <i>old</i> name, which by definition looks like a normal item name. It is not detectable after the fact by inspecting names — only by comparing an item's name against what some phase <i>said</i> it renamed it to. So "no failures found" here means "no anomalies visible", not "no failures occurred", and no future sweep should treat this as a clean bill of health.<br><br><b>A live instance of the same class was found this pass, in a different place.</b> The two index documents both carry a stale <code>set_name</code>: the Phased Build Plan's <i>content</i> was at v14 while the <i>document title</i> still read v13, and the decision queue's content was at v7.0 while its title read v6.9. Nothing failed silently here — the doc rename was simply never attempted, because the convention only ever renames the <b>item</b>. The effect on a reader is identical to a silent failure: the title says one version, the first line says another. Both are now corrected, and the standing rules carry the rule.<br><br><b>Recommendation, unchanged in substance and now with a cheaper form:</b> keep recording outcomes by rename where the name still fits, but <b>read the name back after writing it</b> — one query, and it converts a silent failure into a visible one. Where the outcome will not fit in 255 characters, put it in an item update, which has no such limit, and keep the name short. The standing rules in the plan document now say this.

CLOSED 31 August 2026 by the Phase 47 sweep. The investigation is complete, the preventive rule is in force, and this sweep hit the limit in practice.

### 31 August 2026, 17:05:55 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5506498709

Confirmed again on 31 Aug 2026 (Phase 53) — and it is not only item renames. DOC renames do it too.
-----------------------------------------------------------------

This item was written about change_item_column_values silently no-op'ing an item name over 255 characters. Phase 53 hit the same shape on a document:

* update_doc set_name on the plan doc (18427857409) with a 257-character name returned [OK] set_name: Renamed to "..." — echoing the new name back — and the document kept its old name.
* Verified by a direct GraphQL read of docs { name }, which still showed v21 after the "successful" rename to v22.
* A 169-character retry took immediately.
Why this one is worse than the item version. The item API at least fails quietly. update_doc echoes the name it did not set, so the confirmation line is affirmatively misleading: a phase that renames a doc to record an outcome, reads its own tool result, and moves on will believe it recorded something it did not.

The rule to work to: keep doc and item names under about 200 characters, and where an outcome matters, record it as an item update or a document section, not as a name. Then verify the rename with a read rather than trusting the tool result. This is the third time a "success" response has been found not to correspond to a change on this board.

<b>What to do, and why.</b> Part A of the Governance Policies document on board item 12552682456 is a Complaints Policy, DRAFT v1.0 dated 26 August 2026. It is a good policy about <i>service and fee</i> complaints. It is not about data protection complaints, and three of its statements are wrong if read as covering them.<br><br><b>The provision it does not account for.</b> DPA 2018 s.164A, inserted by DUAA 2025 s.103(2), in force 19 June 2026 (S.I. 2026/82 reg. 3(a), with reg. 7). It gives a data subject a right to complain to the controller about an alleged infringement of the UK GDPR, and puts three duties on the controller: facilitate the making of complaints, including by providing a form completable electronically and by other means; acknowledge receipt within 30 days beginning when the complaint is received; and respond without undue delay, making enquiries to the extent appropriate, keeping the complainant informed of progress, and informing them of the outcome.<br><br><b>The three statements to correct.</b><br><b>A2</b> defines a complaint as one "made by a client or a client's representative". A s.164A complainant is a data subject. The realistic one at Ledgerstone is not a client at all — the Retention Procedure section 5.1 describes them as a stranger with no client relationship, no account and possibly no idea how their name reached Ledgerstone.<br><b>A4</b> says the acknowledgement and response targets "are internal service standards, not a statutory or regulatory requirement — Ledgerstone is not a regulated firm (see A8)". Correct for the service limb. Wrong for the data protection limb, where s.164A(3) is a statutory 30-day duty and s.164A(4) a statutory duty to respond.<br><b>A8</b> says there is "no sector regulator and no professional ombudsman scheme that covers Ledgerstone's own conduct", and lists the client's accountant, mediation and the courts as the genuine independent routes. Correct for the consultancy service. Wrong for data protection: the Information Commissioner is a regulator, DPA 2018 s.165(2) (as amended 19 June 2026 to cover the UK GDPR) is a real independent route, and s.166 gives a Tribunal backstop if the Commissioner does not deal with the complaint.<br><br><b>What the fix is, and what it is not.</b> Do not rewrite Part A and do not merge the two regimes — they have different definitions, different clocks, different decision-makers and different onward routes, and merging them produces a policy that satisfies neither. Add an explicit data protection carve-out: a short section saying that a complaint about how Ledgerstone has handled personal data is a s.164A complaint, that it is handled by the DPO under the separate procedure, that it carries a statutory 30-day acknowledgement, and that its onward route is s.165 and not the routes at A8. Then correct the three sentences above so they read as being about the service limb rather than about everything. A9's complaints log should also cross-refer to the s.164A complaints log rather than implying one log covers both.<br><br><b>Where the source material is.</b> The classification rule (what is and is not a s.164A complaint, with three worked distinctions on Ledgerstone's own facts) is at section 3.2 of the Phase 35 document on board item 12927908435. The complaints log fields are at 3.4, the 30-day clock at 3.3, and the onward-route wording — which is largely prescribed by Article 12(4) rather than a drafting choice — at 5.7.<br><br><b>Note on status.</b> Part A is DRAFT, NOT APPROVED, and its parent item sits in group Z marked Done. ## A-4 OVER-CLAIM — no disposal value statement branch anywhere in the engine. s.187A(3)(c), (10) and (11) are unreachable, so the s.196 item 2/3 and s.61 item 7 cases return a figure where the law returns nil

`12921347004` · 1 comment

### 31 August 2026, 15:09:59 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5505984026

<b>A-4 built — Phase 50, 31 August 2026.</b><br><br>

<b>What was wrong.</b> There was no disposal value statement branch anywhere in the engine. s.187A(3)(c), (10) and (11) were unreachable, so the s.196 item 2, item 3 and s.61 item 7 cases returned a figure where the law returns nil.<br><br>

<b>What changed.</b> <code>LS_S187A.dvsAssess()</code> implements the requirement, reached whenever A-6's derivation puts the past owner's disposal on the statement track. Three new fields — <code>dvs_statement</code>, <code>dvs_statement_date</code>, <code>dvs_stated_value</code> — captured by three plain questions about a document the client is either holding or not. The requirement is satisfied only where the statement was made within two years of the past owner <b>ceasing to own</b> (not from any later sale) AND the client has actually obtained it, per s.187A(11) and the s.187B(1) burden.<br><br>

<b>The nil cases, which are the point of the defect:</b><br>
• No statement was ever made → <b>NIL</b>, both ends of the range, with the reason named.<br>
• Statement made more than two years after cessation → <b>NIL</b>. The period cannot be extended and an election is not an alternative on these facts.<br>
This is the third clock, and the one most often already expired before anyone looks — HMRC's CA26482 case is exactly it: an owner who discontinued, brought in a disposal value without selling, and sold years later by which time both this period and any election were long out of time.<br><br>

<b>Unknown never becomes "satisfied".</b> Four separate ways the position can be unproven all return INDET with the floor at nil and a named capture step, rather than either a nil or a figure: statement believed to exist but not produced; "not sure"; statement held but the cessation date unknown (so the two years cannot be tested); statement held but undated. A fifth — held and in time but no figure captured — also returns INDET, because the cap cannot be sized. "Not sure" and "no statement was ever made" are deliberately different answers and are asserted to be different.<br><br>

<b>One correction the harness forced on my own test, worth recording.</b> I first asserted that CAP-DV pins both ends of the range to the stated value. It does not, and should not: a cap is a ceiling, not a target. Where the survey range already sits below the stated disposal value the floor stays where it is — the statement is not evidence that there IS that much plant. Same convention as <code>LS_ELECTION.scopedCap</code>. Both behaviours are now asserted.<br><br>

<b>Harness.</b> 321 pass / 0 fail / 14 xfail, up from 238/0/14. New suite L adds 83 checks including every nil branch and every unknown branch. phase3 unchanged at 287 pass / 0 fail across nine suites. Both re-derived per suite. Verified end-to-end through the shipped engine: an undervalue disposal with no statement now returns [0, 0] where it previously returned a figure, and the report names which requirement failed.<br><br>

<b>One residual, flagged not fixed.</b> The statement branch runs inside the existing Stage 5 gate (<code>prior_owner_claimed === "yes"</code>), the same gate the election cap already used. Widening it to cover the case where the past owner's claim status is unknown is A-3 (12921346994), gated on B-Q4 — so the gate was left exactly as found rather than quietly widened.

## A-1 OVER-CLAIM — the FVR question runs the two-year clock from the CLIENT's acquisition. s.187A(9) runs it from the acquisition by the purchaser FROM THE PAST OWNER. With an intervening owner the engine shows a live window on a claim that closed

`12921346992` · 1 comment

### 31 August 2026, 15:09:37 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5505982580

<b>A-1 built — Phase 50, 31 August 2026. This was the over-claim, and it is now closed in both places it lived.</b><br><br>

<b>What was wrong.</b> The fixed-value question asked whether two years had passed since <i>the client</i> took on the property, and treated the answer as decisive. s.187A(9) runs the relevant two-year period from the acquisition by <b>the purchaser from the past owner</b> (items 1 and 9), or from the grant of the lease to that lessee (item 5). Where a developer, charity, housing association or non-claiming propco sits in between, the period opened and closed around a transaction the client was not party to — and may have expired before they were involved at all. The engine reported a live window on a claim that died years earlier.<br><br>

<b>Why the engine got it wrong.</b> HMRC's own pages disagree. CA26480 states the statutory rule. CA26478, one page earlier in the same chain, glosses it as running from the date the new owner is treated as acquiring the fixture. The shipped question paraphrased the gloss.<br><br>

<b>What changed — two parts.</b><br>
<b>1. The start date is now derived properly.</b> <code>LS_S187A.windowStart()</code> returns the s.187A(9) date and says which basis it used: the client's own completion only where they bought direct; the intervening purchaser's acquisition where someone is in between; the lease grant on item 5. New fields <code>intervening_owner</code> and <code>intervening_owner_acquisition_date</code>. The intervening-owner position is derived from what the engine already knows — an entitled seller IS the past owner, so nobody is in between; a non-entitled seller in front of an entitled owner IS an intervening owner — and only asked where that derivation is not conclusive.<br>
<b>2. The shipped question no longer declares the route shut on the wrong date.</b> Its "that route is shut for good" flag now fires only on a direct purchase, where the client's date and the statutory date are the same event and the finding still stands. Where anyone is in between, the client's answer is discarded (<code>fvr_window_closed</code> set to null) and replaced by a capture step. Nothing else read that field, so those flags were the whole of the question's behaviour.<br><br>

<b>Unknown is not resolved in the client's favour.</b> Where an owner is in between and their purchase date is not known, the window is "not derivable" — not "open". That returns INDET with the bottom of the range at nil and a capture step naming the Land Registry title register and price paid data. Per the rulebook, the engine does not accept a client answer about someone else's completion date. The demonstrating test is one comparison: same client, same completion date of January 2026, window open on a direct purchase and NOT reported open with one owner in between; and with that owner's purchase dated 2015, positively closed.<br><br>

<b>A closed window is INDET, never a settled nil.</b> s.187A(6)(b) is a third satisfaction route with no time limit, and it is defect A-2 (12921346993), gated on A-Q8 and deliberately not built. Returning nil on a closed window would decide A-2 against the client without anyone having ruled on it, so the output hands off to A-2 by board id instead.<br><br>

<b>One thing the harness caught in my own work.</b> The first integration dropped the floor to nil even where a valid, in-time election existed — which would have understated every clean two-party case. A valid election IS a relevant apportionment (row A-F12) and satisfies the requirement; I had skipped that limb of the decision order. Added as <code>relevantApportionmentMade()</code>, guarded so it only settles the position where nobody is in between.<br><br>

<b>Harness.</b> 321 pass / 0 fail / 14 xfail, up from 238/0/14. phase3 287 pass / 0 fail across nine suites. Both re-derived per suite. Confirmed end-to-end in the browser: on an intervening-owner path the "shut for good" text is gone and the capture step appears in its place.<br><br>

<b>No rules-defect incident.</b> The site states the company is not yet incorporated and no client has been shown a figure, so item 12927557335 is not engaged.

## A-6 STRUCTURAL — nothing records which s.196 Table item the past owner's disposal fell under, so the engine cannot choose between the fixed value and disposal value statement requirements, or between the two s.187A(9) start dates

`12921347006` · 1 comment

### 31 August 2026, 15:08:51 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5505979550

<b>A-6 built — Phase 50, 31 August 2026.</b><br><br>

<b>What was wrong.</b> Nothing recorded which item of the s.196 Table the past owner's disposal fell under. That item is the fork in the statute: items 1, 5 and 9 lead to the fixed value requirement, items 2 and 3 and s.61 item 7 lead to the disposal value statement requirement, and they are different tests on different clocks. With no record of it the engine could not choose, so it always behaved as though the first fork had been taken.<br><br>

<b>What changed.</b> New shared module <code>LS_S187A</code>, sitting above the five sector IIFEs so the rule is stated once rather than five times. <code>LS_S187A.disposalItem()</code> derives the item and the requirement track. Built first, because A-1 and A-4 both read what it captures.<br><br>

<b>The classification is DERIVED, never asked.</b> "Which item of the s.196 Table did the disposal fall under?" is not answerable by a lay person, so it is not asked. The client is asked one question about what actually happened, with five plain options — they sold it normally / they transferred it for less than it was worth / they granted a new lease for a lump sum / they stopped owning it some other way without selling / they permanently stopped trading but kept it — plus a follow-up on the lease case about whether a joint election was made. The statutory classification is done in code. This follows the precedent already set on this board by the amendment window (12829962267), which is derived from the acquisition date and accounting period rather than put to the client.<br><br>

<b>Unknown routes to capture, not to the favourable branch.</b> "Not sure", and a lease whose election position is unknown, both return UNKNOWN — not the fixed-value track. UNKNOWN drops the bottom of the range to nil and raises a capture flag naming CPSE replies and the title history. This is the F-2 trap (an unknown grant defaulting to nil) and it is tested explicitly in both directions.<br><br>

<b>Harness.</b> 321 pass / 0 fail / 14 xfail, up from a 238/0/14 baseline. New suite L adds 83 checks; no xfail changed state. phase3 unchanged at 287 pass / 0 fail across nine suites. Both totals re-derived per suite rather than read off the previous row. Also verified end-to-end in the browser: the new questions render and gate correctly in all five sector flows.<br><br>

<b>What was wrong.</b> There was no <code>past_owner_cessation_date</code> anywhere. Both FA 2012 Sch 10 para 13 transitionals gate on when the PAST OWNER ceased to be treated as owning the plant — para 13(1) for whether the s.187A regime applies at all, para 13(2) for whether the pooling requirement does. The engine had only the client's own acquisition date, which is a different date whenever anyone sits between the two.<br><br>

<b>What changed.</b> New date field <code>past_owner_cessation_date</code>, captured in all five sector flows by a plain question ("On what date did that earlier owner stop owning the property?", with the help text pointing at the Land Registry title register and saying it is fine to leave blank). Three functions in <code>LS_S187A</code> read it:<br>
• <code>commencementDate()</code> — 1 April 2012 for a company, 6 April 2012 otherwise, following the client's own charge because para 11 speaks of the current owner's new expenditure.<br>
• <code>regimeOff()</code> — para 13(1).<br>
• <code>poolingRequirementInForce()</code> — para 13(2), cessation no later than two years after commencement.<br><br>

<b>One simplification worth recording.</b> Para 13(1) speaks of a period of ownership that <i>began and ended</i> before commencement. A period cannot end before it begins, so a cessation date earlier than the commencement date is by itself sufficient — no separate ownership-start field is needed, and none was added.<br><br>

<b>Unknown does not relieve.</b> Both transitionals REMOVE a restriction, so both fire only on a date that is actually known. An absent or unparseable cessation date leaves the regime on and the pooling requirement in force, and raises a capture flag. Tested in both directions at both gates, including the three-day CT/IT boundary: a cessation of 3 April 2012 puts the regime off for an individual and leaves it on for a company.<br><br>

<b>Harness.</b> 321 pass / 0 fail / 14 xfail, up from a 238/0/14 baseline. phase3 unchanged at 287 pass / 0 fail across nine suites. Both re-derived per suite.<br><br>

<b>Note on direction.</b> The item is titled "both directions" and that is right, but worth being precise: coding these transitionals is claim-INCREASING where the date is known and satisfies them, because each removes a requirement. That is not a reading of an ambiguous provision — Rulebook A Addendum 1 T24 states both flatly and its decision order puts para 13(1) at step F0 — so it is not held with the gated ten. Where para 13(1) fires, the output says s.187A is off <b>and that s.185 can still cap the claim</b>, so "off" is never presented to a client as "free".

## DECIDED 1 Sep (Q51-Q54) - WordPress is the WHOLE back end AND front end; uploads go to the custom back end; DPO logs (tamper-evident, not tamper-proof). Scope is now a rebuild not a config - see Phase 61. Backup-exclusion question still open with the host

`12937301773` · 1 comment

### 31 August 2026, 17:06:31 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5506500791

Four questions, in plain English. They come from one sentence you wrote on 29 August.
-----------------------------------------------------------------

"invoice with bank transfers, CRM will be a custom WordPress back end"The first half is clean and is now built into the plan. No card processor, no direct debit, nothing in the customer journey takes money — the invoice follows the claim, because our fee is a percentage of a tax saving that has to be quantified first. One house rule to put in writing before we send a single invoice: bank details on an emailed invoice are the standard way this kind of fraud works, and the sums here are percentages of tax refunds. Details get confirmed on a channel other than the invoice email, and are never changed because an email asked.

The second half needs you and the data protection officer. WordPress puts uploaded files in a folder that the web server hands to anyone with the address, with no login check at all. Fine for a photo on a web page. Not fine for a client's lease, their sale contract, or their property enquiries — documents naming people who are not our clients and never agreed to anything.

This is not a reason to abandon WordPress. It is three questions that must be answered before anybody builds the upload page. Everything else can be built today.

Q51 — do client documents stay out of WordPress's own file library entirely?
The fix is to put them where the web server will not serve them, and hand them out only through a page that checks who is asking. There is no cheaper version of this. If the answer is "use what WordPress gives us", the honest description is that client leases sit at guessable public web addresses — and the right response to that is not a smaller safeguard, it is not accepting client uploads.

Q52 — who controls the backups, and can one folder be left out of them?
We promise in writing that the unredacted original is deleted. Most managed WordPress hosting takes a nightly copy of the whole site that the customer cannot pick apart. A file deleted from the disk and alive in a thirty-day backup has not been deleted — and our deletion record would say it had. That is worse than not making the promise.

Q53 — where does the tamper-proof log live?
We need a log of who saw what that cannot be quietly edited. Inside WordPress, anyone with an administrator account can edit the database, including the record of what they themselves did. Two honest answers: pay for a separate write-only log outside WordPress, or have the DPO record in terms that the log is tamper-evident rather than tamper-proof and that administrators are trusted. For a business this size the second is perfectly respectable. Saying nothing is not.

Q54 — does WordPress replace the rest of the system, or sit next to it?
Two readings are live. (a) WordPress is the whole back end. (b) WordPress is the customer-management screens, sitting beside the calculation engine we have already built. Everything built so far — the engine, the eleven rulebooks, the document controls — is in a language WordPress does not run, so (a) means rebuilding all of it and (b) means none of it. Different quotes. Nobody should be asked to price this until it is answered.

What is NOT blocked: the whole client journey, the estimate engine, the reports, the ops screens, the invoice, the accountant handoff. Only the client-document upload page waits on Q51 and Q52.

Full detail in Developer Brief §3.0 (attached to item 12937209644) and in Part 5 of the decision queue, item 12919337890, Document 3.

## Q34 offers RETAIN_REDACTED_DELETE_ORIGINAL as an option and nothing anywhere can produce a redacted file — applyReceiptPolicy returns text segments, not a redacted PDF. The option is unimplementable as built and neither Q34 nor the module says so

`12928215019` · 3 comments

### 29 August 2026, 19:06:51 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5502455825

Found by Phase 42 (sweep & stress-test), 29 Aug 2026.

The gap. RawFileRetentionRule in phase3/ledgerstone-client-doc-ingestion.ts offers three options. One is RETAIN_REDACTED_DELETE_ORIGINAL — "Keep a copy with the receipt strip applied; delete the unredacted original". Nothing anywhere produces that copy.

applyReceiptPolicy returns Segment[] — extracted text — not a redacted PDF or image. There is no PDF, image or OCR redaction function in the codebase (grep for redact across phase3/ returns only the enum member, a doc comment, and the redacted_copy_retained boolean). That boolean is something a caller asserts, not something the mechanism creates. deletionDueAt treats the option as identical to DELETE_ON_EXTRACTION_COMPLETE, so even the clock does not distinguish it.

Why it matters. This is not a dormant enum member. It is the option Phase 40 §7.7 measure 2 recommends as the alternative where deleting the source early is unacceptable, and it is offered to Lakhbir and the DPO inside Q34 as one of the answers they may choose. If they choose it, the developer inherits a rule name with no mechanism behind it — and the fail-closed design guarantees nothing, because the guarantee was that a redacted copy survives.

This is a decision being put to a human with an option that cannot be performed. Q34's text does not say so, and neither does the module.

What to do — pick one, do not leave all three live.
1. Build the producer: a redaction step that emits a new file with the removed segments' page regions obliterated (not merely covered — a black rectangle over selectable text is not redaction), and set redacted_copy_retained from it rather than trusting a caller.
2. Or withdraw the option from RawFileRetentionRule and from Q34, leaving the two that are implementable, and record why.

### 26 August 2026, 07:16:19 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5492257832

What this is
An open decision, and the board flags it as the highest-value one still unanswered. Only you can make it.

In plain English
Two different businesses are possible here:

• We advise the client. We tell the client what they can claim and they act on what we say. Higher fees, but we are giving tax advice, which means serious professional indemnity insurance, and we carry the risk if a claim fails.
• We support their accountant. We hand a technical pack to the client's own accountant, who makes the filing decision and signs it. Lower risk, lower fee, and the accountant becomes our referral source rather than our competitor.

Why it changes everything downstream
It sets the level of insurance we need, the wording of the engagement letter, and the tone of every report template. A report written for a client to act on reads very differently from one written for an accountant to file from.

The reports built so far assume the second model — they are addressed to "the owner and their accountant" and say the accountant files. If you choose the first model, they all need rewriting.

Claude can help by writing a comparison paper covering the insurance, regulatory and commercial consequences of each route.

Original wording: "T8 — DECIDE: do we ADVISE the client or SUPPORT their accountant? Drives PI cover, engagement letter, and every report template. HIGHEST-VALUE OPEN DECISION."

The reasoning turns on a distinction worth stating plainly. "Here is what is in your building and what your entitlement position is" is insight. "Put this figure on your return" is advice. A surveyor gives the first without giving the second and nobody thinks they are being evasive. Your steer is satisfied by the first; the entire risk sits in the second.

What each pure model costs:
• PI. Cover has to be sized against the claim, not the fee. A failed care-home claim is £202,500 against a £10,125 fee — twenty times over. And if a rule in our engine is wrong it is wrong on every job that touched it, so the aggregate limit matters more than the per-claim one. The uplift ADVISE earns is per job; the premium is annual — at current volume it plausibly costs more than it earns.
• Regulatory. Tax advice is not itself restricted, and that is usually where the argument stops. But I have flagged an AML supervision point that I have not verified and no regulation text was read: a firm giving tax advice by way of business may fall within the regulated sector and need supervision, which we have no professional body to provide. It is flagged because it is a registration obligation with real consequences, not because I can stand behind the detail. This is the single item most worth putting to the solicitor first.
• Referral channel. The strongest argument in the paper, and it needs no regulatory question to work: if ADVISE earns 20% more per job but costs half our referral volume, we are worse off at any volume. The board calls accountant referral the primary acquisition route.

Which deliverables assume which — evidenced, not asserted: everything built so far assumes SUPPORT, and in the report architecture it is structural. The Report Pack spec defines two outputs (client report and accountant report) with the production line ending [ACCOUNTANT/CTA] → [CLIENT] and a whole section on "what the accountant adjusts". Business flow v2 says the accountant "files or amends the returns" and closes the loop as the acquisition channel. The sample report says their accountant "can choose what suits". The site says "alongside your own accountant". Switching to pure ADVISE makes every "not tax advice" disclaimer false — worse than having none.

One thing that is already broken today. The s.203 section tells clients to notify "through their own accountant", which assumes one exists. Under your steer some will not have one. We currently surface a three-month statutory duty and point it at someone who may not be there. It is also open question C-Q8 in the CTA pack, where I have asked the reviewer whether we should be surfacing that duty at all without a route for the client to discharge it.

The engagement letter does not exist yet. That is the one artefact that has to state this in terms, and it is the one not written — so there is no rework, but it cannot be written until this is settled.

What I need: a broker conversation about whether tax-advice PI is available to an unregulated firm at a limit matching a £200k claim (availability before price — it can close the branch on its own); the AML question to the solicitor; and confirmation of what you meant on 25 August. If you meant genuinely telling clients what to file, the paper is wrong about your intent and section 10 becomes the live list of six things that then have to be funded.

A decision that has already been made, kept here as a record.

When a client types their address, we need a service that turns it into one exact, official property record. We chose Homedata. It has a free tier of 100 lookups a month, and a paid tier at about £49 a month if we need more.

## Decision made — National Insurance is left out of all client figures

`12804368578` · 1 comment

### 26 August 2026, 07:16:07 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5492257582

What this is
A decision that has already been made, kept here as a record.

In plain English
Self-employed people pay National Insurance as well as income tax, so a capital allowances claim can reduce their National Insurance too. We decided not to include that in any figure we show a client. We quote income tax only.

Why
It keeps our numbers conservative. A client who is told a smaller number and then gets a bigger one is happy; the reverse is a complaint. It also avoids us having to model National Insurance thresholds, which change every year.

What this means in practice
Every client-facing document must say in its assumptions that National Insurance is excluded — so the real benefit may be slightly better than we have shown.

Original wording: "D4 — DECIDED: Class 4 NIC EXCLUDED from all client-facing figures. Income tax only, stated in assumptions."

Why this item exists, and it is a worked example rather than a projection. Q55 was answered on 3 September: the fee is 5% of the allowances identified. The competitor deliverable in Desktop\reports shows what that can do on a small job.

The numbers, from the Eureka invoice and Tax Implication Summary for 1A Albert Street:

Allowances identified GBP 73,740 (main pool 34,075 at 18%, special rate pool 39,665 at 6%).
Fee at 4% of allowances: GBP 2,949.60, plus VAT GBP 589.92 = GBP 3,539.52.
Tax actually saved across both open years, 2022/23 and 2023/24: GBP 1,010.00 repayment + GBP 1,673.20 reduction in payments on account, less the profit interaction = GBP 2,509.80 total tax saving.
Remaining pools carried forward at 2024/25: GBP 18,788 and GBP 32,945, unwinding at 18% and 6% out to 2029/30 and beyond.

So the client paid GBP 3,539.52 to receive GBP 2,509.80 now, with the balance arriving slowly over a decade. Nothing here is improper — it is the arithmetic of a fee that crystallises at once against relief that unwinds over years. But it is our exposure too, and it lands hardest on exactly the client we tell to expect a cash repayment: the small, low-rate or loss-making one.

### 1 September 2026, 16:14:56 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5510332724

PHASE 59 — DONE, 1 September 2026 (L.Dhillon-WIN11). Identity verification for a rights request, both routes.
-----------------------------------------------------------------

The note this phase was asked to leave, stated plainly: Route B was added because the answer as given covered only organisational requesters. The identity standard given on 1 September — their name, affiliation with the organisation, approval from the company owner or director to speak on the company's behalf, captured on the back end system — is adopted in full, unchanged, and is now Route A. It is a good test for somebody asking on behalf of a business: a client company's director, a practice manager. It is no test at all for the population this control was written for. A private individual whose name appears in a lease or a property enquiry reply that a client uploaded has no company, no affiliation with us, and no director who could approve them. Applying the business test to that person refuses every request they could ever make, and a refusal by that route is itself a breach of Article 12(2), the duty to facilitate. So the gap was closed rather than inherited.

What was built. Section 5.5 of the Retention and Rights-Request Operating Procedure, now v1.3 (item 12818099921, Document 2 — doc 18428630726) is replaced by a two-route standard: 5.5.1 classifies by whose personal data is asked about rather than by who is asking, with the tie-break that an unclear case is Route B; 5.5.2 carries Route A verbatim; 5.5.3 carries Route B; 5.5.4 stops identity becoming refusal by attrition; 5.5.5 adds five register fields; 5.5.6 states the approval position.

Route B's shape — the shape the phase specified, and the shape the complaints pack had already recommended at Q26. Public matching data is enough to FIND the record and is not enough to RELEASE it, because for a Companies House person with significant control the matching data is a name plus a birth month and year, and Companies House publishes both: anyone who can use a search box can quote them back. Release needs one corroborating fact only that person would hold — the property or instruction, a reference from us, who supplied the document, the nature or date of the dealing, or a reply to a one-time code sent to an address already on the record — or a narrower disclosure giving everything Article 15(1) requires except the non-public content. What does not count is written down too: name, birth month and year, nationality, company number, registered office, officer appointments, PSC status, and the HM Land Registry title number and proprietor name. A fact anyone can buy is not a shared secret, and recording one as a check is worse than recording no check, because it looks like a control.

Three things follow from Route A, and none of them changes it. (1) It is an authority test, not an identity test — "approval from a director" answers may this person speak for the company, not is this person who they say. In practice the identity half comes free from an account we issued; where the representative has no account, Route B's corroborating check is applied to them as well. (2) The grantor must be somebody we can already place — a person on the instruction, or an officer on the Companies House record we already hold. An approval from a name that appears nowhere is a second unverified stranger, and the record has to be able to say so rather than swallow it. (3) Company authority is not a third individual's mandate — Article 15(4). That is Q67.

Neither route may become refusal by attrition, and 5.5.4 gives that teeth rather than stating it. Ask once and early; a doubt first raised in week four reads as a delaying tactic. A nil return — "we hold nothing that matches" — discloses nothing and needs no check at all, because it is the same answer to the real person and to an impostor. An acknowledgement is never held for identity, and neither is a s.164A complaint acknowledgement. A failed identity check is not "manifestly unfounded" under Article 12(5)(b). Every outcome short of what was asked for carries all three Article 12(4) onward routes. And the standard applied is recorded per request — not "identity confirmed" but what was asked for and why it was proportionate to that request.

The point that makes the recording load-bearing. Article 12A(2)(b) restarts the whole month from the day identity information is received, so an identity request gains us time: one made on day 2 and answered on day 19 hands back all nineteen days, not the seventeen in between. That advantage is real and legitimate, and it is exactly what makes an unjustified identity request profitable. The register field exists to make that visible to a reviewer, and the developer brief asks for a dashboard warning where an identity request is raised more than seven days after receipt.

Developer brief — v3.1 to v3.2, new §5.2a (00-START-HERE/Ledgerstone-Developer-Brief.md). §5.2 listed "data-subject requests" as one line under Profile and consents; that line is a whole statutory process. §5.2a specifies the RightsRequest and RepresentativeAuthority records — including grantor_placement with a storable NEITHER value, per-instruction scope, and expires_at as a field rather than a convention — and flags in terms that Route B is handled by a person, not a form: no code path may release record content on matching data alone, no identity-document upload field is to be built, and the /notices/ form must accept rights requests as well as complaints. Both entities added to the §9 data model; §12 item 22 records what is genuinely open.

Corpus consistency — occurrences counted, not documents (the Phase 43 lesson). Four other places carried the old position and all four are corrected: the complaints pack (12927908435) gains Addendum 1 moving readiness C8 from "NOT DECIDED" to PART-DECIDED; the response letters pack (12927850552) gains Addendum 1 filling the slot §3.5 had explicitly reserved for this answer, and records that §3.5's conservative rule was confirmed rather than replaced — worth saying about a section that predicted its own replacement; DECISIONS goes to v14.0 with a new Part 13; and the Blockers map on the Desktop, whose "a second route is needed" now reads as built.

Law read first-hand for this on legislation.gov.uk, 1 September 2026, rather than carried over from the earlier packs: UK GDPR Article 11(1) and (2) — which is what makes "we cannot tell which record is yours" a lawful answer rather than a fudge — Article 12(1) to (6) including 12(2)'s cross-reference to 11(2), and Article 15(1A), 15(3) and 15(4). No ICO guidance is cited anywhere.

Status, stated honestly. Route A is decided — it is the controller's own answer and needs no approval. Route B is drafted and NOT approved: it is readiness item C8 and the open limb of Q26, and it closes when the DPO signs 5.5.3. It is the operating rule in the meantime, deliberately, because the alternative to an unapproved Route B is applying Route A to a private individual, which is a certain breach rather than an unapproved control. And "captured on the back end system" names a destination, not a running control — the back end does not exist, none of §5.2a is built, and until it is, both routes are recorded by hand.

Questions raised: Q67 (does company authority reach a third individual's data — drafted "no" on Article 15(4), needs confirming rather than deciding) and Q68 (may an identity document ever be required — drafted DPO-only and exceptional). Both sit with the DPO. Nothing new is waiting on Lakhbir.

### 2 September 2026, 09:18:21 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5512705258

PHASE 67 — DONE, 2 September 2026. The condensed front door and the derivation layer are built. The layer is switched OFF and the reason is not an engineering one.
-----------------------------------------------------------------

Harness: 392 → 437 pass, 0 fail, 4 xfail. Suite O is new. Nothing in the existing flows changed, and that is deliberate — see "switched off" below.

What was built
--------------

LS_REGISTRY — the derivation layer. The finding that created this phase was that both journey documents named Companies House, HMLR, EPC and CQC 76 times between them and neither derived anything from any of them. They were cited as sources in the output and never used to skip a question. This is the layer that takes them seriously: one address, and the purchase price and completion date, floor area, building age, bed count, service type, entity type and year end stop being questions and become confirmations.

It is not a connector and makes no network calls. It is the contract the connectors fill. Three things in it are load-bearing: a missing register value falls back to asking, never to a default; personal fields are classified by field name and refused by default with only the two permitted exceptions; and derivation is jurisdiction-aware, so a Scottish address gets a question rather than a wrong purchase price.

LS_FRONTDOOR — six questions to a range, with the three corrections. LS_BOOKING — call booking on four channels from three entry points, including the gated exit. LS_FEE — built, and refusing to render.

The three corrections — and the thing worth knowing about them
--------------------------------------------------------------

Two of the three were already right in the engine before this phase started. That was not what anyone expected, and it changed what the phase had to guard against.

* April 2014 is already correct, and it is not one date. The engine derives it as the regime commencement plus two years, which lands on 1 April 2014 for companies and 6 April 2014 for income tax payers. A single hard-coded date would have flattened that split.

* The two-year clock's start was never hard-coded. It is derived: direct purchase runs from the client's completion, an intervening owner runs from theirs, and where the chain cannot be established it returns "not derivable" and says in terms that it is not safe to assume the client's own date.

* Only the Q1 gate needed building, and it is built: it gates on your own prior claim on these fixtures, and a previous owner's claim never gates on any answer. A previous owner having claimed is normally what makes the current claim possible.

So the risk was never that the corrections were missing. It was that a new front door would reimplement them and get them wrong, in the half of the system nobody reads. Every date test in the front door therefore delegates to the engine, and Suite O asserts the delegation rather than the answer — including a source check that the front door computes with no year of its own.

Two corrections to the phase brief itself
-----------------------------------------

The brief said the two-year clock's starting point is "one of the ten switches". It is not. The ten are C-4, D-5, E-4, E-5, E-8, F-3, F-6, F-10, A-2 and A-3, and none of them is the clock start. The brief also said not to hard-code it — which was right to say, but it was never hard-coded. No eleventh switch was invented for something that is already derived correctly.

The brief's premise that two journey files are in conflict is half right. They were never alternatives: one is a screen specification and the other was a question specification. What actually conflicted was narrower — where the register calls happen — and that is now decided.

The supersession decision (Q77 to ratify)
-----------------------------------------

Written up in full on item 12552691606, Document 2. In short: the live site is the build and always was; the condensed journey supersedes the front door of both older documents; the Wireframe & Build Spec keeps screens 8–19 and must not be archived — it is the only place the four non-happy-path states are written down; and the 251 questions in the site are not deleted, they move to after the engagement letter.

One thing found while deciding it: the Client Journey (FINAL) file is not on disk. Not in the working folder, not in the archive. The only trace is a shortcut pointing at a path that no longer holds it. Its "269 questions" is another document's count of it and nobody has verified it. The site defines 251.

A contradiction in the corpus, now resolved on the record
---------------------------------------------------------

The Developer Build Order said in two places that no external lookup happens before the engagement letter. The condensed front door derives at question 2. Those cannot both stand.

It was resolved in favour of derivation, and §1 and §2 of that document are amended to say so. The reasoning: the old sentence was never a recorded decision — it is not in the Decided-And-Not-Decided register — and §11 of the Developer Brief already required register lookups to be "async with optimistic UI" and to "degrade gracefully — fall back to asking", which describes lookups running inside the funnel. The corpus was inconsistent before this phase; the amendment resolves it in the direction the engineering requirements already pointed.

Switched off, and the switch is not ours (Q76 — new item 12955356558)
-----------------------------------------------------------------

Running those lookups processes personal data — the HMLR proprietor, Companies House persons of significant control — at a point where no contract exists. The lawful basis is the legitimate interests assessment, not the engagement letter, and that assessment carries a condition that a privacy notice be published and reachable at the point of collection. That condition is recorded as unmet.

So the layer ships the way the ten adviser switches ship: branch built, branch tested, branch defaulting to today's behaviour. While it is off every question stays asked. Unblocking it is publish the notice, link it from the address question, confirm the assessment covers pre-contract lookups, then one line of code.

Without it the front door is not six questions — it is the same fifty in a different order. This is the highest-value thing on the board that is not the fee basis.

Q55 is still the blocker on quoting
-----------------------------------

The fee basis is unanswered. No fee display was built, as instructed. LS_FEE computes both readings — £25,000 and £6,250 on a £500,000 allowance at 25% — renders neither, and states why. Nothing is quoted to anybody until it is settled.

Phase 67. Code in 03-app/ledgerstone-site.html; assertions in Suite O of ledgerstone-regression.cjs; backups at .bak-phase67.

Correct the worked example so the location factor is applied once, to the total, and not per element line; check whether the engine's own cost model does the same thing; and reconcile the base — the code comment declares "Regional location factors, mean 100" while Spon's is indexed to Outer London = 1.00 and the Mechanical and Electrical book uses a third base again. The base question and the contract-size range (declared valid £2m–£5m against a standing £6m worked example) stay on 12804374707, because those two do wait on the data.

### 7 September 2026, 19:54:38 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5525634263

Done, Phase 97, 7 September 2026.

The premise held and it was wider than stated. The prompt asked whether the code applied the factor to a total. It did not — residualApportionment multiplied loc.factor into every element inside the costing loop, so the defect was in the code as well as the specification.

But the arithmetic was never wrong. One factor, uniform across every element, multiplies straight out of the sum, so A and B came to the identical figure either way. That is why nothing caught it in seven months, and it is why no equality test on a total could ever catch it. The tests added here assert the shape instead.

In the engine (phase9/caprebate-cost-model.cjs): element lines are now quantity × rate × depreciation × prelims × index and nothing else; each carries location_adjusted: false and no location_factor field at all, so a report generator cannot find one to print. The single factor is applied once to the summed total, before the fee band is looked up — the VOA fee scale is banded on construction cost, so applying it after would read the wrong band near an edge. Two live guards raise E_LOCATION_FACTOR_NOT_APPLIED_ONCE: one requires every line to be explicable by the factors it declares, the other requires the totals to be the line sum times one location factor and one fee factor.

The guard was proved rather than asserted. Test D10 rebuilds the module from source with the defect put back and checks it refuses. It also checks the mutant passes with the gate off — which is the honest reason this survived, since every shipped configuration is one the defect hides in.

In the specification (caprebate-full-specification-v8.html): the five element rows lost their "Cardiff 94" source labels; a new §10a shows the adjustment as the single step it is; and — the cause, which the item did not name — the design rule at "The rule that makes this work" had required the per-line adjustment, giving "Cardiff factor 94" as its model citation. Five rows were following the rule. That paragraph is corrected, or the defect would have been designed back in.

The index base was left alone on purpose and stays on the price-book item. Where the factor is applied and what it is indexed to are two different defects.

Suites after: site harness 632 pass / 0 fail / 4 xfail, phase3 358 / 0, phase9 142 → 151 / 0. Drift checker green.

### 7 September 2026, 19:54:39 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5525634292

Phase 97, 7 September 2026 — this item was two things and they have been separated.

Built, and this item now covers only this half. The contract-size scale interpolates instead of stepping, and converts the percentage the source publishes into the factor the model multiplies by.

The table shipped as bands: [floor, ceiling, factor] read through bandLookup, which was wrong twice over. The published scale is a curve, not a step — a step function makes two jobs £1 apart across a band edge get materially different replacement costs, which the source does not say and could not be defended. And the slot held a factor where the source publishes a percentage: loading published figures straight in would have multiplied every cost by roughly minus five and still returned a number. quoted_as now states which the points hold and one function does the conversion.

It refuses rather than extrapolating. The book declares the adjustment valid only over roughly £2m to £5m of contract value. Outside that there is no published adjustment, and continuing the publisher's curve past where they stopped drawing it is our figure wearing their citation. This is the path that fires first when the book is bought — the standing worked example is a £6m contract.

Built against the empty table, as the rest of phase9 is: the mechanism ships, the data does not, and the gate is still off. Nine new tests (D11–D16 and the malformed-scale refusals). phase9 went 142 → 151 pass / 0 fail.

## Decide whether the "AIA used against other spending" fact needs its own question, or stays folded into the headroom one

`12991117818` · 2 comments

### 7 September 2026, 19:09:01 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5525470636

<p><b>Created 7 September 2026 by Phase 96, which made this decision and needs it visible rather than buried in a code comment.</b></p><p><b>The fact.</b> Gate 4 of the cash-benefit gates reads <code>aia_used_elsewhere</code>. Nothing sets it. Phase 96 captured the neighbouring fact — how much of the £1m annual investment allowance is left — but deliberately did NOT set this one, and this item exists so that the decision can be looked at by someone other than the person who made it.</p><p><b>Why it was left.</b> The new allowance question already sets the headroom to "none" when a client says it has all been used, which closes gate 2. Setting gate 4 on the same answer would close two gates on one fact and print the client two near-identical reasons for it: "no Annual Investment Allowance headroom left this period (used elsewhere, or across the group)" and "AIA already claimed against other expenditure this period — no headroom left for this spend". That is a cosmetic defect on a client-facing report.</p><p><b>Why it might still be wrong, and this is the part worth a second opinion.</b> The two are not actually the same fact. Gate 4 is specifically <i>AIA spent on OTHER expenditure</i>; gate 2 is <i>no headroom, for any reason</i> — including a group company having used it, which is not the client's own spending at all. A client could have headroom of their own and still be caught by the group. So there is a real case for asking the narrower question separately, and the honest reason it was not built is that the reporting would need reworking at the same time, which is more than the item it sat inside was asking for.</p><p><b>What to do.</b> Either capture it with its own question and make the two reasons read as one coherent explanation rather than two overlapping ones, or confirm the fold and say so on the gate. <b>Do not simply set both from the same answer</b> — that is the outcome this note exists to prevent. The reasoning is written beside gate 4 in the engine.</p>

### 8 September 2026, 08:13:59 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5527453099

DECIDED 8 September 2026, and the second opinion this item asked for reached a different reason from the original.

The fold is confirmed: this fact gets no question of its own. But not for the reason Phase 96 gave. Phase 96 held off because a second question would print two near-identical reasons — a cosmetic argument. The stronger reason is that as a boolean this fact cannot decide anything at all. "Some of the allowance went elsewhere" does not tell us whether any is left, so a question capturing it would produce an answer that still could not size the relief. The fact that WOULD decide it is the numeric headroom, and that is already open as its own question. Capturing a boolean would add a client question, add a second reason to the report, and change no figure — the worst of the three outcomes available.

AND THE ITEM TURNED UP A REAL DEFECT, which is why it was worth a second look. Gate 4's reason read "AIA already claimed against other expenditure this period — no headroom left for this spend". A boolean cannot support that conclusion: a client who spent some of the allowance elsewhere may have plenty left. And the harness already pins exactly that case — headroom of £250,000 stated, flag set — so the wrong sentence was being printed to a client in the one scenario the suite asserts.

Fixed, without moving a number. The reason now reads that we cannot tell how much of the allowance is left for this spend, so none is modelled. The gate still closes, because closing it understates the benefit and that is the safe direction; only the explanation changed.

Two assertions added so neither decision can silently reverse: one that gate 4's reason no longer claims there is no headroom when a headroom is stated, and one that a client saying the allowance is all used gets one reason and leaves gate 4 open — which is the fold itself, asserted rather than commented. Proved by reverting the wording and watching the first test fail.

Harness 632 → 634 pass / 0 fail / 4 xfail. The decision and its reasoning are written beside gate 4 in the engine, as this item asked.
