## When an external data call may fire — free on permission, paid after signature

`12977632344` · 2 comments

### 4 September 2026, 17:56:38 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5521476238

WHERE THIS LANDED. This single update replaces the four notes posted on 4 September 2026 as the rule was worked out; those have been deleted. Nothing in them is lost — the two that were superseded were superseded by their own successors, and one of them contained a factual overstatement I corrected an hour later.

THE RULE, as Lakhbir set it across four messages on 4 September 2026.

1. "Commercial only" means the CLIENT, not the building. Settled. Our clients are trading businesses — not buy-to-let landlords, not homeowners. It says nothing about the property, so supported living is unaffected and nobody drops that sector on this rule. The engine classifies it residential on purpose, because those buildings often are, and that is precisely what earns it the one free purchase-price route the other four sectors cannot use. No code change and no document change follows from this half.

2. Free calls fire once the client has given permission to use their data. Lakhbir: "all free API fire once a user gives us permission to use their data."

This is already built and already switched off, and the switch says almost exactly this. CB_REGISTRY.precondition, verbatim: enabled: false, requires: "a published privacy notice reachable from the address question, because the legitimate-interests basis for these lookups depends on it". So do not build a second gate. Publish the notice, link it at the address question, flip one boolean.

The legal point, and it is a legal point not a wording one: "permission" here means INFORMED, not CONSENTED. The lawful basis is legitimate interests and the assessment is already written. A consent tick at the address question would misdescribe the basis and is the weaker position — consent is withdrawable, an assessment is not, and anyone who declined could not be given a figure at all. If an actual tick box is ever meant, that is a different instruction, it rewrites the legitimate-interests assessment, and it must be said explicitly.

3. A paid call fires only after the engagement letter is signed, and only when an operator clicks. Lakhbir: "paid APIs should only fire when an engagement letter has been signed — this is something more for the back end which a user clicks and any paid APIs auto run."

Two preconditions then full automation: a signed engagement asserted server-side, never in the UI; a person in the back office clicks Run the research; and on that click every paid call runs automatically. The operator picks the moment, not the calls — do not build a per-call confirmation.

Nothing refuses and nothing throws. Pre-signature a paid source is simply not consulted and its facts stay asked, which the fourth non-negotiable already requires of every unknown. If a build of this makes an estimate fail, a screen error, or a source read as unavailable, it is built wrong.

4. NOTHING IS FIRING TODAY, and this is a specification for the developer, not a fix to running code. The engine makes zero network calls — a grep for fetch( on the site returns 0. derive() consumes a bundle of what connectors already returned and the connectors do not exist; assertSignedEngagement is named in four documents and implemented nowhere. My first two notes said the address lookup "fires pre-gate on every property" — that describes the design, not the software, and it was an overstatement.

5. The one open question, and it is narrower than it first looked. The address lookup is paid and its UPRN is what the free registers are keyed on, so tier 2 appears to depend on tier 3. It does not, quite: EPC, the care regulator, Companies House and Price Paid can all be searched on a typed postcode or name. The paid UPRN buys match certainty, not access. So the two tiers work — free calls run early on a fuzzy match with a confidence threshold, and the paid lookup after signature upgrades it. What decides it is a measurement nobody has taken: the matching spec says to measure the real failure rate on 200 properties and nobody has. Do not assert the fuzzy match is good enough, and do not assert it is not.

Where this lands: the Developer Brief, the Build Order and the Provenance Map — whose instruction to fire the title register "without thinking about it" is now wrong and must be corrected. It is also recorded as a standing business rule at the top of the action plan, so it outlives this item.

What actually unblocks the free half: one page. The public notices page is already specified, already required for two separate statutory duties, and is not gated on the WordPress question.

<b>Done 8 September 2026. The rule is now written into all three documents, where it had been in none of them.</b><br><br><b>The premise was re-derived before anything was written, and it held.</b> Searches for the phrases the rule was recorded in returned zero across the developer brief, the developer build order and the API and data provenance map. They now return matches in all three. ## BUILD 1 of 7 — the engine as a shared package. Acceptance: the harness reports the same totals against the package as against the single file

`12984660315` · 2 comments

### 6 September 2026, 08:58:39 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5523180397

Created 6 September 2026. Part of a seven-phase run that builds a WORKING DEMONSTRATION PROTOTYPE to put in front of a developer — the full specification for this item is the correspondingly numbered phase in CAPREBATE ACTION PLAN, phases 102 to 108. Read it there; it is not duplicated here, because a second copy is how this corpus produces drift.

What the prototype is. Three surfaces sharing one engine and one mock store: the existing public site and assessment, a client portal, and a Caprebate staff portal with five roles. Mock data, no live external calls, no authentication, no payment processor. It exists so a developer can see what the thing is and how it works, and so the handover document can say precisely which parts are real and which are scaffolding they must replace.

Three decisions were taken before any of it was written, on 6 September 2026. The Accounting role is Caprebate's own finance — it sees the client name, claim value, fee, invoice and payment status, and NOT the questions and answers, the register data or the surveyor's workings. Firing the research is ONE button that runs everything outstanding, with per-source status shown beside it, which keeps the 4 September rule intact — an individual retry appears only on a call that actually failed. And the engine is lifted into a shared package first, so all three surfaces compute from one estimate rather than three copies.

The four non-negotiables apply in full, and one of them is how a prototype goes wrong badly. The surveyor must never receive our estimate — and hiding it with CSS teaches the developer the exact opposite of the control, because they will copy whatever pattern they find. It is enforced in the store, and the surveyor phase proves it by inspecting the payload rather than by looking at the screen.

Two standing rules for every phase in this run. Invented demo data only — no real client, person or property, ever, in a file that will be emailed to a third party. And every mock is labelled as a mock, on screen: a convincing fake that is not in the handover table is the failure mode the whole exercise exists to prevent.

It goes in a NEW folder, 09-prototype/. Folders 00- to 08- are not renamed or restructured — two NTFS junctions point into 04-phase-work by absolute path and every numbered folder name is a literal path in a dozen documents.

### 6 September 2026, 09:21:28 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5523192485

SCOPE CHANGED 6 September 2026, after this item was created. Read the phase in CAPREBATE ACTION PLAN, not the earlier update below it.

It is no longer a prototype. Lakhbir: build it as if it ships, and the developer finishes what could not be finished here. The end state is three things — Caprebate HTML (public site, assessment, customer login, client portal), the Caprebate back end (Sales, Admin, Accounting, Surveying, super user), and the Caprebate Developer Spec (user cases, wireframe, and what every API does).

The stack is Node and TypeScript, because the engine, the eleven data modules, the upload handler and all 1,063 assertions already are. This partially reverses the 1 September decision that WordPress is the whole back end, and the reversal is recorded rather than assumed. The fallback is defined: if the host can run a Node process this ships behind WordPress; if it cannot, it becomes the executable specification the PHP rebuild is tested against, so nothing is thrown away. Whether the host can run Node is still unanswered and it is the question that most changes the developer's price.

What is real and what is stubbed. Real: authentication with hashed passwords and revocable sessions, authorisation enforced server-side per object, SQLite with parameterised statements, the upload handler and its twelve-step receipt contract, the anchor quarantine, the name exclusion register, an append-only audit log. Stubbed, and it is a short list: outbound email, the register connectors, document signature. Each stub is one named module behind an interface.

Two gates stay shut and the build must show them shut. Free register calls wait on a published privacy notice; paid calls wait on a signed engagement asserted server-side plus one operator click that then fires everything outstanding. Do not open either to make a screen flow.

The security baseline is in the action plan, in THE BUILD section, and no phase repeats it. Authorise on the server for that requester and that object; client documents outside the web root; uploads allow-listed, size-capped and content-sniffed; argon2id or bcrypt; escape on output; parameterised queries only; no personal data in URLs or logs.

Fifteen superseded files fold into the three deliverables and are ARCHIVED, not deleted. The twelve rulebooks, twenty code and test files, eight policy documents and 219 governance exports are not touched — that is the evidence four professionals sign off, and the harness reads it.

BUILT — Block C, Phase 104, 8 September 2026. The public site, the six-screen assessment, the customer login and the client portal, in 09-app/backend/src/web/. One process, one session store, one can() — mounted ahead of the JSON API in src/server.ts.

The opening move works end to end. Six screens → the engine's figure → the funnel close → a business, an assessment, one row per question and a booking the back end can see. The client-facing copy, the question wording and the order were transcribed from the site's own renderer, not rewritten. Every gate, band and channel still comes from the engine package: src/web/engine.ts is the only file that imports it and it is one line to grep.

THE UPLOAD HANDLER RAN, UNMODIFIED, FOR THE FIRST TIME. 945 lines and 38 tests that had never had a caller since 31 August. It now discharges steps 1 to 7 of the receipt contract against a real ObjectStore: the strip runs, the unredacted original is deleted from quarantine with evidence, and under fail-closed settings the raw file is never promoted. Nothing in 04-phase-work/phase3/ was touched — there is no .bak-phase104 in that folder and the modification dates are unchanged.

Requirement W1: five of the six acceptance tests pass here and are named in the test file. W1-T1 (no path reaches a document, and the router provably has no static file route), W1-T2 (authentication is not authorisation), W1-T3 (checked per request — the test moves a document to another business mid-session and the very next request is refused), W1-T5 (no execute bit, server-side sniffing refuses a PHP payload named .pdf, size cap, single-key capabilities) and W1-T6 (every serve writes an access record, allowed or refused). W1-T4 needs the real host — it is about the WordPress Media Library and there is no WordPress in this build. It is declared and NOT counted as a pass.

The engagement letter is rendered from the .docx, and its eight unresolved terms are shown blank on purpose — derived from the document rather than listed, so one that gets filled in disappears without anybody editing code. The break fee, the fee basis, the abort fee and clause 13's three terms all sit with you on item 12984553034. Signing is stubbed and says so; there is no payment processor anywhere in this build.

Three findings worth the phase on their own. The engine package could not be imported by Node at all — import x = require() is refused in type-stripping mode, so Block A had never actually been loaded by anything; fixed without touching a generated file. Migration 002's bookings.channel allowed only telephone and virtual, which is a second booking vocabulary AND re-admits the video channel CB_BOOKING deliberately removed on 3 September; rebuilt onto CB_BOOKING's three real channels. And the developer handover pack's two file reads were by array index, so archiving the journey wireframe silently pointed one of them at the wrong document — now looked up by name.

Suites, every figure re-derived by running it: site harness 634/0/4 xfail, and 634/0/4 in --package mode (the two must match); phase3 379/0; phase9 245/0; the new back end 100/0 with SQL lint and a clean strict typecheck; engine verify 21/0; drift checker GREEN. Total 1,358 passing assertions.

Archived, not deleted: the journey wireframe, the client script, the business flow and the supersession note, all to _archive/superseded/ with a note saying where each one's content went — the business flow's eleven step titles are now the portal's stage vocabulary and that mapping is the only reason the portal can say where a claim is in the client's own words.

### 9 September 2026, 08:35:31 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5531409059

DONE 9 September 2026, Phase 107. Block F of the Developer Build Order. The done-when for this block was that a surveyor session's response body contains no estimate output, verified by inspection rather than by reading the code — and here is what was captured.

THE PAYLOAD INSPECTION, against the seeded application over real HTTP. GET /staff/survey/<job>/payload.json signed in as the surveying user returned HTTP 200, 2,540 bytes. Top-level keys: job_id, business_id, business_name, sector, answers, register_records, properties, quarantine — and 'estimate' in body is false, so the key is not present at all rather than present and empty. It carried 5 answers, 2 register records and 1 property; quarantine.state was SEALED with its own notice.

The sealed estimate for that job, read straight out of the estimates table, was qualifying_expenditure_pence 30000000, qualifying_pct 0.3, pool_split_main_pence 18000000, pool_split_special_pence 12000000, bare_land_pence 5000000, multiplier 0.25, indicative_lifetime_saving_pence 7500000. The captured body was searched for every one of those, three ways: by field name 0 found, by value at any depth under any name 0 found, by raw text 0 found. The rendered HTML page (28,768 bytes at the last capture — that figure moves whenever a word on the page does, and only the zero matters) was searched the same way: 0 found.

THE NEGATIVE CONTROL, which is what makes those zeros mean anything. The identical searches as ADMIN, where the estimate IS released, returned 7, 7 and 7 — every field name, every value, every string. A search that cannot find the figure where it is definitely present proves nothing when it finds nothing elsewhere.

Re-run it: cd 09-app/backend && CAPREBATE_ALLOW_SEED=1 node tools/payload-proof.ts. It prints what was captured rather than a tick, runs against the seed rather than a fixture, and ends with that control.

What was built. The surveyor review-and-sign workspace at /staff/survey: the property and the client's own answers, the sector's room schedule with the surveyor's counts, the ten tracked rate fields, the evidence and what their pack still waits on, their own figures, and the hash-chained record. Committing figures releases our estimate automatically and there is no route that releases without one. Amending afterwards carries a mandatory reason and does not overwrite the commitment, because that pair is what the drift measurement reads. The accounting view at /staff/finance: the client name, the claim value, the fee, invoice and payment state, the VAT position, and the fee-versus-benefit comparison — with a test for each of the five refusals. Both CB_FEEGUARD switches are off and the rendered fee is untouched. Signature is stubbed and says so; no payment is taken anywhere.

Suites at the close, every figure re-derived by running it: site harness 634 / 0 / 4 xfail (both modes), phase3 379 / 0, phase9 245 / 0, back end 284 / 0, extraction 21 checks 0 failures, drift checker GREEN with zero present-tense failures. 1,542 passing assertions.

Three files archived to _archive/superseded/ with a note saying where each one's content went. Three loose ends went to a new item, Phase 107a.

Found by the Phase 95 sweep, 6 September 2026, while verifying that the two rename items on the build queue were actually done. They were — Phase 88 cleaned every body. It did not clean the names.

The five, read from the live Files column on each item:

* 12552682421__Ledgerstone-Business-Plan.md — the business plan
* 12552682538__Ledgerstone-Brand-Guidelines.md — the brand book, which is the one that reads worst
* 12830178449__AML-KYC-Position-Paper-Ledgerstone.md — goes to a solicitor and an accountant
* 12830181513__ASA-CAP-Code-Claim-Audit-Ledgerstone-Pre-Launch.md — the advertising-claims audit
* 12921255840__Ledgerstone-Statutory-Rules-Register.md — a second file on the rulebook A addendum item
All five have clean bodies. Verified against Phase 88's own pre-rename snapshots on disk. This is a filename defect only.

Why it is not already covered. Phase 92 job 2 lists seven rulebook attachments by name and re-uploads them from disk. Four of these five are not rulebooks and are not on that list; the fifth (12921255840) sits on an item that job 2 touches, but the specific file is not the one named. So nothing in the current plan reaches them.

## The funnel's Q1b gate never stops a non-taxpayer, and if it did their call from the reasoned negative would be lost: the close fails with no property

`13022911228` · 2 comments

### 11 September 2026, 01:38:32 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5538579015

Found by CRM 2 of 10 on 11 September 2026, while re-deriving the premise that a gated exit is already a lead. Housed in Phase 117a, which runs next.

1. The gate never stops. The engine's claimant gate returns gated: true for a business that pays no UK tax or is a charity. The funnel's renderer (nextScreen in 09-app/backend/src/web/assessment.ts) reads a field called stop, which the engine never returns, and the TypeScript declaration names stop too. Reproduced on the Mac copy over HTTP: answering "No, or we're a charity" at the tax question sends the prospect on to the next question and, in the end, to a figure.

2. The call would be lost. The reasoned negative page offers "Book a call" to the close. Reproduced over HTTP: closing with no property answers HTTP 500, because the submission takes its sector from the first property and there is none. Nothing is written, so the back office never sees the enquiry.

Nothing blocks this: it is buildable today. Phase 117a says how, including the one decision it has to take — where a prospect's own name and channel live before an organisation exists.

### 11 September 2026, 07:50:44 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5538906951

Built and in force on the Mac copy, 11 September 2026 — the gated-exit repair.

Both faults were reproduced over HTTP before anything changed, and each reproduction is now a test that was red and is green. (1) The funnel read a field the engine never returns, so a business with no UK tax bill went on to a figure — before the repair a "no" at the tax question redirected to the next question. (2) Asking for a call from the reasoned negative answered with a server error (HTTP 500) and wrote nothing.

What changed. The funnel now reads the engine's own answer: "no" (which covers charities) stops at the reasoned negative, and "not sure" and no answer at all both carry on, identically, with the condition printed on the figure. A stopped prospect cannot reach a later question or a figure by typing the address. The reasoned-negative page now gives the engine's reason in its own words. The engine itself is untouched — the mistake was in a hand-written type declaration beside it.

The call is kept. It is recorded as a lead from the website with no organisation (there is no property or sector to make one from). The person who asked and how they want to be reached are held on a contact and a booking that belong to that lead until it is linked to an organisation, when the same rows move across. A telephone slot is held where the calendar checks for clashes, and the call appears in the calendar's queue. The thank-you page prints no range, because none was shown. The decision and its reasons are written into the CRM disposition table; no question was needed for the data protection officer, because the draft privacy notice already covers contact details taken at a prospect's request.

Evidence. Back-end check 450 pass / 0 fail (441 before); nine tests in a new file; five controls broken on purpose, each seen red and restored byte-identical; extraction verifier and the extractor's check green; engine type checks clean; surveyor payload proof passes; drift checker green, project total 1,938. ## Make the professional-fee rate depend on building type

`12927234375` · 3 comments

### 4 September 2026, 17:54:49 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5521469626

Why this item exists, recorded here before the name was shortened (Phase 83, 4 September 2026).

Phase 10 finding F-1. From the Activation Test Plan; gated on the VOA licence.

The VOA professional-fee scale carries a +4% adder for highly serviced buildings and +3% for hospitals. Our feesFactor takes a construction cost and returns one banded rate with no building-type parameter at all.

So loading the VOA base bands alone would under-read fees on every job we do, because our whole client base is highly serviced or hospital. This is a mechanism change with its own tests, not a table load — and it must be built before the LEG-E3 gate can be flipped.

## DPO to approve six years' retention on the client's uploaded document

`12955088177` · 2 comments

### 2 September 2026, 08:10:41 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5512590592

<b>Raised by Phase 65, 2 September 2026. For the DPO. It exists because answering Q56 changed what an unapproved retention period costs.</b><br><br>

<b>What is being approved.</b> RET-7: <b>six years from the later of (a) the end of the accounting period or year of assessment the claim relates to, and (b) the date Health Tax Partners delivers its report.</b> Derived by Phase 55 from FA 1998 Sch 18 para 46(2) and TMA 1970 s.36(1), matched by Limitation Act 1980 s.2 and s.5. The derivation is Retention Determinations v1.1 on item 12945903194, section 4.3 and section 11; the parameter sits at Retention Procedure v1.5 section 2.3C.<br><br>

<b>Why it is now urgent when it was not.</b> Until 2 September the client's uploaded file was deleted once extraction was complete, so RET-7 governed only the extracted facts and an unapproved period delayed nothing operational. <b>Lakhbir answered Q56 on 2 September: the file is kept.</b> RET-7 is now the rule for the file itself, and the mechanism is built so that an unapproved period computes nothing:<br>
• <code>settings.ret7_approved</code> defaults to <b>false</b>;<br>
• with it false, <code>deletionDueAt()</code> returns null for every retained file;<br>
• <code>assertNoOverdueUndeleted()</code> then reports each one as held with <b>no computable deletion date</b>, which is the sweep working correctly and must not be silenced.<br><br>

<b>So this is not a document waiting for a signature. It is a switch that has to be thrown before client uploads can be accepted with a defensible retention position.</b> That is deliberate: the alternative was to let the answer create a six-year retention period nobody had approved, which is exactly how a schedule comes to look finished when it is not.<br><br>

<b>Three things the DPO should see before signing, because each could change the number.</b><br>
<b>1. Q61 — the single assumption the six years rests on.</b> The 20-year deliberate-behaviour window and the 15-year latent-damage longstop are excluded and handled by legal hold rather than by the schedule. If that is rejected, this row is twenty years and the design of the defence pack changes with it.<br>
<b>2. Q59 — which event starts our own clock</b>, delivering the report or the client's accountant filing the return. The drafting takes the later of the two so the answer holds either way, but it should be confirmed rather than inherited.<br>
<b>3. Q60 — Item 5 section 10 names the wrong window.</b> It is built on the 12-month enquiry window and never mentions the discovery windows. That defect used to sit on the defence pack alone; it can now reach the client's own document, because the raw file takes a supplied defence-pack date where one exists.<br><br>

<b>What approval does NOT do.</b> It does not reach every document. A document whose ingestion strip removed content there is no lawful basis to hold stays on the extraction clock under condition D4, is deleted, and is never promoted to durable storage at all. <b>That carve-out cannot be waived by approving RET-7</b> — it is a lawful-basis condition, not a retention preference.<br><br>

<b>Blocked, not merely waiting:</b> the appointment itself sits behind incorporation (DECISIONS Part 8), so this cannot be signed until Companies House is done. It is on the board now so that it is not discovered late.<br><br>

<b>Two fields still do not exist anywhere.</b> <code>claim_period_end</code> and <code>report_delivered_at</code> are declared on the raw-file record and populated by nothing. RET-7 computes null without both, by design — one limb is not half a rule. That is the Developer's, with the CTA.

## Age each piece of plant separately, not the building as a whole

`12804317685` · 4 comments

### 27 August 2026, 09:46:31 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5496125897

Phase 9 — the depreciation model is prepared and is NOT shipped. This item stays Blocked.

Where the code is

phase9/ledgerstone-cost-model.cjs — gate leg_e5_per_element_depreciation, shipped false.

Both tables empty: LS_VOA_OBSOLESCENCE.scales = {}, LS_CIBSE_PLANT_LIVES.lives_years = {}.

Tests: 51 assertions passing. Harness 216 pass / 0 fail / 14 xfail. Shipped site unchanged.

═══ Two sources, two blocks — clearing the VOA licence does NOT unblock this ═══

This item needs VOA obsolescence scales (licensed) and CIBSE plant lives (a separate source, on its own separate terms). They are different publishers with different agreements. If the VOA licence lands and someone assumes E5 is now free to ship, they will be wrong.

Test E8 pins this: it loads CIBSE, leaves the VOA table empty, and confirms the model still refuses. The two stubs are deliberately separate objects for exactly this reason.

The dependency on the valuation basis is now cleared

This item was also blocked on the D5 valuation-basis choice (item 12804374838). That item was not actually blocked — its own text said "NOT BLOCKING — build both branches behind a config flag, surveyor picks" — and it is now built, tested and Done. Depreciation runs on the DRC branch only, and the switch is already there waiting for it. So E5's remaining blocks are the two data sources and nothing else.

Why per-element and not per-building — the part that matters for tax

A single building-wide depreciation factor is wrong in a way a valuer might tolerate and a tax adviser must not. Plant lives differ by an order of magnitude across the taxonomy: a lift, a boiler, a nurse-call system and the drainage under the slab do not age together.

Depreciating everything at one rate moves value between the pools — main (14%), special rate (6%) and the non-qualifying residual (SBA, 3% straight-line). A pooling error is a permanent timing error, not a rounding one. Test E3 shows three elements at the same age depreciating differently, which is the whole argument for building it this way.

The chain

age_years → CIBSE expected life (per element) → age_ratio → VOA obsolescence scale → surviving proportion of replacement cost.

The guard that matters most

An element older than its expected life does not depreciate to zero. It is still there and it still works — depreciating it to zero would strip a working asset out of the claim entirely. Two protections:

• age_ratio is clamped at 1.0, never extrapolated. Extrapolating a scale past its last band is inventing data (test E4).

• A residual floor, taken from the scale and never assumed, puts a bottom under the factor (test E5).

Both cases are flagged in the output (ELEMENT_BEYOND_EXPECTED_LIFE, RESIDUAL_FLOOR_APPLIED) rather than handled silently.

Other refusals

No CIBSE life for an element → E_PLANT_LIFE_NOT_IN_TABLE (it will not assume a life). No age → E_ELEMENT_AGE_REQUIRED. Gate on over an empty table → E_TABLE_NOT_LOADED, naming the gate and the licence.

What has to happen to ship

VOA licence cleared and CIBSE terms cleared → load both tables with verified_at dates → flip the gate. The model is done and tested; only the two data sources are missing.

## Minimum fee - RETIRED 16 Sep 2026: the flat 3% fee has no minimum. Both papers record the old floor as retired, re-costed at 3%

`12830205390` · 5 comments

### 26 August 2026, 07:16:25 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5492257963

What this is
An open decision. Only you can make it.

In plain English
At a 5% fee, a small job does not pay for itself. A dental practice bought for £500,000 would earn us roughly £2,200 — and out of that we still have to pay a surveyor, pay a tax adviser to review it, and cover your own time. That is a loss.

The two ways to fix it
• Set a minimum fee — for example, "5%, or £4,000, whichever is greater."
• Set a minimum job size — for example, "we do not take properties bought for under £750,000."

A minimum fee keeps more clients but risks a client feeling stung on a small job. A minimum job size is cleaner and easier to state publicly, but turns away work.

Why it matters now
The website and the assessment tool both need to know this. Right now the assessment will happily give a quote on a job we would lose money on.

This is tied to the fee-basis decision elsewhere on this board — best decided together.

Original wording: "DECIDE: minimum fee or minimum purchase price — at 5%, a £500k dental job grosses ~£2.2k before surveyor + CTA + your time."

### 26 August 2026, 09:00:41 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5492447784

Options paper drafted. Your decision — item ownership and status left untouched.

Doc: Options paper — minimum fee, or minimum job size?

Recommendation: a minimum fee, set per sector — £5,000, or £7,500 for care homes and private hospitals — plus an internal gate that tests the expected fee rather than the purchase price.

Your £2.2k figure reconciles exactly. A £500k dental purchase at the band midpoint gives £112,500 QE; at 40% income tax that is £45,000 of lifetime relief and 5% is £2,250. But it is the optimistic case — held in a company at 25% the same job yields £1,406.

True cost per job. Direct cost ranges £2,630 (dental) to £5,750 (private hospital) — a 2.2x spread on surveyor, CTA, internal time and data. The item's framing leaves out two real costs: overhead, and the failed enquiries that converting jobs have to carry. At 100 jobs/yr with £60k overhead and 1-in-4 conversion that is a £960 loading on every job; at 25 jobs/yr it is £2,760. So the £500k dental job does not lose £400 — it loses £1,340.

Break-even purchase price, loaded: £798k to £1,717k — a 2.2x spread. Two counterintuitive findings. Claimant type moves the threshold more than sector does (incorporating raises it ~60%, because the fee is a share of tax saved and 25% is a lot less than 40%). And the care home — our biggest job — has almost the highest threshold at £1,667k, despite the better band, because corporation tax is lower and the survey costs more.

Minimum job size fails at every value. A £750k floor excludes not one of the eight sector-claimant combinations. £1m still loses on six. You have to reach £1.7m to make the whole book profitable, and at £1.7m you have excluded essentially all of dental. It also throws away good work (an £850k unincorporated dental practice is profitable) while accepting bad (a £1.5m company-held GP surgery is not) — and it damages the accountant channel, because a referrer refused once stops referring.

The finding that matters most, and it goes beyond what the item asked. Set a £5,000 minimum and a dental practice has to reach £1.1m — or £1.8m if company-held — before 5% overtakes it. Dental practices do not trade at those prices. Across dental and GP the minimum is not a floor, it is the price. We are not a 5% business with a floor underneath; for two of five sectors we are a fixed-fee business that has not noticed. That argues for leading with the fixed number on the pricing page and treating the percentage as the exception — which is also the cleaner advertising position, since a headline of 5% against an effective 17.8% on a small company-held practice is a qualification that cannot sit in small print.

Why a minimum fee alone is not enough either. It protects the bottom, not the middle. A £1.5m company-held care home yields a £5,625 fee against a £6,250 loaded cost — above any sensible minimum, so no floor catches it. The loss band runs roughly £1.33m–£1.67m and is invisible to both options as framed. Hence the second mechanism: the assessment should test expected fee against loaded cost plus target margin and route to "we'll come back to you" rather than issuing an automatic quote. The engine already computes expected relief, so it can compute this. It also fixes live behaviour — the assessment currently quotes on jobs we lose money on.

Caveats I want to be plain about. The cost figures are my estimates, not quotes, and they are the weakest input — every threshold moves with them. The £60k overhead is a placeholder. And the asymmetry matters: of the five things that could change the conclusion, only one makes it better (a cheaper small-job survey) and it is the one I can least verify. These numbers are the optimistic reading.

Needs from you: real surveyor quotes by sector for the smallest job in each; your actual overhead; a realistic year-one volume; and a call on whether GP sits at £5,000 (£170 margin — not a margin) or £7,500.

Assumes 5% of lifetime relief, per the companion paper on 12804368154. The two decisions belong together, as your note here says.

Status and owner unchanged. "Claimed by (machine)" cleared.

### 1 September 2026, 15:46:40 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5510199610

<h2>THE INCORPORATION CHAIN — nine numbered steps. Added 1 September 2026 (Phase 58)</h2>

<p><b>Why this update exists.</b> On 1 September 2026 Lakhbir answered the question "who handles a data protection complaint until the DPO appointment is signed?" with <b>"the company is not live; when it is live Saddique will be DPO"</b>. That is a sequencing decision and a reasonable one, and it is not being reopened. <b>Its consequence is that the DPO appointment is now downstream of this item</b> — and behind it sit thirteen finished data protection documents that name the DPO as their approver, and three duties that are live and unperformed right now:</p>

<ul>
<li><b>Article 37(7), limb one</b> — publish the DPO's contact details. Not done; no page exists.</li>
<li><b>Article 37(7), limb two</b> — communicate them to the Commissioner. Not done; runs through ICO registration, item 12552682424.</li>
<li><b>DPA 2018 s.164A(2)</b> — a means of making a complaint, completable electronically AND by other means. <b>Live and unmet since 19 June 2026</b>, throughout, and not met by a placeholder.</li>
</ul>

<p><b>None of that argues against the sequencing. It argues for incorporating quickly</b> — which is what item 12937561331 records as the intention, with a review if it slips past 8 September 2026.</p>

<h3>The chain, in order</h3>

<p><b>1. Incorporate.</b> Certificate obtained. Record company name, number, registered office and accounting reference date on THIS item. (The update of 29 Aug 2026 confirms none of them exists anywhere on this board.) — <i>Lakhbir</i></p>

<p><b>2. Transcribe</b> the company name, number and registered address into the DPO instrument (item 12927221812 — header, §1, §11) and the privacy notice (item 12818279787 — header, Section 1, Section 5). Closes blank 1 of the instrument's §10. <i>Not a decision — a copy-and-paste that has been waiting on Companies House.</i> — <i>Lakhbir</i></p>

<p><b>3. Create and monitor the dedicated mailbox</b> on healthtaxpartners.com, and confirm the local part (§8.1 recommends privacy@ — it is a recommendation, not yet a decision). Control-panel task, not a purchase: item 12927874161. Closes blank 4 of §10, breach-procedure readiness B6, Article 33(3)(b), and the first half of what s.164A(2) needs. <b>The blank closes when the address is MONITORED, not when it exists</b> — breach procedure §3.1: an unmonitored inbox does not stop the clock. — <i>Lakhbir</i></p>

<p><b>4. ANSWER THE FIVE BLANKS AT §10.2, THEN SIGN THE DPO INSTRUMENT.</b> Both signatures at §11; the appointment takes effect on the later of them. The five are listed by name in the update on item 12927221812 — they are five sentences, not a project. Closes the appointment itself and breach-procedure readiness B2. — <i>Lakhbir and Saddique</i></p>

<p><b>5. Publish the DPO's contact details</b> on the public notices page specified at item 12946752268. Closes Article 37(7) limb one. — <i>Lakhbir and DPO</i></p>

<p><b>6. Complete ICO registration</b> (item 12552682424) and communicate the DPO's details to the Commissioner through it. Closes Article 37(7) limb two and breach-procedure readiness B7. — <i>Lakhbir; DPO confirms the route was used</i></p>

<p><b>7. The DPO approves, and Lakhbir countersigns, the documents that name the DPO as approver</b> — Item 5, the Retention and Rights-Request Operating Procedure, the pipeline DPIA, the breach register and procedure, the letters pack, the communications pack, the retention determinations. <b>This is where the "DRAFT — NOT APPROVED" headers come off. They are not to be edited before then.</b> — <i>Saddique and Lakhbir</i></p>

<p><b>8. Give the DPO a monday.com account</b> with write access to the restricted breach register board 18429145787. Breach procedure ADDENDUM 2 §A2.3. <b>Until this exists, Saddique cannot open a register entry at all, and the deputy route added on 1 Sep is the ONLY operable route into the register.</b> — <i>Lakhbir</i></p>

<p><b>9. Answer Q28</b> — how the signatory of a statutory data protection letter is described, now that the instrument is executed and Article 37(7) is discharged. Retires the conservative rule at §0.4 of item 12927850552. — <i>DPO and Lakhbir</i></p>

<h3>Step 4 is the step this chain exists to protect</h3>

<p>Steps 1, 2, 3 and 6 will get done because something external chases them — Companies House, the host, the ICO. <b>Nothing external chases step 4.</b> No registrar refuses a filing because a DPO instrument is unsigned; no supplier withholds a service. It is two signatures on a document finished since 29 August, and steps 5, 7 and 8 are all behind it.</p>

<p><b>If step 4 is not carried as a numbered step in its own right, it will be found months later by a sweep</b> — which is exactly how the thirteen DRAFT headers came to be sitting there. That is the whole reason this is written as a chain rather than as a note.</p>

<p><i>The same chain is recorded in the DPO instrument at §10.3 (v1.2, 1 September 2026), so it survives if this update is scrolled past.</i></p>

## Set up one shared OneDrive folder holding all current documents

`12852031760` · 4 comments

### 26 August 2026, 07:17:14 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5492259046

What this is
A piece of housekeeping that is quietly limiting how fast this project can move.

In plain English
The working documents for this project live in several places — some on a Desktop, some attached to Monday items, some in Teams. There is no single place holding the current version of everything.

Why that is a problem
When more than one person or session works on this at once, they can each edit a different copy of the same file and neither knows. There is no version control and no locking. The practical rule right now is that only one machine at a time may touch code or engine files; everyone else has to take document work. That is a real cap on throughput.

What "done" looks like
One shared Google Drive folder that holds the current version of every live artefact — the rulebooks, the sector modules, the engine files, the report templates — with old versions moved to an archive subfolder so there is never a question about which one is live.

Original wording: "SET UP SHARED FILE STORE (Google Drive) — one folder holding the CURRENT version of every live artefact. Until this exists, only ONE machine may do code/engine work; others take document work only. This is the constraint that limits parallel working."

## Phase 148 — three of the sign-off register check's four evidence columns can never fire, because a document column's text is always empty

`13119191965` · 2 comments

### 23 September 2026, 18:54:33 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5573291722

Found by the sweep, 23 September 2026. The sign-off register check's fourth check says it looks for "an update, a file or a document" on every item the board calls finished, and its failure line reads "no update, no file and no document". It has never been able to see a document.

Why. A document column on this board returns an empty string in its text field even when a document is attached — the document is in the value field instead. Proved today on all six hub items: each one's Document column reads text: "" while its value carries the document's own identifier and link. The snapshot the check reads is captured by a query that asks only for text, so all three document columns arrive empty for all 420 items, and the check's list of four evidence columns is really a list of one.

What it costs today: nothing, and that is the point. The only items carrying documents are the six hub items, and every one of them also carries updates, so no item is wrongly passed right now. The defect is that the check states, in its own output, that it did something it cannot do — and the day an item's only evidence is a document, it will be reported as having none.

The fix, and it is small. The refresh plan's prescribed board query asks for { id text }; it needs { id text value } on the three document columns, and the check needs to count a document column as evidence when either field is filled. Then plant the fault and prove the check catches it: an awaiting item with a document, no file and no update must pass, and the same item with nothing at all must fail.

Two other traps the same run found, both worth writing into the coordinates block rather than a note. An items(ids: [...]) query silently returns only the first twenty-five items whatever the length of the array — thirty-five identifiers in, twenty-five out, no error and no warning. And a docs(object_ids: [...]) query with six identifiers returns an empty array, as the coordinates block already says, but six single-identifier docs queries aliased into one call return all six; that has now worked once.

Nobody has to answer anything for this. It is written up as a phase in the action plan and runs before the sweep. Status: Ready - Claude can build.

## ⚠️ DPO: does the backup risk need prior consultation with the ICO?

`12949133781` · 5 comments

### 1 September 2026, 17:04:30 · Lakhbir Dhillon · comment 5510562893

<p><b>Raised by Phase 60, 1 September 2026. For the DPO. Not resolved here, deliberately.</b></p><p>Revising the DPIA for the data-holding reversal surfaced one risk rated <b>High with no measures at all</b> — R10 at DPIA v2.0 §7.2. The house rule is that a residual high risk that cannot be mitigated is an Article 36 question for the DPO rather than something Claude resolves, so it is here.</p><p><b>The risk.</b> The retention rule requires the client's uploaded document to be deleted once extraction is checked, and the built mechanism refuses a deletion that is not evidenced. Managed WordPress hosting commonly takes a whole-site nightly copy the customer cannot pick apart. <b>A file deleted from disk and alive in a thirty-day backup has not been deleted — and our deletion record would say it had.</b> That falsifies the retention determination, the Article 14 position, and any breach assessment resting on "that file was already deleted". It bites hardest on the quarantine object, whose entire safety argument is that it lives for sixty minutes.</p><p><b>Article 36 has now been read</b> in the current UK text on legislation.gov.uk (1 September 2026), closing the gap DPIA v1.2 recorded as "the prior-consultation Article was not read". Art 36(1): consult "where a data protection impact assessment under Article 35 indicates that the processing would result in a high risk <i>in the absence of measures taken by the controller to mitigate the risk</i>". <b>Two readings are live and the difference matters here:</b> on the face of the words, consult where the unmitigated risk is high; on the conventional reading, consult where a residual high risk survives the measures. The first taken literally would engage Article 36 for nearly every DPIA. <b>The DPIA proceeds on the second and flags that it is a reading, not a finding.</b></p><p><b>Three things to decide.</b> (a) Which reading governs. (b) Does R10 as it stands today engage Article 36 — provisional view <b>no</b>, because it is high pending a question nobody has asked rather than high after mitigation failed. (c) <b>Is this the right trigger: if the host answers "we cannot exclude the folder, and our copies do not expire inside the deletion clock" and the business proceeds on that host anyway, does that require consultation rather than a risk acceptance?</b> Provisional view yes.</p><p><b>The recommendation is not to accept the risk.</b> The cheaper answer by a wide margin is to move the document store off the WordPress host to storage the business controls — which is what the Developer Brief's stack table assumed before WordPress became the whole platform. <b>And note the timing:</b> Article 36(2) gives the Commissioner eight weeks, extendable to fourteen. A consultation started after a launch date is set will not finish in time. The host question (item 12949133180) should be asked now.</p><p>Sources: DPIA v2.0 §10 (item 12910861459, Document 2); Dashboard Data Specification §10.2 (item 12948738680); Retention Procedure v1.4 §2.3B.</p>
